0.title: Christ Is All: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
0.overview:
Colossians is the most christologically concentrated letter in the Pauline corpus. Its central argument can be stated in five words: Christ is all you need. The church at Colossae was being seduced by a sophisticated religious system — a blend of Jewish legal observance, angel veneration, ascetic practices, and esoteric philosophy that scholars call the “Colossian heresy.” The false teachers were not asking the Colossians to abandon Christ; they were proposing to supplement him, to add the fullness they implied Christ alone could not provide. Paul’s response is the great Christ hymn of chapter 1 and the devastating theological logic of chapter 2: in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (2:9–10). There is nothing to add. He is enough.

Paul wrote the letter from prison, most likely in Rome, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon — the so-called “Prison Epistles.” The church at Colossae had apparently been founded not by Paul himself but by Epaphras (1:7), one of Paul’s co-workers, during Paul’s extended ministry in Ephesus (Acts 19). Paul had never visited the church personally (2:1), and yet he writes with the pastoral urgency of a father: he is “struggling” for them (2:1), praying that they would have “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” hidden in Christ (2:3), warning them against the plausible-sounding deception that threatens to take them captive (2:8).

The letter’s structure is elegant. Chapters 1–2 are theological: the supremacy of Christ over all creation (1:15–20), the mystery of Christ in you as the hope of glory (1:27), and the fullness of deity in Christ as the demolition of every religious supplement (2:9–15). Chapters 3–4 are ethical: if Christ is everything, if you have died and been raised with him, if your life is hidden with him in God, then certain things must be put to death and certain things must be put on. The theology of chapters 1–2 always produces the ethics of chapters 3–4 in Pauline thought. Indicative before imperative; who you are before what you do.

The Christ hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 is one of the most majestic texts in the entire New Testament. In six verses it covers the entire scope of Christ’s lordship: he is the image of the invisible God; the firstborn over all creation; the one through whom, for whom, and in whom all things were created and cohere; the head of the body; the firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell; the one through whom God reconciled all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross. This is not merely elevated religious poetry; it is the most comprehensive christological statement in Paul’s letters, and it provides the theological foundation for everything else the letter argues. If Christ is who the hymn says he is, then the Colossian heresy — and every supplement to Christ in every generation — is not merely unnecessary but absurd.

Did Paul write Colossians? Some scholars doubt it, pointing to vocabulary and style unlike his undisputed letters, to the soaring hymn of 1:15–20, and to its close relation to Ephesians. But the letter names Paul three times (1:1, 23; 4:18), closes with his own signature, and is tied by its list of names to Philemon, which almost no one doubts is his. Differences of style are well explained by the subject, a new error to answer, and by the help of a co-writer, Timothy (1:1). The church received it as Paul’s from the beginning, and the more likely conclusion is that he wrote it.

Colossians is the answer to every form of Christianity that adds to Christ. It speaks directly to the believer who feels that faith in Christ alone is not quite enough — that additional spiritual experiences, additional practices, additional revelations are needed for full access to God. The letter says: you have been filled in him. You are complete. The fullness you are seeking is already yours, in the one in whom all fullness dwells. Seek more of him — not more beyond him.

1.title: The Supremacy of Christ: Hymn, Mystery, and Ministry
1.overview:
Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus. Paul had never visited; the church was planted by Epaphras, a local man converted probably during Paul’s years in Ephesus. Now, writing from prison, Paul hears that teachers are offering the Colossians something “more”: secret knowledge, angelic powers to be honoured, food laws and festivals, and harsh treatment of the body (2:8–23). Paul’s answer is not a better technique but a bigger Christ.

Chapter 1 thanks God for their faith, love and hope, and prays that they will know God’s will so as to live worthily, strengthened by his power, thankful that the Father has already qualified, rescued, transferred, redeemed and forgiven them. Then comes the great hymn (vv. 15–20): Christ is the image of the invisible God, the Creator and sustainer of everything, including every spiritual power; the head of the church and firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all God’s fullness dwells, who made peace by the blood of his cross. Finally Paul applies it: you who were God’s enemies are reconciled, if you continue in the faith, and the great mystery now revealed is “Christ in you, the hope of glory”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul had not founded himself; it was planted by Epaphras. Paul thanks God for their faith in Christ and their love for all believers, both springing from the hope stored up for them in heaven, which they heard in the gospel now bearing fruit across the world. He prays that God will fill them with knowledge of his will, so that they live in a way that honours the Lord, growing in good works and in knowing God, strengthened to endure with patience and joy, and thankful to the Father, who has rescued them from the power of darkness and brought them into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Knowledge of God’s Will: Wisdom vs. Esoteric Speculation

Paul’s prayer for “knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (v. 9) directly counters the false teachers’ offer of special knowledge. The knowledge Paul seeks for the Colossians is not mystical or esoteric; it is practical and ethical: “so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord.” Reformed theology has always insisted that true wisdom is not the accumulation of specialized spiritual information but the God-given capacity to live well in the world as God has made it, according to God’s own revealed will. The wisdom from above, as James says (3:17), is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits.” It is visible in life, not in the possession of secret knowledge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered a form of spiritual wisdom that was speculative, esoteric, and attainable only through special initiation. Paul’s prayer shows what genuine spiritual wisdom looks like: it produces fruit, builds endurance, and generates thanksgiving. Now: The contemporary church is perennially attracted to special spiritual knowledge — prophetic insights, mystical experiences, hidden wisdom that the ordinary believer does not possess. Paul’s prayer is the corrective: true knowledge of God’s will is measured not by the height of its claims but by the quality of life it produces. Does it make you fruitful? Does it make you endure? Does it make you thankful? Those are the tests.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.

Meaning first. Colossians is Paul’s great letter on the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ. A teaching at Colossae was adding to Christ: special knowledge, mystical visions, the worship of angels, food laws and festivals. Paul answers not with a better technique or a deeper secret but with a bigger Christ, so that believers see they need nothing more. Chapter 1 moves in four steps: thanks for the Colossians’ faith, love and hope, and for the gospel bearing fruit among them (vv. 1–8); a prayer that they will know God’s will, live worthily, endure with joy and give thanks to the Father, who rescued them into the kingdom of his Son (vv. 9–14); one of the Bible’s highest passages on Christ, the image of the invisible God, Creator and sustainer of all things, head of the church, firstborn from the dead, in whom all God’s fullness dwells and who made peace by the blood of his cross (vv. 15–20); and the application: once enemies, now reconciled, if they continue in the faith, while Paul suffers to make known the mystery, Christ in you, the hope of glory (vv. 21–29).

The setting. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13), once important but now overshadowed by its wealthier neighbours. Paul had never visited (2:1). Epaphras founded the church, probably during Paul’s three years in Ephesus, when all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord (Acts 19:10). Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon, sending the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus (4:7–9). So the greatest description of Christ’s lordship over the universe was written by a man in chains, to a small church in a fading town that he had never seen.

An apostle sent by the risen Christ. Paul writes to a church that does not know him personally, so he states his authority, and he roots it not in achievement but in calling. “By the will of God” is not a modest disclaimer; it is a theological anchor. His authority does not come from the Colossians’ recognition, or from the approval of the Jerusalem church, or from his own sense of vocation. It comes from the sovereign pleasure of God, and from the risen Christ himself, who stopped him on the Damascus road while he was hunting Christians and said, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (Acts 9:5). An apostle is a sent man, and the sender is the point: the letter that will set Christ above every power in heaven begins by putting its own writer under him. That matters for everything that follows. When Paul tells the Colossians that the new teachers are wrong, he is not one opinion competing with another. He is an envoy speaking with the authority of the one who sent him.

And Timothy our brother. Timothy was with Paul in prison, and he is named as co-sender, though Paul is the writer (notice the “I” of 1:23–25). The ministry is never solitary. And Paul’s word for him is not assistant or junior colleague but brother. The apostle and the younger man belong to the same family before they belong to the same team.

To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae. The recipients are called saints (hagiois), holy ones, set apart for God; and faithful brothers, believing and trustworthy. Both designations matter: they are holy by God’s action, and faithful in their own continuing trust. Neither truth cancels the other. Then come two addresses. In Christ: their true location, the place where their life is hidden (3:3). At Colossae: their earthly address, a small town with its markets, its temples and its ordinary pressures. Every believer has both, and the whole letter is about living at the second address as someone who belongs to the first.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father. Paul’s standard greeting, but not merely conventional. Grace (charis) takes the ordinary Greek hello, chairein, and fills it with the gospel: God’s free, undeserved favour. Peace is the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything set right with God. Grace is the source; peace is the fruit. The order cannot be reversed. No one arrives at the peace of God by working up to it; it flows from grace received. And both come from God our Father: not from Paul, and not from the Colossian church’s good standing, but from the Father himself. Here only the Father is named; Christ fills the rest of the letter.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only special Christians are saints. All believers are. Saint describes what God has done in setting a person apart for himself, not a level of achievement reached by a few.

Why is Paul so formal with people he loves? Because he has to be. A rival teaching was claiming a higher authority than the gospel the Colossians first received, and a church that does not know Paul’s face needs to know that this letter is not one man’s view. Apostolic letters were read aloud in church as the word of the Lord (4:16), and they still are. When you open Colossians, you are not reading a pious friend’s advice. You are receiving what Christ’s appointed envoy was given to say.

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to God’s holy people in Colossae, the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ: grace and peace to you from God our Father.

On a Tuesday. You live at two addresses: in Christ, and in your town. Let the first shape how you live at the second. When you walk into work, into the shop, into the family kitchen, you carry the first address with you. The neighbours see only the second. God sees both, and he names you by the first.

For worship. The God who could have written to the Colossians as a judge writes to them as a Father. Before a word of correction, before a line of argument, he pronounces grace and peace over a little church in a declining town, and calls them holy. That is how he always begins with his people: not with what we have done for him, but with what he has made us in his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited; the church was founded by Epaphras. Paul wrote from prison, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon.

verseByVerse.quote: We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,

We always thank God. Paul begins with thanks for a church he has never seen, and he gives thanks not for good weather or success but for what God has done in human lives: the faith, love and hope produced in the Colossians by the gospel. Every evidence of grace in another person is a reason to exalt God, because it is entirely his doing. The Christian who has grasped the gospel never runs short of things to thank God for. Thanksgiving is a theme of the whole letter: giving thanks to the Father (1:12), abounding in thanksgiving (2:7), and be thankful (3:15–17), continuing steadfastly in prayer with thanksgiving (4:2). A church that has forgotten how to give thanks is already open to the teachers who say it does not yet have enough.

The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul directs the thanks to the Father because the Father is the source, the fountain of all grace, who planned salvation before time began (Ephesians 1:3–4). And he does not say briefly God the Father. He names him the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the choice is loaded. It identifies exactly which God he addresses: not a philosophical abstraction, not one deity among many in the crowded religious marketplace of Asia Minor, but the God who has revealed himself definitively in Jesus Christ. Christ’s relationship to the Father is eternal and unique. And the phrase names the only basis on which we approach him at all: the God who is Father of the Lord Jesus is, by adoption, Father of all who are in the Lord Jesus (John 14:6; 20:17).

When we pray for you. Paul’s thanks rise in his prayers. He prayed regularly for churches far away, and for people whose faces he had never seen. His praying was not a vague goodwill toward the church in general; it had names and places in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thanked God for everything about them. He goes on to warn them sharply (2:8, 16–23). But he starts with God’s work, because what God has begun in a church matters more than what is still wrong with it.

Should I thank God for Christians I find difficult? Yes, and Paul shows how. You do not have to approve of everything they do, or pretend their faults are not there. You thank God for what he has truly given them: their faith in Christ, the love they do show, the hope they hold. That is not flattery, because the gifts are real and the credit goes to God. And it changes you. It is very hard to keep resenting someone you have honestly thanked God for that morning.

In a sentence. We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,

On a Tuesday. Make a short list of believers you know, near and far, and thank God for one specific grace you can see in each of them. If you cannot think of one, ask God to show you what he has done in them before you next see them.

For worship. The Son himself once lifted his eyes and thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children (Matthew 11:25). Every thanksgiving Paul offers for a church he has never seen is an echo of that prayer. Faith in a Phrygian town, love in a fading market, hope in hearts once dark: none of it was manufactured there. It came down from the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who shares his Son’s own sonship with beggars, and who delights to be thanked for what only he could have done.

verseByVerse.quote: since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,

Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus. Epaphras had reported it (v. 8). Faith and love are the two great marks Paul looks for when he hears about a congregation. Faith in Christ Jesus is the vertical: the soul resting its entire weight on the person and work of Christ. Notice that its value lies in its object. Faith is not strong because the believer is strong but because Christ is; a trembling hand that holds a strong rope is safe.

And of the love that you have for all the saints. Love for all the saints is the horizontal, the evidence that the vertical is real. And Paul says all of them, not just some: not only the believers who are like us, or easy to be with, or of our own background. These two are inseparable throughout Paul’s letters: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; 1 Timothy 1:14). Faith that produces no love for people is not yet the genuine article; John says that whoever does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20). And love without faith in Christ has no inexhaustible source to draw on. Together they are the signature of a church where the gospel has truly taken root.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love earns salvation. It is the fruit of faith. We are not saved because we love; we love because we have been saved, and because God first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Does loving all the saints mean I have to like them all? No. Love in the New Testament is not first a feeling of warmth but a settled commitment to another person’s good. You may never find a particular believer easy company, and that is not a sin. But you can pray for him, speak well of him, help him when he is in need, forgive him when he wrongs you, and refuse to join in when others run him down. That is love, and over time God often adds the warmth to the obedience.

In a sentence. because we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all God’s people,

On a Tuesday. Is your faith visible in love for all believers, including the difficult ones? Think of the person in your church you most naturally avoid, and do one concrete thing for their good this week.

For worship. The Christ who receives our faith is the Christ who loved us first, and every act of love between his people is his own love flowing on. He did not choose the easy ones to die for. He loved us while we were enemies, and that love is now the life of his church.

verseByVerse.quote: because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,

Because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Paul roots the Colossians’ faith and love in the hope laid up for them in heaven. Biblical hope is not the modern wish, as in I hope it does not rain, but confident expectation grounded in God’s promise: not uncertain, only unfinished. The outcome is guaranteed; it simply has not arrived. And it is specifically the hope of resurrection and the full inheritance of God’s children at Christ’s return (Romans 8:23–25; Colossians 3:4). “Laid up” (apokeimai) means stored, reserved, kept safe, the language of a secured deposit set aside and waiting (2 Timothy 4:8), kept where nothing can spoil or steal it (1 Peter 1:4). Your circumstances may be terrible; your hope is untouched, beyond the reach of anything this world can do to you.

Hope is the fuel. Notice that Paul says faith and love spring from the hope, which seems backwards. He is describing not the order of salvation but the dynamic that sustains faith and love day by day. This is the famous triad of faith, love and hope (1 Corinthians 13:13), and here hope fuels the other two. A believer who has lost sight of what is coming, living as if this world were all there is, finds faith shrinking and love growing cold. But one gripped by the certainty of what God has stored up has a reserve that makes persevering faith and costly love possible. Those sure of heaven can afford to love sacrificially on earth. The martyr who loves his enemies, the missionary who stays in the hard place, the ordinary Christian who keeps forgiving: all are drawing on hope.

A hope with a face. What is laid up in heaven is finally not a thing but a Person. Paul will soon call Christ in you the hope of glory (1:27), and tell the Colossians that their life is hidden with Christ in God (3:3). The hope is kept in heaven because Christ is in heaven, risen and seated, holding it in his own hands. That is why it cannot spoil: it is as safe as he is. And it will not be posted to us from a distance. It arrives when he does.

Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel. They heard of this hope when the gospel first came to them. Against a teaching that paraded itself as a higher wisdom, Paul offers no competing philosophy. He anchors everything in the gospel’s own character: it is the word of the truth, not one opinion among many, because it corresponds to what God has actually done in Christ. The alternatives are attractive; they are not true. And gospel (euangelion) was the language of imperial announcement: an heir born, a victory won. A King has won the decisive victory; he is Lord, and the world must answer (Isaiah 52:7; Romans 1:16–17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian hope is only for the future. It shapes life now. The hope is stored in heaven, but its effects are felt on earth every day, in the faith it steadies and the love it frees.

Is heaven a place I go to, or something that comes here? Both, in their order. When a believer dies, he goes to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). But the final hope is larger: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, and God will make a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4). What is laid up in heaven now is kept there for us, and will be revealed when Christ appears (3:4). You are not hoping to float away from creation for ever, but to live in it renewed, with God.

In a sentence. the faith and love that spring from the hope stored up for you in heaven and about which you have already heard in the true message of the gospel

On a Tuesday. When love feels too costly, look up before you look in. Ask what you are actually hoping for, and whether it is big enough to pay for what Christ is asking of you today. A forgiven grudge, a hard kindness, a long patience: none of them can bankrupt someone whose inheritance is kept in heaven.

For worship. The inheritance was not laid up cheaply. The Son went down into poverty and death to buy it, rose to take possession of it, and now sits at the Father’s right hand as its keeper. No thief breaks in there, no market crashes there, no diagnosis reaches there. The hands that hold our hope still bear the marks of the nails, and nothing laid in them has ever been lost.

verseByVerse.quote: which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,

Which has come to you. The gospel travelled to them, as it travels everywhere. They did not go looking for it in some distant shrine; it came to them, carried by a man from their own town.

As indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing. Paul speaks of the gospel in the language of a living plant, and he means it. The gospel is not an idea humans spread by their own energy but the living word of God, carrying within itself the power to produce what it announces. Bearing fruit: changing lives. Increasing: spreading to new people. Jesus taught the same: the seed has life in itself, and the farmer’s job is to sow, not to manufacture the growth (Mark 4:26–29); and Isaiah had said that God’s word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11). We carry it; it works (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). And the whole world means that this is not a local cult or secret teaching but a worldwide message, the opposite of the false teaching, which was for an elite few.

As it also does among you, since the day you heard it. The same gospel, at work among them from the first day. The fruit in Colossae is the same fruit as everywhere else, because it grows from the same seed.

And understood the grace of God in truth. “Understood” (epiginōskō) is a strong word: not merely having heard information, but coming to know fully, a personal, life-reordering recognition. What they grasped was the grace of God, the sheer undeserved generosity of God toward sinners in Christ. They grasped that salvation is God’s grace, not human achievement. To understand grace is to understand that you brought nothing, deserved nothing, and received everything. And it took root the day they understood it. There is nothing deficient in a straightforward reception of the gospel (Galatians 1:6–9).

What does “in truth” add? The Greek en alētheia carries two ideas, and Paul probably means both. First, truly: their understanding was real, not a passing interest or a surface agreement, and it showed in the fruit growing in their lives since that day. Second, as it really is: they understood God’s grace accurately, in its true form, not a distorted version of it. Paul has just called the gospel the word of the truth (v. 5), and he adds that they learned it from Epaphras, a faithful minister of Christ (v. 7). That matters because false teachers were now offering the Colossians plausible arguments, philosophy and empty deceit (2:4, 8), and rules about food, festivals and self-denial (2:16–23).

Why it matters. Grace can be misunderstood in two opposite ways. Some turn it into permission to sin: if God forgives, why not carry on? (Romans 6:1; Jude 4). Others add something to it, so that Christ is not quite enough without extra rules, rituals or experiences: the very danger in Colossae (2:20–23; Galatians 5:4). Understanding grace in truth means holding both halves together: it is entirely free, given to those who deserve nothing, and it changes those who receive it. The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).

Grace with a name. The grace the Colossians understood was not a general mood of kindness in heaven. It has a name and a history. John says that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), and Paul that the rich Son became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). To understand the grace of God is to understand the manger, the cross and the empty tomb. That is also why grace cannot be topped up with rules or experiences. It is not a quantity God measures out but the gift of his Son, and the Son is not given in part.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world had heard. It means the gospel was spreading everywhere across the known world of Paul’s day, and that it is by nature a message for all nations (compare v. 23).

How can I tell whether I have understood grace in truth? Look at both halves. Do you rest your hope before God on Christ alone, with nothing of your own added: not your church attendance, your good record, your feelings, your spiritual experiences? And is that grace changing you, so that you hate the sins you once excused and want to please the God who forgave you? If you find yourself thinking that God accepts you because you are doing well, grace has been distorted one way. If you find yourself thinking it does not matter how you live because you are forgiven, it has been distorted the other. Grace in truth gives you peace and makes you new.

In a sentence. that has come to you. In the same way, the gospel is bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, just as it has been doing among you since the day you heard it and truly understood God’s grace.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is still bearing fruit worldwide. Pray for its growth in a nation you care about. And when you share it, remember whose seed it is: your task is to sow it faithfully and clearly, not to make it grow. That frees you to speak without pressure and to wait without despair.

For worship. The word that reached a small town in the Lycus Valley was the word of the cross, and it is still running across the earth, alive with the life of the risen Christ it proclaims. When Greeks first came asking to see Jesus, he spoke of a grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies and bears much fruit (John 12:20–24). Every believer in every nation is that fruit. He gave everything to people who brought nothing, and from one death a harvest is still being gathered that no one can number.

verseByVerse.quote: just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf
verseByVerse.commentary:
just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf

Just as you learned it from Epaphras. Epaphras was a native of Colossae, one of you (4:12), who probably heard the gospel from Paul in Ephesus and then took it home to the Lycus Valley (4:12–13). Paul endorses his teaching: what you learned from him is the true gospel. Do not abandon it for the new teachers. The point is sharp: the Colossians did not receive a beginner’s version that now needs upgrading. They received the real thing from a faithful man.

Our beloved fellow servant. “Fellow servant” (syndoulos) is literally fellow slave. It is not a polite title. A doulos was a slave, someone with no rights of his own, whose whole existence was defined by belonging to a master. Paul regularly calls himself a slave of Christ (Romans 1:1), and here he names Epaphras his fellow slave: the same Master, the same total obligation. He honours him as an equal in service. Far from a degradation, Paul wears it as the highest honour: to be the slave of this Master is to be freer than any emperor. And he calls him beloved, which tells you that Paul’s praise is not a strategic endorsement but affection.

He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf. “Minister” (diakonos) is the word for a table servant, one who waits at another’s direction. In a world obsessed with status, the Christian leader is a table waiter: Epaphras came not to build his own platform but to serve, carrying a message that was not his own (Mark 10:44–45). Some manuscripts read on our behalf, as the ESV notes, which would mean that Epaphras represented Paul among them, doing in Colossae what Paul could not do in person. Either way, his faithfulness is the point.

Why a minister of Christ, and not of the Father? There is a pattern in Paul. When he speaks of the source of salvation and the ultimate purpose of all things, he tends to name the Father (as in v. 3). When he speaks of the content and commission of the ministry, what is preached and served, he names Christ. Epaphras is a minister of Christ because it is Christ who commissioned him, Christ whose death and resurrection is the substance of the message, and Christ who sends those who go in his name, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18–20). The Father, when speaking of source and purpose; Christ, when speaking of the mission.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel depends on the messenger. It means faithful messengers deserve honour. If Epaphras had been unfaithful, the gospel would still be true; but because he was faithful, the Colossians received it pure.

What if the person who brought me the gospel later failed badly? It happens, and it is painful. But the gospel you received does not stand or fall with the messenger. What saved you was Christ, not the person who told you of him. Paul says he could rejoice that Christ was preached even when the preachers had poor motives (Philippians 1:15–18). Grieve the failure, pray for them, and if they wronged you, take it seriously. But hold on to what was true in what they gave you: the Christ you trusted is unchanged.

In a sentence. You learned it from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf,

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the person who first brought you the gospel, or taught you it most clearly. Pray for them by name, and if you can, write and thank them. Faithful servants are rarely told what their faithfulness did.

For worship. Christ the Lord took the form of a slave and came among us as one who serves (Philippians 2:7; Luke 22:27). Every faithful Epaphras is only following his Master to the table, and every gospel that reaches a town like Colossae is carried by the servants of the greatest Servant of all.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who probably heard the gospel during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.

And has made known to us your love in the Spirit. Epaphras reported their love, and Paul describes it with a phrase that rewards a closer look. Love in the Spirit does not mean love that feels spiritual, or love expressed in a religious setting, or even simply love between believers. It means love whose source and energy is the Holy Spirit himself. Romans 5:5 is the clearest explanation: God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. And Paul goes straight on to say what that love looks like: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). The Spirit does not merely encourage us to love. He is the one who pours God’s own love into the believer, so that what flows out toward others is not simply a human effort to be kind but something with a divine origin. Galatians 5:22 confirms it: love is the first fruit of the Spirit, the primary evidence of his presence in a life. This is the only explicit mention of the Spirit in Colossians, which focuses on Christ. But that is fitting, because the Spirit’s work is to make Christ known and to produce love.

Two kinds of love. This matters because it distinguishes two kinds of love that can look similar from the outside. Natural human love, affection for friends, loyalty to family, generosity to those who are like us, is real and good, but it has limits. It falters under pressure, it prefers the lovable, it dries up when it is not returned. Love in the Spirit has a different source and therefore a different staying power: it can love the difficult, the undeserving, the enemy, because it is not drawing on human reserves but on the inexhaustible love of God flowing through the Spirit.

The surest evidence. For Paul, this love is also the most reliable evidence that the gospel has truly taken root. Anyone can adopt new religious beliefs; not everyone is transformed at the level where they genuinely and practically love people they would not naturally love. When Epaphras reported the Colossians’ love, Paul heard: the Spirit is at work here. The gospel did what it does. As John says, everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God (1 John 4:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit is unimportant in Colossians. His work is assumed throughout: the spiritual wisdom of v. 9 is wisdom the Spirit gives, and the spiritual songs of 3:16 are songs he inspires.

May we pray to the Holy Spirit? The normal pattern of Christian prayer in the New Testament is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit: through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18; Matthew 6:9; John 16:23). No prayer in the New Testament is addressed directly to the Spirit, and many Reformed Christians therefore keep to that pattern, as this note does. But it is not wrong to address the Spirit. He is fully God: lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3–4). We are baptised into the one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). The Westminster Confession says that worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and to him alone (21.2), and the Nicene Creed confesses the Spirit, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified. That is why the church has long sung prayers to the Spirit, such as Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire, and Breathe on me, breath of God. So: pray ordinarily to the Father, in the Spirit’s strength; and if you sometimes say, Holy Spirit, fill me with love, you are speaking to God.

What if I do not feel much love for other believers? Then ask for it, because that is exactly what the Spirit gives. Love in the Spirit is not something you manufacture by trying to feel warmer. Begin where you are: confess the coldness honestly, ask your Father to pour his love into your heart by the Spirit (Luke 11:13), and then act in love toward someone specific, even before you feel it. The feelings often follow the obedience. And look again at the cross. The Spirit’s way of producing love is to show us how much we have been loved (1 John 4:10–11).

In a sentence. and who also told us of your love in the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Ask your Father to produce love in you today by his Spirit, for someone specific, and name them.

For worship. The love of God is not rationed. The Father loved us, the Son gave himself for us, and the Spirit pours that same love into hearts that were once closed and cold, until it overflows toward people we would never have chosen. Every act of such love in a church is the Holy Spirit making Christ visible.

verseByVerse.quote: And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,

And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you. Constant prayer for people he had never met. Paul prays rather than merely explains, because accurate teaching alone does not change a life. God must open the eyes and bring the truth home to the heart, or the clearest explanation lands on the surface and slides off (1 Corinthians 2:14). That is why the most faithful teachers are the most persistent in prayer, as Epaphras was, always struggling on their behalf in his prayers (4:12).

Asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will. The false teachers promised special knowledge (gnōsis). Paul prays for true knowledge (epignōsis, full knowledge) of God’s will: what he has revealed about salvation and how to live. This is not abstract theology but a deep, personal, practical grasp of what God wants and is doing. And notice the word filled. The false teachers implied that the Colossians were half empty and needed topping up from their secrets. Paul prays that they will be filled from the source they already have, Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (2:3).

In all spiritual wisdom and understanding. Wisdom (sophia) and understanding (synesis) are near partners, and Paul uses them as a pair. Spiritual means given by the Spirit, not human cleverness, which was precisely the counterfeit the false teachers were selling. This is not secret knowledge for a few, but wisdom for all.

Which word means applying God’s word? In the Bible, it is chiefly wisdom. The Old Testament word behind it (ḥokmah) means skill: it is used of craftsmen (Exodus 31:3–6), and in Proverbs it is the skill of living well in God’s world, choosing the right thing in a real situation. James says the same: who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works (James 3:13). Understanding is closer to insight: seeing what a situation really is, discerning, grasping how truths fit together (Proverbs 2:2–6; 1 Kings 3:9–12). So roughly: understanding sees, and wisdom does. Some interpreters, notably J. B. Lightfoot, described understanding as the critical faculty that grasps the bearings of things, how a truth bears on a particular case, which is why it is sometimes explained as applying truth; but the words overlap heavily, and in Scripture it is wisdom that is most clearly the skill of living. The pair comes from Isaiah’s promise that the Spirit of wisdom and understanding would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2). What Christ has fully, his people receive from his Spirit. And the purpose follows at once: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord (v. 10). Knowledge of God’s will is meant to be lived.

What it does not mean. It does not mean seeking private revelations about God’s will for every decision. God’s will is revealed in Scripture, and wisdom applies it.

Does this mean God will show me which job to take or whom to marry? Paul means God’s revealed will: the wisdom and understanding to live a life worthy of the Lord (v. 10). Within that will, God gives his people freedom to make wise choices, praying, seeking counsel and weighing what is good. He guides by his word and his providence, not usually by special messages about particular decisions. So if two jobs are both honest and both open to you, you are not missing a secret answer. Ask which would let you serve God and love others best, take advice from mature believers, decide, and trust him with the result. Scripture does settle some questions for you: a believer is to marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39).

In a sentence. For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you. We continually ask God to fill you with the knowledge of his will through all the wisdom and understanding that the Spirit gives,

On a Tuesday. When you face a decision today, do three things in order. Ask what God has already said about it in Scripture. Ask what love and wisdom would choose within that. Then pray this prayer for yourself: Lord, fill me with the knowledge of your will. And pray it by name for someone else, because Paul prayed it for people he had never met.

For worship. The God who knows all things does not keep his will locked away from his children. He has spoken it once for all in his Son, and he gives his Spirit to make it plain and to make it live. The Son who said on the night he was betrayed that eternal life is to know the only true God (John 17:3) now intercedes for his people at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34), and every prayer like Paul’s for Colossae rises inside his.

verseByVerse.quote: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;

So as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord. Knowledge of God’s will is never meant to stay in the head; Paul prays for it so that the Colossians will walk, which in the Bible means the whole of daily life. “Worthy” (axiōs) first meant of equal weight, what balances the scales. A worthy life is one that fits, that matches the one it belongs to. Paul uses the same word for a life worthy of the gospel (Philippians 1:27), worthy of your calling (Ephesians 4:1), and worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory (1 Thessalonians 2:12). Think of an ambassador, whose conduct abroad either honours or shames the king who sent him (2 Corinthians 5:20).

The order of the walk. The worthy walk is grounded in everything before it: grace received, love poured in, prayer for wisdom. And its order matters: we please God because he loves us, not so that he will. The motive is never to earn a favour already secured in Christ; it is the response of a loved child to a Father who has given everything (1 John 4:19). And it flows from what Paul prayed in v. 9. The grammar is explicit: he prays for knowledge and wisdom so that they may walk worthily. A person trying to live for God without that Spirit-given knowledge is like someone navigating without a map. This is why prayer is not a supplement to discipleship but its engine.

What does a worthy walk look like? Paul does not leave us to guess. He defines it in the same sentence, with four marks: bearing fruit in every good work, increasing in the knowledge of God (v. 10), being strengthened for endurance and patience with joy (v. 11), and giving thanks to the Father (v. 12). Fruitful, growing, enduring with joy, thankful. Later he fills it in: compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiving one another, and above all love (3:12–14), lived out in marriage, in the family and at work (3:18–4:1). And the measure is the Lord himself: not any lord, but the one Paul is about to describe, the image of the invisible God, the one through whom all things were made, who made peace by the blood of his cross (vv. 15–20). He is gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). A life that fits him will look like him.

Fully pleasing to him. “Fully pleasing” (areskeia) is the desire to please in every way. The aim of life is to please Christ (2 Corinthians 5:9). Here is a staggering thought. The Lord who holds the universe together (v. 17), who needs nothing from us (Acts 17:25), takes pleasure in the obedience of his children, as a father delights in a child who loves him. Our small, ordinary acts of faithfulness can please him (Hebrews 13:16).

Bearing fruit in every good work. Like the gospel (v. 6), believers bear fruit: good works flowing from new life, the works God prepared beforehand for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). The same word for fruit is used of the gospel and of the believer, because the fruit in the believer is the gospel’s own fruit. And “in every good work” means exactly that: not only the public acts of faith but the whole texture of daily life. The honest word when a lie would be easier, the patience when irritation is natural, the kindness to the person nobody notices, faithfulness in small tasks nobody praises. No category of life falls outside it.

And increasing in the knowledge of God. Knowing him better and better: not accumulating information but deepening a relationship with the living God. And it is a living spiral. Knowing God better produces a worthy life: you do not struggle as much to forgive once you have reckoned with how much you have been forgiven. And living worthily deepens the knowledge: if anyone wills to do God’s will, Jesus said, he will know whether the teaching is from God (John 7:17). The one who trusts in a dark season finds God more real at the end than at the beginning. The growth has no ceiling this side of glory: the elder of forty years still has more of God to know, and to stop growing is not to stand still but to drift (2 Peter 3:18).

What it does not mean. Christians have filled this phrase with very different ideas, so it is worth being clear.

Not earning God’s approval. We are already accepted in Christ, reconciled and presented holy in his sight (1:22). We aim to please him as children please a father, not as servants anxious for their wages.

Not a list of human rules or a Christian look. A worthy walk is not measured by a dress code, by avoiding particular foods, drinks or films, or by keeping special days. That is exactly the religion Paul rejects in this letter: do not handle, do not taste, do not touch, rules that have an appearance of wisdom but no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (2:16–23). Such customs differ from church to church; Scripture does not make them the test.

Not mere respectability. The Lord himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19). A life that fits him will sometimes look out of place to polite society, and even to religious people.

Not perfection. The worthy walk is one of increasing (v. 10): it is growing, not finished. It includes failing, confessing and getting up again (1 John 1:9). And endurance and patience (v. 11) assume a struggle.

Not only the spectacular. Enduring a long illness with patience and joy (v. 11), giving thanks in a hard season (v. 12): that is as worthy of the Lord as any public ministry.

Not in our own strength. Paul prays for this walk (v. 9), because it is God’s work in us. We are strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might (v. 11).

Can someone as ordinary and inconsistent as me really please God? Yes, and Scripture says so plainly (2 Corinthians 5:9; Hebrews 13:16). You please him not because your obedience is flawless but because you are in his Son, so that your imperfect works are received through Christ, as a father treasures the crooked drawing his child brings him. The Westminster Confession says that believers’ good works, though imperfect, are accepted in Christ, God looking upon them in his Son (Westminster 16.6). So the smallest honest act done for his sake gives him pleasure. That is not a reason for pride. It is a reason to begin.

In a sentence. so that you may live a life worthy of the Lord and please him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God,

On a Tuesday. Ask before each task today: how can I please the Lord in this? Not how can I avoid displeasing him, but how can I give him joy. Then notice, at the end of the day, one thing you learned about God through doing it.

For worship. The Lord of glory, who holds the stars in place, is pleased by the faithfulness of his children. He has accepted us in his Son, he walks with us in the ordinary day, and every good work he finds in us is fruit of the seed he planted. There is more of him to know than a lifetime can exhaust, and he means to show us all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;
verseByVerse.commentary:
being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;

Being strengthened with all power. “Strengthened” (dynamoō) is receiving language, and continuous: being strengthened, kept being strengthened. The Christian does not receive a deposit of power at conversion and then live off it; it is an ongoing supply from outside himself. Paul does not pray that they dig deeper or try harder, but that they be strengthened, assuming plainly that the Christian life needs more than human resources can provide.

According to his glorious might. Not according to our weakness, but his might, the power of his glory. The measure is not a fraction, not enough to get by, but God’s own might, the same power that raised Christ from the dead (Ephesians 1:19–20). The one who thinks he needs only a little of God’s help has not understood how much genuine love, sustained faithfulness and real forgiveness actually cost.

For all endurance and patience with joy. Now the surprise. God’s mighty power is given not for spectacular feats, not for dramatic success or miraculous gifts, but for endurance (hypomonē) and patience (makrothymia), the two great staying-power graces. Hypomonē holds up under the weight of circumstances: not gritted-teeth stoicism but a forward-leaning perseverance, the runner who keeps going. Makrothymia is patience with people: the long-suffering that does not retaliate but waits for God to act. A church under pressure, as Colossae was, most needs not the spectacular graces but the quiet, costly ones: keep going, do not retaliate, do not give up. It takes nothing less than that resurrection might to keep a tired believer gentle with a difficult neighbour for twenty years.

With joy. Two words that should stop us. Not grim endurance, and not forced cheerfulness, but the deep gladness of one who knows God is sovereign and the inheritance is secure, so that no present suffering is the final word. The joy comes not from good circumstances but from knowing the One who holds them (James 1:2–4; Romans 5:3–5). Patience with joy is a miracle of grace.

Endurance first seen in the Lord. Both graces were Christ’s before they were ours. He endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). And Paul says that in his own conversion Christ Jesus displayed his perfect patience (1 Timothy 1:16), bearing long with the man who was hunting his church. So endurance with joy is not a Stoic ideal admired from a distance. It is the shape of the Saviour’s own life, and the power that strengthens us is his risen life at work in us, making us like him in the long, quiet places.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes trials. It means he gives strength to endure them joyfully. Nor does joy mean pretending: the psalms of lament are in the Bible, and Jesus wept. Joy can sit alongside tears, because it rests on something deeper than the day.

How can I have joy when I am suffering? Not by denying the pain, but by looking past it to what it cannot touch. Your sins are forgiven (v. 14), your inheritance is kept in light (v. 12), you have been moved into the kingdom of the Son the Father loves (v. 13), and the Lord who holds all things together is holding you (v. 17). Joy in suffering is often quiet, more like a steady floor under your feet than a feeling of happiness. If you cannot find it today, ask God for it, because Paul is praying here for exactly that, and it is a gift, not an achievement.

In a sentence. being strengthened with all power according to his glorious might so that you may have great endurance and patience, and joyfully

On a Tuesday. Name the trial you are enduring and the person who most tries your patience. Ask God for his glorious power, not to escape your trial, but to endure it with joy, and not to change that person first, but to make you patient with them.

For worship. The might that flung out the galaxies and rolled the stone from the tomb is put to work in the quiet places of a believer’s life: a hospital bed, a hard marriage, a long wait. God is not too great to bother with our endurance. He counts it worth his glorious power.

verseByVerse.quote: giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.

Giving thanks to the Father. Thankfulness, the fruit of grace, is the fourth mark of the worthy walk, and it is no small thing. A thankful heart is one that has understood it has received everything as a gift.

Who has qualified you. “Qualified” (hikanoō) means made sufficient, made fit. The choice is pointed. The false teachers were suggesting the believers were not yet fully qualified: that they needed additional experiences, angelic mediators, or ascetic practices to be complete (2:18, 23). Paul cuts it off at the root: the Father has already qualified you, fully, not provisionally. There is nothing left to add, no credential to acquire, no rung still to climb, and it rests entirely on God’s act in Christ, not on your spiritual performance. This is the pastoral heart of the whole letter.

To share in the inheritance of the saints in light. Paul draws on the Old Testament language of the promised land, the inheritance God gave Israel as his gift, where the LORD himself was the portion of his people (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 32:9). Like Israel’s inheritance, believers share an inheritance: eternal life in God’s kingdom. But in Christ it is transformed beyond all proportion: nothing less than a full sharing in the life of God himself, the new creation, the resurrection body, the face of God seen unveiled, what no eye has seen nor ear heard (1 Corinthians 2:9). Not earned but inherited, and an inheritance comes by relationship and gift, not by merit. And it is in light because it is in the full, unmediated presence of God, who is light (1 John 1:5; Revelation 21:23). That sets up the deliberate contrast with v. 13: the domain of darkness we were rescued from, the inheritance in light we are moving toward. Two kingdoms, two destinations.

Heirs because of the Heir. Why should strangers inherit anything from God? Because the Father has appointed his Son heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and everyone joined to the Son shares his portion: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). Canaan was divided by lot among the tribes; this inheritance is not divided at all, because each of the saints receives it whole, in him. The qualification is Christ’s own fitness, counted as ours; the inheritance is Christ’s own estate, shared with us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we qualified ourselves. The Father did it, through Christ. Nor does it mean that some believers are more qualified than others. The weakest believer has the same qualification as the apostle, because it is the same Christ.

What if I feel unworthy to stand before God? You are right that you are unworthy in yourself, and so is every believer. But the question is not whether you are worthy but whether God has qualified you, and if you trust Christ, he has. Your fitness for heaven does not rest on your feelings, your progress or your record this week. It rests on what the Father has done in his Son. Feeling unworthy can be a healthy humility, but it must not become a doubt about God’s verdict. Bring the feeling to the cross and leave it there.

In a sentence. giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of his holy people in the kingdom of light.

On a Tuesday. When you feel unqualified before God, remember: the Father has qualified you in Christ. And when someone offers you a spiritual extra, a technique, an experience or a rule that will finally make you complete, ask whether it is adding to what the Father has already done. If it is, you do not need it.

For worship. The Father did not wait for us to become fit for his presence. He made us fit, at the cost of his Son. And the inheritance he has qualified us for is himself: the light of his face, the life of his kingdom, and a share with all his saints in everything that is his.

verseByVerse.quote: He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,

He has delivered us from the domain of darkness. “Delivered” (rhyomai) is a rescue word, used in the Old Testament for God snatching his people from Egypt, from situations of complete helplessness. You do not use it for someone who found his own way out, but for one who was trapped, had no exit, and was pulled free by another. Paul’s whole diagnosis is that without Christ we were dead, captive, bound: not struggling toward the light but at home in the dark (Ephesians 2:1–5). The initiative and the power were entirely God’s; we contributed nothing to our rescue.

The domain of darkness. What we were rescued from is the domain (exousia, authority, power) of darkness, a word of governance. Not merely a moral condition but an organised realm with a ruler, under the one Jesus called the ruler of this world (John 12:31) and Paul the god of this age (2 Corinthians 4:4). Before Christ, we were under Satan’s authority (Ephesians 2:2; Acts 26:18). This domain has real power. It blinds minds and holds people captive while presenting itself as normal and even attractive. The person living in it does not feel trapped, which is part of the darkness. He cannot see that he cannot see, which is why rescue requires a power from outside.

And transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son. “Transferred” (methistēmi) was used of deporting whole populations from one country to another, as ancient empires did with conquered peoples. God moved us from one kingdom to another, and it is a completed action. The kingdom of the Son is not only a future hope; it was inaugurated in his resurrection and ascension, and everyone who is in him by faith has already entered it. A glorious visible consummation is still to come, but the transfer has already happened. You are a citizen of a different kingdom, under a different King, even while your feet still stand on the old earth (Philippians 3:20; Ephesians 2:6).

The Son of his love. And it is the kingdom of his beloved Son, literally the Son of his love, echoing the Father’s voice at the baptism: this is my beloved Son (Matthew 3:17). You have been brought inside the Father’s own love for the Son. The warmth and delight the Father has in him is the very atmosphere of the kingdom you now inhabit, and you are secure there, because nothing can remove the Father’s love for Christ, and you are in Christ (John 17:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are free from all spiritual struggle. But Satan has no rightful authority over them. He may tempt, accuse and trouble a believer; he cannot take him back.

If I have been rescued, why do I still struggle with sin and temptation? Because the transfer is complete but the war is not over. You have changed kingdoms, but you still live in enemy-occupied territory, with old habits that still pull and an enemy who still tempts. The difference is that sin is now a rebel in your life, not your rightful ruler (Romans 6:12–14). Every struggle against it is the struggle of a free citizen of Christ’s kingdom, not the hopeless effort of a captive. Fight it, confess it, and remember whose kingdom you belong to.

In a sentence. For he has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves,

On a Tuesday. When a temptation comes dressed as normal life, call it by its name: that is the old country. You do not live there any more. And when you pray for a friend who does not believe, pray as Paul would: not merely that they will improve, but that God will rescue them, because that is what it takes.

For worship. The Father reached into the dark and carried us out. He did not leave us at the border, but brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves, so that the love that has passed between the Father and the Son from eternity is now the air we breathe. You belong there now, and no power of darkness can deport you again.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

In whom we have redemption. Redemption (apolytrōsis) comes from the slave market and the practice of ransom: captives could be freed if someone paid the price demanded, bought back, their status changed by another’s payment. We were held captive by sin, by the debt owed a holy God, by the domain of darkness of v. 13, and we could not pay our own way out. Christ paid, and the price was his blood (Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18–19). The captive walks free, not because the debt was overlooked but because it was met in full. This is not cheap grace; it is the costliest possible grace. And Paul says we have it now: present tense. Some later manuscripts add through his blood, borrowed from Ephesians 1:7; the earliest manuscripts do not have it here, but the truth is the same, as v. 20 will say.

The forgiveness of sins. Redemption defined: forgiveness. Forgiveness (aphesis) means release: the letting go of a claim, the cancellation of a debt, the dropping of a charge. In the law court of God every sin is a real offence on the record. Forgiveness does not pretend the offences did not happen; it declares the charge answered and the record cleared, legally, finally, completely. Our debts are cancelled, the record nailed to the cross (2:13–14). It is not something to be achieved by rituals or experiences, as the false teachers implied, but something believers already have in Christ.

One event, two angles. The two are not separate transactions but one event seen from two angles. Redemption answers the question, how did we get free? A price was paid. Forgiveness answers the question, what is our standing now? The debt is gone, the record clear. You cannot have the forgiveness without the redemption, and the redemption means nothing except in the forgiven standing it secured (Romans 3:24–25). And notice the two words: in whom. Redemption is not a commodity Christ hands over and leaves us to manage. It is found in him, and we have it because we have him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean redemption is only future. We have it now. There is a final redemption still to come, of our bodies at the resurrection (Romans 8:23), but the forgiveness of sins is already ours, full and complete.

Does God forgive sins I commit after I become a Christian? Yes. The forgiveness Christ won covers your whole life, because he paid for all your sins on the cross, when every one of them was still future. That does not make sin small; it cost his blood. When you sin as a believer, you are not cast out of the family, but you do grieve your Father, and you should confess it to him honestly. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Confession does not buy the forgiveness again; it brings you back into the enjoyment of it.

In a sentence. in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

On a Tuesday. You are forgiven. Live free of guilt today. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not argue with your feelings; answer with the fact: in Christ I have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. And because you are forgiven so much, forgive the person who has wronged you a little (3:13).

For worship. The Son of the Father’s love paid the ransom in his own blood. The charge sheet that stood against us is cancelled, and the One who cancelled it is the Judge himself. We do not hope for forgiveness. In him, we have it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In what may be an early Christian hymn, Paul describes who Christ is. He makes the invisible God visible. He holds the rank of the firstborn over all creation, because everything, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including every spiritual power, was made through him and for him. He existed before all things and holds them together. He is also head of the church, the first to rise from the dead, so that he has first place in everything. The whole fullness of God was pleased to live in him, and through him God made peace with all things by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as Creator and Redeemer: The Cosmic Scope of the Gospel

The Reformed tradition has always insisted on the unity of Christ’s work as both the agent of creation and the author of redemption. The hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 grounds this insistence: the same one through whom all things were made is the one through whose blood all things are reconciled. This means that redemption is not the rescue of souls from a material world that God has abandoned; it is the renewal of the entire creation that God originally made through Christ. The scope of the atonement is cosmic, not merely individual; the goal of redemption is “all things,” not merely individual souls. Abraham Kuyper’s famous claim — “there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’” — is exegetically grounded here.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian heresy apparently involved a hierarchy of spiritual powers — angels, thrones, dominions, rulers — through whom one had to navigate to reach God. The hymn annihilates this hierarchy: all these powers were created by Christ, are sustained by Christ, and are subject to Christ. There is no mediating hierarchy between the believer and God; Christ is the direct and only mediator. Now: Every form of Christianity that introduces additional mediators — saints, angels, spiritual powers, ecclesiastical hierarchies — between the believer and God is doing what the Colossian heresy did. The hymn says: Christ is the image of the invisible God. To see God, look at Christ. To reach God, come through Christ. There is no other way, no additional hierarchy, no further mediation required.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.

The turn to Christ. For fourteen verses Paul has given thanks and prayed. Now, without warning, he stops speaking of the Colossians and speaks only of Christ, and does not stop until v. 20. This is his whole strategy against the error threatening the church: he answers false teaching not with a better technique or a deeper secret but with a bigger Christ. Keep Christ in focus and the rivals shrink to their true size; lose sight of him and everything else swells to fill the gap (Hebrews 12:2).

The Christ hymn. Verses 15–20 are often thought to be an early Christian hymn, in two stanzas: Christ and creation (vv. 15–17), Christ and the new creation (vv. 18–20). Whether Paul wrote it or quoted something the churches already sang, it is one of the highest statements of Christ’s person in Scripture, aimed at a teaching that made Christ one spiritual power among many. Notice how the stanzas mirror each other: firstborn of all creation (v. 15), firstborn from the dead (v. 18); all things created through him (v. 16), all things reconciled through him (v. 20). The one who made the world is the one who remakes it.

He is the image of the invisible God. The word is eikōn: not a weak likeness that resembles its subject from a distance, not a mere copy, but the exact, living representation and revelation of the original. God is invisible; no one has ever seen him (1 Timothy 1:17; John 1:18). And yet the invisible God has made himself visible, not in a symbol or a sound but in a Person. Jesus said: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3; 2 Corinthians 4:4).

Three echoes. Paul’s readers would feel three echoes at once. An eikōn was the emperor’s head stamped on a coin, carrying the sovereign’s own authority (Mark 12:16). Humanity was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27): Adam was made in God’s image; Christ is God’s image, the true image Adam failed to be, the last Adam in whom the broken likeness is restored (3:10). And Jewish wisdom writing had called Wisdom an image of God’s goodness. Paul lands all of it on one man: Jesus of Nazareth.

The firstborn of all creation. “Firstborn” (prōtotokos) speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place in the family. Not first created, but first in rank, heir and ruler over all creation. God called Israel his firstborn (Exodus 4:22), and he made David his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (Psalm 89:27), though David was the youngest son of Jesse. Rank, not birth order. “Of all creation” means over all creation, as verse 16 explains: because all things were created by him. He is not the eldest member of creation’s family; he is the heir of the whole estate.

Where Christians differ: is Christ a created being? Ancient Arians and modern Jehovah’s Witnesses take firstborn to mean that Christ was the first being God created, through whom he made everything else. Verdict: Verse 16 gives the reason he is firstborn: “for by him all things were created.” If he created all things, he is not one of them. Firstborn here means supreme heir, not first created; Paul had another word for “first created” and did not use it. And verse 19 says all the fullness of God dwells in him. Christ is the eternal Son, uncreated, fully God, of one substance with the Father (John 1:1–3; Nicene Creed).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ had a beginning. He is before all things (v. 17). Nor does image mean that the Son is a lesser copy of the Father. He is the image because he shares the Father’s nature fully; he shows us God because he is God.

How do I answer a Jehovah’s Witness at my door about this verse? Gently, and from the passage itself. Ask them to read on to verse 16, and ask how someone who made all things can himself be one of the things made. Point out that the Bible calls David the firstborn although he was the youngest, so firstborn can mean first in rank. Then show them verse 19 and 2:9, where all the fullness of deity dwells in Christ. Their own translation adds the word other (all other things), which is not in the Greek; you can ask them why. Above all, be kind. You are not winning an argument but pointing a person to the Christ who made them.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? By looking at Jesus. You do not have to guess what God is like, or build a picture from your feelings, your upbringing or your fears. Read the Gospels and watch him: touching lepers, welcoming children, rebuking hypocrites, weeping at a grave, forgiving the men who crucified him. That is what God is like. Whatever picture of God you carry that does not look like Jesus is not the true God.

In a sentence. The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation.

On a Tuesday. When your picture of God grows cold, distant or harsh, put it beside Jesus in the Gospels and let him correct it. Read one Gospel story today and ask: what does this show me about God?

For worship. The God no one has ever seen has stepped into view in his Son, with a human face and nail-scarred hands. Moses asked to see his glory and was hidden in the cleft of a rock while it passed by (Exodus 33:18–23); fishermen from Galilee ate breakfast with it on a beach (John 21:12). He is not one of the things God made; he is the heir of everything, and he is God, and the face that shows us the Father is turned toward us in mercy.
verseByVerse.note: “Firstborn” speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place — not that the Son was created.

parallels.desc: I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him.

For by him all things were created. Literally in him: creation happened in the sphere of the Son. All things: no exceptions. Christ is the Creator (John 1:3; Hebrews 1:2). Paul says creation came about by him, but he is not crowding out the Father and the Spirit. Scripture presents creation as the work of the whole Trinity: from the Father, the source (1 Corinthians 8:6); through the Son, the agent (John 1:3); by the Spirit, who hovered over the waters and gives life (Genesis 1:2). So why put Christ alone in the spotlight here? Because of what was being denied. The false teachers were evidently crowding Christ in among the spiritual powers they urged the Colossians to reverence (2:18). Paul plants him unmistakably on the Creator’s side of the line that divides Creator from creation. The very One they would reduce to a creature is the One by whom every creature was made.

In heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. The whole universe, seen and unseen. Paul spells out the scope exhaustively, not as a flourish but to shut every door. Visible and invisible adds the unseen realm explicitly, and that is the decisive stroke, because the unseen spiritual world is exactly where the Colossian error located its powers.

Whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers, angels good and evil, which the false teachers honoured or feared (2:15, 18). The four terms are the vocabulary of angelic ranks, the kind of hierarchy that speculative teaching arranged to govern access to God. Paul is not teaching a doctrine of angelic grades. He is borrowing their impressive-sounding vocabulary and sweeping the whole catalogue into a single sentence: all of it, every rank, created by Christ. They are his creatures, under him.

You do not tremble before what your Lord made. This is the pastoral heart of the verse. The Colossians were taught that these powers controlled the road to God and had to be appeased, and Paul pulls the ground from under that fear with one fact: Christ made them. And it cuts further. Some of these powers are now hostile, fallen, arrayed against the believer: the same ranks Christ disarmed at the cross (2:15; Ephesians 6:12). So it matters enormously that even the rebel powers owe their existence to him. They are not an independent dark kingdom locked in even combat with him. They are creatures, defeated creatures, and their Maker is their Master.

All things were created through him and for him. Through him: he is the agent of creation. For him: he is its goal, the one toward whom it all moves, made to find its meaning and end in Christ. Everything exists for Christ’s glory. And notice: in Romans 11:36 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 it is God the Father from whom and for whom all things exist; here Paul says it of Christ. Only God can be the purpose of creation, so this is a quiet but unmistakable claim to his full deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father did not create. The Father created through the Son, by the Spirit.
