What it means to be made for Christ. If all things were created for him, so were you. He is not only where you came from, but what you are for. The Westminster Shorter Catechism puts it this way: man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever (Q. 1). Colossians adds that this God is known in Christ, the image of the invisible God (v. 15). Four things follow.

Your life has a purpose that does not depend on success. You are not for Christ only when you are useful, healthy or impressive. A bedridden grandmother who trusts him, or a child with severe disabilities, is as truly made for him as a missionary or a preacher.

You belong to someone. You are not your own; you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). None of us lives to himself: whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s (Romans 14:7–8).

Nothing else will finally satisfy. That is why career, money, relationships or pleasure, good as they are, leave us restless when they are made the point of life. Augustine prayed: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (Confessions 1.1).

Ordinary things are for him too. All things were made for Christ, not only spiritual things: work, food, marriage, music, science, a garden. Everything created by God is good, and to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). Living for Christ does not mean leaving ordinary life behind, but living it for him.

What living for him looks like. Paul spells it out later in this letter. Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks (3:17). Work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (3:23). And then he applies it to marriage, children and work (3:18–4:1), the most ordinary parts of life. In practice: you do your job well because he is the one you serve. You speak in a way you would be glad for him to hear. You enjoy his gifts and thank him for them. You make decisions by asking what pleases him (2 Corinthians 5:9, 15). And when you fail, you come back to him, because he has already forgiven you (1:13–14).

What it does not mean. Not that you must become a pastor or missionary to live for Christ. Not that you must be doing something religious every minute. Not that God needs you: he is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). He made you for his glory and for your joy, and those two are not rivals. And not that your standing with him depends on how well you manage it: you are reconciled and presented holy in his sight through Christ’s death (1:22). Living for him is the response to that, not the price of it.

Like a key in its lock. Think of a key: made for one lock, it turns smoothly in the right door; forced into the wrong one, it jams. The van you drive, the shelves you stack, the bill you pay honestly, the patience you keep with a difficult workmate: done consciously for Christ, the key slides into its lock, and the most ordinary Monday becomes the thing you were made for.

Should I be afraid of evil spirits? No, not if you belong to Christ. Scripture takes them seriously: they are real, they deceive, and believers are to resist the devil and put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). But they are creatures, made by Christ, defeated at the cross (2:15), and unable to separate you from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39). You do not need charms, rituals, special formulas or anxious precautions. You need to stay close to Christ: pray, trust his word, refuse sin, and leave the powers to their Master. The safest place in the universe is in the hands of the One who made them.

In a sentence. Everything that exists, in heaven and on earth, seen and unseen, including every power and ruler, was made by Christ and exists for his glory.

On a Tuesday. You were made for Christ. So was everything you see today. Live accordingly: before your work, your meals and your conversations today, say quietly, this is for you, Lord. Then do it as if he were the one you are serving, because he is (3:23).

For worship. Every star, every atom, every angel that stands before the throne, and every fallen power that trembles before it, owes its existence to the Son. He is the reason there is something rather than nothing, and the reason it all has a point. And the One for whom all things were made did not wait for his runaway creatures to come looking for him. He came looking for them, wearing the dust he had made, so that a world made for him might be brought back to him.
verseByVerse.note: Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.

And he is before all things. Paul means two things at once. Before in time: Christ existed before anything was made, existing eternally. And the present tense is startling: not he was before all things, but he is, the same grammar Jesus used when he said, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). And before in rank: to be before all things is to stand above them, first in authority and dignity. Paul presses it because the false teachers were fitting Christ into the created order, one exalted being among the powers. If Christ is before all things, he is not on the list at all; every angel and authority came after him and stands under him. There is no rung of the ladder higher than Christ, because Christ is not on the ladder. He made it.

And in him all things hold together. The shift from v. 16 is deliberate. There all things were created through him, the language of agency; here they hold together in him, the language of centre. The word (synistēmi) means to cohere, to be kept from flying apart, and its tense means has held together and goes on holding. Christ upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3). He is not a watchmaker who wound the world and walked away. The atoms cohere, the planets keep their orbits, your next heartbeat comes, because Christ is actively holding it all. Withdraw his hand, and reality would not merely stop; it would unravel into nothing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean scientific explanation is unimportant. It means the order science discovers is sustained by Christ. The scientist who measures the laws of nature is measuring the faithfulness of the Son, whether he knows it or not.

If Christ holds everything together, why do things fall apart: illness, disasters, death? Because we live in a world that is held but also fallen. Christ sustains creation, but it has been subjected to futility because of sin, and it groans as it waits for its renewal (Romans 8:20–22). He does not prevent every breaking, but nothing breaks outside his hand, and he works even the breaking for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). The same Christ who holds the stars was himself broken on a cross. He knows what falling apart feels like, and he is bringing all things to a day when nothing will be broken again.

In a sentence. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.

On a Tuesday. On the day it feels as though everything is coming apart, say it to yourself: in him all things hold together, including this. Then do the next small thing in front of you, and leave the holding to him.

For worship. The Son is not resting from the world he made; he is upholding it now. Every breath drawn in an operating theatre, every sunrise over a battlefield, every atom in the hand raised to strike him, is held in being by his word. He kept in existence the very soldiers who crucified him while they did it. A Lord like that does not lose his grip on anything entrusted to him, least of all the people he bought.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.

And he is the head of the body, the church. The second stanza: Christ and the new creation. In the ancient world kephalē (head) could carry two ideas English keeps apart: source, like the head of a river, and authority, the one who rules. Paul means both: Christ is the source of the church’s life and its ruler, giving it life, unity and direction (Ephesians 1:22–23; 4:15–16). And he adds the plain gloss, the church, so that no one mistakes the body for the universe at large. Greeks and Romans often compared a community to a body, but Paul says something no one had said: the church is not merely like a body; it is Christ’s body, and Christ himself is its living Head, supplying its life from above.

Why the church comes in here. First, to bring the soaring hymn home. Verses 15–17 lifted our eyes to Christ’s lordship over galaxies and angels, and now Paul says this same cosmic Lord is the Head of this congregation, the little flock at Colossae. Second, the polemical edge. The false teachers were slipping angelic mediators between the believer and God, giving the church other heads to look to. Paul’s answer is that the church has one Head, and life and access to God flow from him alone. To go looking elsewhere is to be not holding fast to the Head (2:19).

He is the beginning. “Beginning” (archē) means origin, source, ruler. Christ is the beginning of the new creation. As he was firstborn over the old order (v. 15), so he is the beginning of the new order that dawned when he walked out of the tomb: first in sequence and the originating source, the doorway and the fountainhead of the new humanity.

The firstborn from the dead. The first to rise from the dead to resurrection life, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:20; Revelation 1:5). First in rank among the raised. Others had been raised before him: the widow’s son at Nain (Luke 7:14–15), Jairus’s daughter (Mark 5:41–42), Lazarus (John 11:43–44). But those were resuscitations, each called back to the same mortal life only to die a second time. Christ passed through death and out the far side into new, glorified, deathless life, the first human ever to do so. Firstborn, as an eldest brother is, the first of a great family who will follow him through the grave (Romans 8:29). His resurrection is the firstfruits and the pattern of ours: because the Head has risen, the body will rise too. His resurrection guarantees ours. The empty tomb is a promissory note with your name on it.

That in everything he might be preeminent. “Preeminent” (prōteuō) means to be first, to hold first place, and this purpose clause crowns the whole hymn. First in creation, first in new creation. Over angels and over death: in everything, without a single exception, first. Paul presses it because the Colossian error was at bottom a quiet demotion of Christ, fitting him in high but not highest, letting him share the platform with angels and rules and special experiences. And it is God’s own settled purpose that his Son be first, with the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ needs the church to be complete. The church needs him. Nor does head mean that any human leader is head of the church. Pastors and elders are servants under the one Head, not substitutes for him.

What does it look like to give Christ first place? Think of a wedding ring. You may love a great many things, your work, your friends, your hobbies, all rightly enjoyed, but the ring says one person comes first, and everything else takes its place around her. A life is not put right by adding Christ to the list of things you love. It is put right when Christ is moved to the head of the list, and everything else, job, family, hobbies, not thrown away but reordered, learns to orbit him. In practice it shows in what you will not give up for anything else: time with him in his word and prayer, obedience when it costs, the worship of his people on the Lord’s Day. And it shows in how you decide: what does he want here?

In a sentence. And he is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning and the firstborn from among the dead, so that in everything he might have the supremacy.

On a Tuesday. Is Christ first in everything in your life: your time, money, relationships, ambitions? Look at your calendar and your bank statement for the last month and ask what they say comes first. Then give him first place in one specific area this week.

For worship. The Lord of galaxies is the Head of a congregation in a small town, and of yours. He went down into death ahead of us and came out the other side as the eldest of a great family. He is first in creation and first in resurrection, and it is the Father’s delight that he should be first in everything. Every knee will one day agree.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,

For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell. The Greek has no separate phrase of God; it reads simply in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell. The ESV rightly supplies of God, because Paul tells us plainly one chapter on that in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (2:9). So in him means in Christ, and what dwells in him is nothing less than the fullness of God himself, the entire divine nature. Not partly, not a share.

Fullness. “Fullness” (plērōma) was perhaps a word the false teachers used for the totality of divine powers, spread out among angels and spirits. Later teachers of this kind certainly pictured the divine fullness parcelled across a long chain of intermediary beings, so that to reach God you climbed the ladder rung by rung, appeasing each being on the way. Paul seizes the word and turns it. All the fullness, nothing left over, nothing residing anywhere else, is concentrated, complete and undivided, in Christ alone. That single word demolishes the whole system. If the entire fullness of God is in Christ, the ladder of mediators is not merely unnecessary but an insult to the Son who holds it all.

To dwell. This indwelling is of the highest order. God dwelt in the tabernacle by a localised presence among his people, and the Spirit dwells in believers by grace, yet we remain creatures. This is different altogether. The word (katoikeō) means to settle down, to take up permanent residence, not to lodge for a season and move on. God did not visit Christ, or rest upon him as upon a prophet. The whole divine fullness took up permanent residence in him, and (2:9 adds) bodily, in a real human body: not part of God, not a copy or emanation, but God himself, complete and entire, dwelling in the man Christ Jesus (John 1:14).

Was pleased. And God was pleased (eudokeō) to dwell so: the language of free, delighted good pleasure, the same root as the Father’s voice at the baptism, with whom I am well pleased. Suppose you had worked for years at a vast firm and never met the owner, getting only fragments of his mind secondhand down a long chain of managers. Then one Monday he walks onto the shop floor, pulls up a stool, and says: I have come myself; everything there is to know of me, you can know by knowing me. That is what God did in Christ. He did not send fragments of himself down a chain of angels. He came himself, the whole of him, in a real man you could have stood beside (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the fullness came to dwell in him at some point, as if he were not God before. It speaks of the incarnate Son, in whom the eternal God fully dwells in bodily form. Nor does it mean that Christ’s humanity was swallowed up by his deity: he is one person, truly God and truly man.

If I have Christ, do I need anything more? Nothing more of God, no. You do not need a second blessing to complete what Christ began, a secret teaching, a special experience, or a higher class of Christian. All the fullness is in him, and you are filled in him (2:10). You do need to grow: to know him better, to obey him more, to enjoy him more fully. But that growth is going deeper into Christ, not beyond him. Whatever claims to take you past Christ is taking you away from the only place God’s fullness is found.

In a sentence. For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him,

On a Tuesday. When something promises to give you more than Christ, a technique, a teacher, an experience, a new rule, ask the question this verse forces: is it offering me something that is not already in him? If so, it is offering less, not more.

For worship. All of God is in Christ. The Father was glad to have it so: not a fragment of himself sent at a distance, but his whole fullness come to live in a man who ate and slept and wept and died. You need nothing beyond him, because there is nothing of God beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.

And through him to reconcile to himself all things. To reconcile is to take two parties at war and bring them back to peace, turning enemies into friends. The Greek (apokatallassō) is intensified: to reconcile fully, to change from enmity to peace, to bring the estranged all the way home. Sin brought disorder and enmity into creation; through Christ, God restores harmony. And the heart of it is this: the breach was not on God’s side. We were the rebels, alienated and hostile in mind (v. 21), yet the offended party is the one who makes the first move. God does not wait for the rebels to crawl back; he reconciles them to himself. Peace is his initiative, his gift, his costly achievement, not our negotiation (2 Corinthians 5:18–19; Romans 5:10).

Through him. Mark that the very words that named Christ as the One through whom all things were created (v. 16) now name him as the One through whom all things are reconciled. The hands that scattered the stars are the hands that were nailed to the beam; the Author of life is the One who bled. The Maker did not send the means; he became the means. He could have left the universe to its ruin and lost nothing. He went to the cross instead.

Whether on earth or in heaven. The whole cosmos, which was created through him, is brought back under him. Paul writes all things, not all people: the same sweeping phrase he used for the whole created order in vv. 16–17. The reach of the cross is as wide as the reach of creation. When Adam fell, the whole world was dragged down, subjected to futility and now groaning (Romans 8:20–22), so the rescue must be as large as the wreck: a renewed creation, the curse lifted, all things at peace.

Making peace by the blood of his cross. The means: not special knowledge or angel worship, but Christ’s sacrificial death. Peace here is not a bare ceasefire but wholeness, a relationship set right. There was real war: God’s holy wrath against sin, and our settled hostility. God did not wave the conflict away. He satisfied his own justice and bore his own wrath in the body of his Son, so the peace is righteous, not cheap (Romans 3:25–26; 5:1). Blood is Scripture’s shorthand for a life laid down in sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). And see how Paul anchors the cosmic in the concrete. Having swept across heaven and earth, things visible and invisible, he lands the whole towering vision on a beam of wood outside a city wall. The reconciliation of the universe was achieved at one particular hill, on one particular afternoon, by one particular death. The cross is the centre of cosmic history.

Where Christians differ: will all things, including all people and demons, be saved? Some read “reconcile all things” as universal salvation. Verdict: Paul means that Christ restores all creation to its proper order under God. Believers are reconciled as friends (vv. 21–22); hostile powers are pacified by being disarmed and defeated (2:15), not saved. The same Paul teaches eternal judgement (2 Thessalonians 1:9). The whole universe will be brought back into peace with God, with evil judged and removed, and creation itself set free (Romans 8:19–21).

Two kinds of peace. Paul himself guards the point three verses on: this hope is yours if indeed you continue in the faith (v. 23). Reconciliation here is the restoration of order and peace to the cosmos, and it happens in two very different ways. For those who come to Christ, it is the reconciliation of glad children welcomed home. For the hostile powers, and for all who refuse him to the end, it is the peace of a conquered enemy, disarmed and put under his feet (2:15). One day every knee will bow, some in joy and some in defeat, but all in submission (Philippians 2:10–11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person will be saved regardless of faith. Reconciliation is received through faith (v. 23).

What does the blood of the cross have to do with my peace with God? Everything. Your peace with God is not a mood you work up or a truce you negotiate by behaving well. It was made, once, outside Jerusalem, when Christ bore the penalty your sins deserved (1 Peter 2:24; 3:18). That is why it is solid: it rests on something finished. And that is why it is free: there is nothing to add by climbing angelic ladders or keeping man-made rules (2:13–15). When your conscience accuses you, do not look first at your feelings or your record. Look at the cross, where peace was made, and rest there.

In a sentence. and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through his blood, shed on the cross.

On a Tuesday. The cross is bringing peace to the whole universe. Be a peacemaker today. If there is a broken relationship you could take the first step to mend, take it, as God took the first step toward you. And when you look at a polluted river or a ruined landscape, remember that Christ died for a creation that will be made new.

For worship. The cosmic Lord is the crucified Saviour, and his throne is shaped like a cross. He who could have spoken peace from a distance made it with his own blood. The rebels did not sue for terms; the King paid the price of the treaty himself and signed it in his wounds. That peace is wide enough to hold the stars and near enough to hold a single forgiven sinner, and the day is coming when nothing in heaven or on earth will be at war with God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Reconciled and the Mystery Revealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Colossians were once estranged from God and hostile, as their actions showed. Now God has reconciled them through Christ’s physical death, in order to present them holy and blameless before him, provided they keep firmly to the gospel they heard. Paul rejoices in suffering for their sake, sharing in the hardships that come to Christ’s people, as the servant entrusted with making God’s word fully known. That word is a mystery hidden for ages and now revealed: Christ among the Gentiles, and in them, the hope of glory. Paul proclaims Christ, warning and teaching everyone, to present everyone mature in him, and he labours at it with the energy Christ supplies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery of Christ in You: Union with Christ as the Heart of the Gospel

The phrase “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) is the most compressed statement of the doctrine of union with Christ in the New Testament. The mystery that was hidden for ages is not merely that Gentiles would be included in the covenant people (though that is part of it); it is that Christ himself would take up residence in his people — that the indwelling of the Spirit would mean the indwelling of Christ himself in the hearts of those who believe. Reformed theology has always understood union with Christ as the foundation of all soteriological benefits: it is because believers are in Christ that they are justified, sanctified, and will be glorified. And it is because Christ is in believers that they have the living presence of the hope of glory dwelling within them now.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that they needed additional spiritual experiences and esoteric knowledge to be “complete” or “mature.” Paul says: the mystery that makes for maturity is already in you. Christ in you is the hope of glory. The treasure the false teachers are selling is already yours, in a far more intimate and certain form than they can offer. Now: The believer who feels spiritually incomplete, who is seeking a second blessing, a higher experience, a deeper initiation, needs to hear this: Christ is in you. The one in whom all fullness dwells is dwelling in you by his Spirit. The seeking is not wrong; but what you are seeking is already present. Seek to know more fully the one who is already yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,

And you. The camera turns. Paul has been gazing upward, lost in the glory of Christ, and now with two small words he swings the whole vision round and points it at his readers. From the cosmic to the personal. It is one thing to say Christ reconciled all things; it is another to hear that this includes you. The great reconciliation has your name in it. This is your story: here is what you were, and here is what Christ has done.

Who once were alienated. “Alienated” (apallotrioō) means estranged, made strangers, shut out from a belonging that ought to be yours. Man was made to walk with his Maker, and sin shattered it, leaving us alienated from the life of God (Ephesians 4:18), without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). Mark the word once. For the believer this is past tense, a country left for good. But it is the present address of every soul not yet in Christ (Isaiah 59:2).

And hostile in mind. Here is the deeper trouble: underneath the estrangement lies enmity, in the very seat of thinking and willing. Enemies of God in their thinking: not neutral, but opposed. This does not mean every unbeliever consciously hates God; most never give him a thought. It means the natural mind is set against his rule. It will not have him on the throne. The mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot (Romans 8:7). The polite indifference of the respectable man and the open scorn of the scoffer are two faces of one enmity.

Doing evil deeds. Their hostility showed in their actions. This was the Colossians’ condition, and everyone’s, before Christ. The deeds are the symptom, not the disease: we are not alienated because we do wrong; we do wrong because we are alienated. And evil here is measured Godward. Not only the obvious sins, but every deed, even the kind and respectable ones, done without reference to God, for self rather than for him. That is why even our righteous deeds can be like a polluted garment (Isaiah 64:6): not because kindness is worthless to a neighbour, but because it is offered by a heart still turned away.

But I was never a bad person. We must clear that protest away, or the verse seems to fit only gangsters. Paul is not saying every unbeliever is a monster, or that the kind neighbour and the cruel criminal are equally wicked. Many outside Christ are genuinely warm and honest, better company on a Monday than many a churchgoer. Paul is not measuring people against each other but against God. The question is not whether a man is nicer than his neighbour, but whether his life is turned toward his Maker or away from him. And every life outside Christ, however charming, is lived with its back to God, running its own affairs, however decently, as though the One who made it were not there. That fits the respectable man and the criminal alike: not equally far down the road, but on the same side of the one line that finally matters.

The decent man on your old street. Think of the most decent man you knew growing up: paid every bill, kept his garden tidy, lent out his ladder, never robbed a soul, and would have said cheerfully that he was not religious, he just got on with his life and did no harm. In that one sentence is the whole of v. 21: not raging against heaven, simply running his own little kingdom from his own front room, himself on the throne and his Maker nowhere in his thoughts. That was every one of us outside Christ: not always wicked by the world’s measure, but always turned away by God’s.

The Son who was shut out for us. What we were, Christ took in our place. The Son who had lived in the Father’s love from eternity was numbered with the transgressors, and on the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). He bore the estrangement our hostility had earned, so that those who were far off might be brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). That is why this dark verse is not a portrait of despair. It is the measure of what he carried.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers are as bad as they could be. It means they are alienated from God and opposed to him at heart. God restrains evil in the world, and unbelievers can do much that is outwardly good and useful to others.

Why does Paul make me remember all this? Not to shame you, but to make you grateful. Paul paints the old life this dark for one reason: so that the grace of the next line blazes all the brighter (Ephesians 2:12–13; Titus 3:3–5). A believer who forgets what he was soon forgets what grace cost, and grows proud, cold or harsh toward those still outside. Remembering keeps you humble before God and gentle with unbelievers, because you know you were once exactly where they are, and only grace moved you.

In a sentence. Once you were alienated from God and were enemies in your minds because of your evil behaviour.

On a Tuesday. When you meet someone today who does not know Christ, remember that you once stood where they stand. Pray for them as someone who has been rescued from the same place, not as someone looking down from above.

For worship. God looked on a race of estranged rebels, with their backs turned and their minds set against him, and he did not wait for us to turn round. He came round to face us, in his Son. The hostile mind was met by a Father’s heart; the evil deeds were answered with a welcome. Nothing in us invited him, and everything in him moved toward us, so that the enemies of God are now called his children.

verseByVerse.quote: he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,

He has now reconciled. Hold v. 22 against v. 21 and the turn is dazzling: once alienated, now reconciled. One word, now, marks the great divide of a life. And mark the grammar, for everything hangs on it. Paul does not write that you have reconciled yourselves, or that you climbed your way back to God. The subject is he: God, in Christ. The offended party is the one who makes peace; we brought nothing to the table but the very hostility that needed reconciling. This is grace with no ladder in it: not God meeting us halfway, but God crossing the whole distance to fetch his enemies home (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

A finished peace. And it is finished. He has reconciled points to a completed act, done for good: not a process you nurse along or a probation you must keep passing, but the peace accomplished at the cross when the Son cried, It is finished (John 19:30). You do not wake each morning to re-earn God’s welcome. You wake already reconciled, and live the day from a settled peace, not toward one you are still trying to win. This is the very heart of the letter’s quarrel with the false teachers: peace with God is achieved, not assembled by rule-keeping.

In his body of flesh by his death. In his real, physical body, which died. Paul is insistent on the physical, for two reasons. The false teachers were spiritualisers who prized mystical ascent and may have despised the body; they would have found something almost embarrassing in salvation coming through a bleeding body on a Roman cross. Paul nails reconciliation to flesh and blood and a real corpse. And it reaches back to the hymn. The One in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (2:9) saved us in a real human body. He had to become flesh in order to die for flesh; God as pure spirit cannot bleed. Our peace did not cost God a word; it cost him a body (Hebrews 10:10).

In order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him. The goal is the last day, when believers will stand before God. The word present (paristēmi) is the language of bringing someone forward and setting them in place: a bride led to her husband, an offering set before God. And the three words pile up the glory. Holy: set apart, belonging wholly to God. Blameless (amōmos): without blemish, the very word for a sacrificial lamb without defect. Above reproach (anenklētos): a courtroom word, unaccusable, a person against whom no charge can be made to stick. All of it before him, under God’s own searching gaze. And all of it through Christ’s work, not their own (Ephesians 5:27; Jude 24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are now sinless. It means God will present them so, perfected in Christ.

But I never feel holy or blameless. How can this be me? Two truths set you free. First, this is your standing, not your feeling. It is not a description of how holy you have become but a verdict about how God sees you in Christ, whose own flawless record was credited to your account while your sin was counted his and paid for (2 Corinthians 5:21). Above reproach is the literal truth of your case in heaven’s court right now: the charge sheet torn up. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; Christ Jesus is the one who died (Romans 8:33–34). Second, what you are now by reckoning you will one day be in full. Paul says to present you, and a day is coming when Christ will set his people blameless before the throne with great joy (Jude 24; Ephesians 5:27): the holiness reckoned to you now finished in you completely, the feeling at last catching up with the fact.

The gap and who closes it. So your sense of falling short is not a contradiction of this verse. It is simply the gap between your standing, already perfect in Christ, and your experience, still being made holy. And the closing of that gap rests not on your grip on God but on his grip on you, for he does not begin a work he fails to finish (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. But now he has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death to present you holy in his sight, without blemish and free from accusation,

On a Tuesday. When your conscience brings up an old charge, answer it with this verse: I have been reconciled in his body of flesh by his death. Then get up and live the day as someone at peace with God, not as someone on probation.

For worship. The One who will present us was first presented for us: led out before Pilate, charged, mocked and condemned, though the governor himself found no guilt in him (John 18:38). He stood in the dock so that we would stand before the throne without a charge. On that day the Judge will look at the people his Son brings forward and find nothing to rebuke, because every reproach already fell on the One who carries them in.

verseByVerse.quote: if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.

If indeed you continue in the faith. That little if can land on a tender conscience like a cold draught. Paul has just promised that Christ will present the believer holy and blameless, and now he adds a condition. “Continue” (epimenō) means remain, persist. The faith means both their believing and the gospel believed. And we must not soften it. It is real, not a figure of speech. The people who will be presented holy are the people who keep believing to the end. A faith that finally and totally collapses and walks away was never the living thing it seemed: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

Stable and steadfast. Building words. “Stable” (tethemeliōmenoi) means founded, set on a foundation, like a building that will not give way. “Steadfast” (hedraioi) means firm, settled, firmly seated. This is aimed straight at Colossae’s danger.

Not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard. “Shifting” (metakineō) means being moved away, budged, carried off. The danger was being drawn away by false teaching: the false teachers were trying to move them off the simple gospel of grace onto some newer, deeper teaching dressed as spiritual progress. Paul’s charge is, in effect: stay put. Do not drift from the message you first believed.

Which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven. Not a statistical claim that every person had heard, but the sweeping language of a man describing something universal and unstoppable. The gospel has gone throughout the world; it is not a secret teaching. The false teaching prized hidden knowledge for an inner circle, but the gospel is the opposite: a public, worldwide announcement. Why trade a place in a worldwide, God-driven gospel for a little local secret society?

And of which I, Paul, became a minister. Paul’s calling. He puts his own weight behind this gospel, the very one they heard, not some rival or improved version. And mark the word: minister (diakonos, servant), not master, not the self-styled expert with the secret. He did not invent the gospel and does not own it; he serves it.

Where Christians differ: does this condition mean believers can lose salvation? Some read “if you continue” as showing that true believers may fall away and be lost. Verdict: Perseverance is the evidence of genuine faith, and the warning is one of God’s means of producing it. Those who are truly reconciled will continue, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). Those who finally abandon the faith show they never truly had it (1 John 2:19). The condition is real and must be heard; it is how God keeps his people steadfast (Westminster 17).

Perseverance and preservation. Look closer, and the cold draught turns to warm assurance. Salvation does come to those whose faith continues, but the continuing is not a weight laid on your own strength, as though you must grit your teeth and hope your grip holds for fifty years. The continuing is itself God’s gift and work: the same God who reconciled you has pledged to finish what he started in you, and to guard you by his power through faith (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). Perseverance and preservation are two sides of one coin: the saints persevere because God preserves them.

The climber and the rope. Picture a climber roped to an expert guide. He must keep climbing, and his effort is real. But he is roped to a guide who will not let him fall, and when his boot slips on the loose rock, as it will, the rope holds. His safety never rested on the strength of his own fingers, but on the rope and the one holding it. So the if is not meant to torment you with the question whether you have enough faith to make it. It is a summons to keep going, and, for the one who keeps clinging to Christ through all his stumbles, the very proof that God is holding him.

Kept by the prayers of Christ. The deepest reason true believers continue lies not in them but in their Saviour. On the night before Peter’s denial, Jesus told him, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:32), and Peter, though he fell, did not fall away. The same Lord always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). For every true believer, the if of this verse is answered by the prayers of the One who died for him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our own strength. It means true faith endures, by God’s grace.

What about someone I know who seemed to be a believer and has walked away? Do not pronounce the final verdict; that belongs to God, and the story is not over. Some who wander are true believers in a season of serious backsliding, and God brings them back, as he brought back Peter after his denial. Others, if they never return, show in the end that their faith was not the living kind (1 John 2:19). You cannot always tell which, and you do not need to. Pray for them persistently, keep the door open, love them honestly, and tell them the truth about Christ when you can. The God who keeps his own is also the God who seeks the lost.

How do I know my faith is the kind that continues? Not by looking for a feeling of certainty about the future, but by looking at Christ now. Are you still trusting him, however weakly? Do you still come back to him when you fail? Do you still want to be his? Those are the marks of a faith God is keeping. Then use the means he uses to keep you: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. A believer who cuts himself off from these is not proving his security but endangering his steadiness.

In a sentence. if you continue in your faith, established and firm, and do not move from the hope held out in the gospel. This is the gospel that you heard and that has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and of which Paul has become a servant.

On a Tuesday. Stay grounded in the gospel you first believed. Do not drift after novelties. If a teaching, a book or a video makes the gospel you first heard seem shallow and promises something deeper, test it against this letter. The deepest thing in the universe is not beyond the gospel; it is the gospel.

For worship. The Christ who sets the guardrail at the cliff edge of grace is the Christ who holds the rope. Real security and real perseverance, the two things anxious hearts tear apart, are bound together in his hands. Behind both stands the Father, who reconciled us at the cost of his Son and will not lose one of those for whom he died. The gospel we first heard is the gospel that carries us home, and the Shepherd who called us will be the Shepherd who brings us in.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,

Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake. The focus turns to the servant, and we must not forget where Paul sits as he writes: in chains (4:18). His life as an apostle was one long catalogue of hardship: floggings, stonings, shipwreck, prison after prison (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). It was the cost of carrying the gospel to the Gentiles, the Colossians among them. And his rejoicing is no grim masochism, as if pain were good in itself.

Three reasons for joy. He rejoices for three reasons folded into the verse. First, the suffering is for your sake: fruitful, spent on people he loves, and a wound borne for those you love is one you can bear gladly. Second, to suffer for Christ is to be drawn into fellowship with Christ himself (Philippians 3:10). The apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer for the name (Acts 5:41). Third, his joy rests not in the pain but in what it accomplishes: through a prison cell the gospel runs free and a church is built.

And in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions. The hardest phrase Paul ever wrote, and we must say firmly what it cannot mean. It cannot mean Christ’s atoning sufferings were insufficient, that his death left a deficit for Paul to make up. The letter has just declared the opposite: he made peace by the blood of his cross (1:20) and has now reconciled us, finished and complete (1:22). To Christ’s sin-bearing suffering not one drop can be added. And the word Paul uses for afflictions (thlipseis) is never used in the New Testament of Christ’s atoning death.

Two kinds of suffering. What it means is this. The New Testament speaks of two kinds of suffering bound up with Christ. There is his atoning suffering, the once-for-all work of the cross, which we receive but never share. And there are his ongoing afflictions in his suffering people as the gospel advances in a hostile world. For Christ is so joined to his church that to strike the church is to strike him: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). There is, as it were, an appointed measure of such affliction still to be borne by the church before the end, and Paul gladly takes up his share. When he is beaten for preaching Christ, the afflictions of Christ’s mission are filled up in his own flesh. He is not adding to the atonement but taking his portion of the cost of spreading it.

For the sake of his body, that is, the church. His suffering builds up the church. That is what turns hardship into joy: Paul’s suffering is not wasted but productive. Through his chains the word runs and believers are strengthened. The cell where Paul sat was not a dead end; it was a pulpit (Philippians 1:12–14).

Where Christians differ: the merits of the saints. Roman Catholic teaching has used this verse to support a treasury of merit: the sufferings of saints added to Christ’s, applied to others through indulgences. Verdict: Christ’s atoning work was complete and finished (John 19:30; Hebrews 10:14). Nothing can be added to it. Paul’s sufferings did not atone for anyone; they were the cost of bringing the gospel to them. There is no treasury of merit and no need for indulgences.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns salvation. It means suffering for Christ serves the church.

Does this apply to my sufferings, or only to Paul’s? In its measure, to yours. What was true of the apostle holds for every believer: when you bear loss or scorn for Christ’s sake, it is not meaningless misfortune but a share in the afflictions of Christ, counted into the great work he is doing and borne for the good of his people. Being passed over at work for refusing to lie, losing a friend because you follow Christ, the long labour of caring for a believer in need: these are not wasted. And even suffering that is not directly for the gospel, illness or grief, can be borne for the church’s sake when you bear it trusting God, because others are strengthened by watching you. But do not go looking for suffering, and do not call the results of your own folly persecution (1 Peter 4:15–16).

In a sentence. Now Paul rejoices in what he is suffering for you, and he fills up in his flesh what is still lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of his body, which is the church.

On a Tuesday. If you suffer for Christ and his church, rejoice. Your suffering is not wasted. Think of a believer you know who is suffering now, and do something for them this week, a message, a meal, a visit, so that you share the weight.

For worship. The Lord who once suffered alone on the cross, bearing what no one else could bear, now walks with his body through every place where the gospel advances at a cost. Paul’s chains in Rome and the scars of nameless believers today are written into one story, and it ends at an empty tomb. Not one blow borne for his church is wasted. The One who counted his servants worthy to suffer for his name will one day wipe every tear from their eyes himself (Revelation 21:4).
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not mean Christ’s atoning suffering was incomplete; he shares in the afflictions that Christ’s people must still endure.

verseByVerse.quote: of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.

Of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you. Paul calls himself a minister, diakonos again, servant, now of the church, and describes his office with a homely word: stewardship (oikonomia), the management of a household, a trust. A steward was not the owner but the servant put in charge of the estate, entrusted with the keys to give out the master’s provisions at the proper time. Three things follow. He does not own what he handles: the gospel is not Paul’s to alter or sell. He did not appoint himself. And he must one day give account. So Paul does not stand over the Colossians as a lord with his own message, but among them as a servant dispensing what belongs to Another, given to him for them, for their benefit, not his prestige (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

All of it comes down. And there is the wonder: the stewardship is from God, given to him. He did not volunteer for the office, invent the message, or earn the trust; it came down to him. Once you see it, you cannot stop seeing it through this whole passage. The gospel is God’s, the mystery is God’s, the revealing is God’s doing, the stewardship is God-given, and even the strength to carry it out is his energy that he powerfully works within me (v. 29). From first to last everything descends from heaven; not one thread ascends from earth. And so it is with the whole of salvation: it is all of God. The same grace that made a persecutor into a steward reached down for you (Ephesians 3:7–8).

To make the word of God fully known. “Fully known” (plēroō) means to fulfil, to complete. The word of God here is first the gospel message, the word God has spoken about his Son (v. 5; 1 Thessalonians 2:13), since the New Testament was still being written. And fully known has a double force: Paul preaches the gospel completely, nothing edited out to please his hearers (Acts 20:27), and he carries it to its full reach, out to the Gentiles. The false teachers wanted to add to the gospel, as though it were lacking. Paul says it is already full: his task is not to supplement it but to declare the whole of it.

The mystery hidden for ages and generations. A mystery in the Bible is not a baffling puzzle but something once hidden in the mind of God and now revealed by him: a truth no one could have worked out, which God has chosen to bring into the light (Ephesians 3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26). Its content Paul gives in the next breath: Christ in you, the hope of glory (v. 27), the plan, hidden for ages, that Christ would be proclaimed among the Gentiles and dwell by his Spirit in all who believe. Note the irony against the Colossian error. The mystery religions and the false teachers traded in secret knowledge for an inner ring. Paul takes their favourite word and turns it inside out: God’s great secret is not hoarded for the few but published to all.

Hidden, yet there all along. It was hidden for ages and generations, yet not absent from the Old Testament. It was there the whole time, but veiled: the offspring who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15), the promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), the Servant given as a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6). The lines were all on the canvas, but in shadow, like a letter sealed and addressed to you, lying on the table for generations, the message real and waiting but unread until the day it is opened. Announced, and still hidden, until Christ drew back the curtain (Luke 24:27).

But now revealed to his saints. The passive matters: the mystery was revealed, by God. The deepest truth in the universe was not unearthed by philosophers or cracked open by the clever; it was unveiled from above by a God who chose to make himself known. Man’s religion is forever a ladder reaching up to find God; the gospel runs the other way: God comes down and tells. And it was revealed to his saints, the ordinary name for all believers, not a spiritual elite: not a truth the saints were sharp enough to grasp, but one their God was gracious enough to give (1 Corinthians 2:14; Matthew 11:25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament was silent about it. The prophets hinted at it, but it was not fully understood until Christ.

Are there still hidden truths God reveals today to special people? Not new truths of the gospel. The mystery has now been revealed and written down by the apostles, and the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God still opens blind eyes to see what is in his word (Ephesians 1:17–18), and a believer may suddenly see a passage he has read a hundred times. But that is illumination of what is written, not new revelation beside it. Anyone who claims to have a secret truth that the ordinary believer with an open Bible cannot reach is offering exactly what Paul refused.

In a sentence. Paul has become its servant by the commission God gave him to present to you the word of God in its fullness: the mystery that has been kept hidden for ages and generations, but is now disclosed to the Lord’s people.

On a Tuesday. God’s great mystery has been revealed to you. Share it with someone who does not know. You hold, in an ordinary Bible on an ordinary shelf, the secret that kings and prophets longed to see (Luke 10:24). Open it today as if that were true, because it is.

For worship. The God who kept his counsel through the long ages did not keep it for ever. He opened it in his Son and put the secret of the universe into the hands of tradesmen, slaves and housewives in a small town. He did not have to tell us. He chose to, and the telling is grace.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.

To them God chose to make known. Before we reach what is revealed, Paul wants us to feel that it was revealed at all. God chose; it was his free choice and good pleasure. The unveiling was not owed to anyone, not earned. God could have kept his secret locked in his own heart through all eternity and wronged no one. Instead he chose to tell, and to tell it to outsiders and rebels. The same sovereign will that called Abraham out of Ur has now flung open his deepest secret. That God should want to share the hidden riches of his glory with people like us is a wonder before it is ever a doctrine (Matthew 11:26).

How great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery. The astonishing part: the Gentiles are included. To a Jewish mind they were the outsiders, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). That God’s richest glory would be displayed among them was the part no one saw coming (Ephesians 3:6). And the Colossians are those Gentiles: this is about them. It is the death of every spiritual snobbery. See how the words pile up: not just the mystery, but its glory; not just its glory, but the riches of it. Paul is straining language, the way a man does when the thing he describes is too large for words.

Which is Christ in you. The mystery revealed: Christ himself dwelling in Gentile believers by his Spirit (Galatians 2:20; Romans 8:9–10). The greatest treasure God ever kept hidden turns out to be a Person. Not Christ far above you, reached only by climbing a ladder of angels and rituals, the very thing the false teachers were selling, but Christ in you: the living Lord himself, taking up residence within his people, now, in the humblest believer. “In you” is plural: among you, and in each of you. The Messiah of Israel living in pagans who had been without hope. You do not need a mediator to reach a distant God, for God in Christ already lives within you.

The hope of glory. Christ in you now guarantees glory to come: resurrection, glorification, sharing his glory. Hope here is not a wistful maybe but settled certainty. Because Christ is in you now, the glory to come is sure: when Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory (3:4; Romans 8:17–18). The present indwelling is the pledge and down payment of the coming splendour.

The King in the cottage. Imagine the King of all the earth leaving his palace to move, in person, into a labourer’s little cottage: not to visit but to live there, day and night. The neighbours would shake their heads and ask why there. But here is what makes the heart race. If the King himself has taken up residence in your cottage now, it is utterly certain that one day he means to bring you home to his palace. He did not move in to leave you in the cottage for ever. Christ in you is the King in the cottage; the hope of glory is the palace that must surely follow. You do not have to climb to God, or earn your way up, or feel worthy enough. The King has already moved in, and that settles where you will spend eternity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers become divine. It means Christ dwells in them by the Spirit, uniting them to himself.

How can Christ be in me if he is in heaven at the Father’s right hand? Both are true, and the link is the Holy Spirit. In his human body Christ has ascended and is in heaven, from where he will return (3:1; Acts 1:11). But by his Spirit he dwells in every believer: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him, and if Christ is in you, your spirit is alive (Romans 8:9–10). This is not a feeling you must produce. It is a fact about every believer, whether you feel it or not, and it is why you are never alone, never beyond his help, and never without hope.

In a sentence. To them God has chosen to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.

On a Tuesday. Christ is in you, the hope of glory. Rejoice in that today. When you feel small, ordinary or unspiritual, remember who lives in you. And when you look at another believer, however unimpressive, remember who lives in them.

For worship. The richest secret of God’s glory is not a doctrine to be filed but a Person to be had. The Son, who fills heaven with his splendour, consents to live in people who were once far off, and he does not find them too small or too stained to dwell in. The glory that is coming will not be a stranger’s glory. It will be the unveiling of the One who has been living in us all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.

Him we proclaim. In the Greek the very first word is emphatic: Him. Not it: not a system, not rules, not a code, not experiences, not a ladder of disciplines. Him. The whole burden of Christian preaching is a Person, Christ himself, to be known, trusted and loved. This lands like a hammer on the Colossian error, which peddled exactly the opposite: regulations, festivals, food laws, angel rituals, secret know-how. Paul will not preach a machine; he heralds a Master. And proclaim (katangellō) is the word for a herald’s open announcement, not the whispered initiation of a secret society. You do not get Christ by keeping the rules; you begin to keep his commands by having Christ (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Warning everyone. True ministry admonishes as well as comforts. “Warning” (noutheteō) means to admonish, counsel, correct: to counsel someone out of harm’s way. It is what Paul did at Ephesus night and day with tears (Acts 20:31). Here it is chiefly the warning against being lured away from the all-sufficient Christ onto the empty promises of the false teachers, and behind that the deceitfulness of sin and the seriousness of standing before God. To warn is not the opposite of love; it is love. The shepherd who never tells the sheep about the cliff is not kind but faithless, and a father shouts at the child wandering into the road precisely because he loves him.

And teaching everyone with all wisdom. If warning turns people away from danger, teaching (didaskō) builds them up in the truth. Both negative and positive. With all wisdom: not the world’s cleverness, but the true wisdom found in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (2:3), and the skill to fit it to each real life so that it takes root. And mark the drumbeat: everyone, everyone, everyone, three times. Unlike the false teachers, who offered maturity only to an elite, Paul offers it to all.

That we may present everyone mature in Christ. “Present” is the word of v. 22, with the great Day in view. “Mature” (teleios) means complete, full-grown, brought to the intended end: the word the mystery religions used for their initiates. True maturity is not initiation into secrets, but growth in Christ. The goal of ministry is to present every believer mature to God on the last day.

What maturity is not, and what it is. Not mere head knowledge: a man can know the whole Bible and be a spiritual toddler. Not religious performance. And not a higher tier for an elite few, the very thing the false teachers dangled. What it is: growing up into Christ, rooted, steady, discerning, Christlike in character, no longer blown about by every new teaching, able to stand and feed yourself from God’s word (Ephesians 4:13–15; Hebrews 5:13–14). A sapling and a great oak share the very same life; the oak is simply that life grown to its fullness. Maturity is not a different Christianity from the new convert’s, but the same Christ-life grown up and bearing fruit. And it is fixed in Christ, for to grow up is simply to become more like him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers reach sinless perfection. It means growth to maturity in Christ.

Is warning only the pastor’s job? No. Paul uses the same word when he tells the whole church to teach and admonish one another in all wisdom (3:16). Every believer is meant to speak the truth in love to others. But how you do it matters. Warn someone you actually love, in private first (Matthew 18:15), humbly, aware of your own weakness (Galatians 6:1), with the aim of their good and not your relief. Begin with Christ, not with a list of their faults. And be willing to be warned yourself. A church where no one ever lovingly says, I am worried about this, is not gentle; it is neglectful.

In a sentence. He is the one we proclaim, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whom are you helping to grow toward maturity in Christ? Warn and teach with wisdom and love. Name one younger believer, or a child in your home, and think of one way this week to help them know Christ better. And ask whether you are still growing yourself: what do you know of Christ now that you did not know a year ago?

For worship. Christ is enough to warn us from every danger, enough to teach us every wisdom, and enough to bring every one of his people to full stature on the last day. The Head who was crucified in weakness will stand at the end with a church grown up into his likeness, and every faithful sermon from Colossae until now will prove to have been one small part of how he did it. He is the beginning, the substance and the end of the message.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.

For this I toil. The shift from we proclaim (v. 28) to I toil lets the Colossians see what the goal costs Paul, a man writing from a prison cell (4:18) for churches he has never met. For this means for the goal just named, to present everyone mature in Christ. He does not toil for fame or comfort, nor merely to win converts and leave them as infants, but that God’s people grow up complete in Christ. “Toil” (kopiaō) means to labour to the point of exhaustion, the bone-weariness of a field hand at harvest.

Struggling. “Struggling” (agōnizomai) means contending, the word for the athlete straining every sinew in the games, from which we get agony. This is worth saying plainly, because some imagine the Christian life is meant to be a gentle, effortless drift. It is not. Following Christ, fighting sin, serving his people, holding fast under pressure: all of it calls for real, costly, wearying effort. Paul does not coast; he agonises.

With all his energy that he powerfully works within me. And yet look how the sentence ends. Paul strains every muscle, but the power he strains with is not his own. “Energy” (energeia) and “works” (energeō) are the same root, doubled for emphasis: God’s might, energising him from the inside. Paul works hard, and every bit of it is Christ’s power working in him. Here is the great balance the whole Bible keeps: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13). Maximum effort and total dependence held together in one breath: not fifty-fifty, but fully Paul’s striving and fully God’s working. Ministry is strenuous, but the strength is Christ’s (1 Corinthians 15:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did nothing. He toiled. It means his toil was powered by Christ.

Two ditches. You can tumble into either of two ditches. The first is the slogan let go and let God: relax, surrender, and wait for God to do everything, since any effort of your own is mere flesh. But Paul did not let go; he toiled to the point of agony, and Scripture never treats hard work as unspiritual. This ditch breeds passivity and a stalled, fruitless faith, and then blames God for the barrenness our own sloth produced. The second ditch is the opposite: it is all up to me. Gritting the teeth and white-knuckling the Christian life on sheer willpower breeds pride when it seems to work and despair and burnout when it does not. At bottom it is self-reliance in religious clothes.

Set the sails. The truth runs between them: work hard, and lean hard. Picture a sailing boat. The crew must do real, sweating work: hoist the sails, trim the lines, lean into the ropes, for a lazy crew goes nowhere. And yet not one inch of progress comes from their muscle alone. It is the wind that drives the boat home, and the wind fills only the sails that hands have laboured to set. So set the sails: pray, fight sin, feed on the word, serve the church, keep going. And let the wind of God’s own power carry you on. The sweat is real, and it is yours; the strength is real, and it is God’s.

I am exhausted. Does this verse mean I should work even harder? Not necessarily. Paul’s toil was aimed at one thing, Christ’s people growing mature, and powered by Christ’s strength, not by guilt or the fear of letting people down. If you are worn out, ask whether you are carrying things God never gave you, or carrying the right things in your own strength. The same Lord who works powerfully in his servants also gave the Sabbath rest and told his tired disciples to come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31). Rest is not a failure of devotion. Sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is sleep, and trust him to hold what you put down.

In a sentence. To this end Paul strenuously contends with all the energy Christ so powerfully works in him.

On a Tuesday. Pick the hardest piece of Christian obedience in front of you today: the conversation, the temptation, the act of service. Before you begin, ask Christ to work powerfully in you. Then work hard by his strength, and at the end of the day thank him for whatever was done, because it was his.

For worship. The risen Christ does not stand at a distance watching his servants strain. He works in them, with all his energy, powerfully. Every sermon faithfully preached, every prayer that struggles for a church, every tired act of love for his people is his own power moving through weak hands. The labour is ours; the might, and the glory, are his.

Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,<sup>6</sup>which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,<sup>7</sup>just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf<sup>8</sup>and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.<sup>9</sup>And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,<sup>10</sup>so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;<sup>11</sup>being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;<sup>12</sup>giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.<sup>13</sup>He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,<sup>14</sup>in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.<sup>15</sup>He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.<sup>16</sup>For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him.<sup>17</sup>And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.<sup>18</sup>And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.<sup>19</sup>For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,<sup>20</sup>and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.<sup>21</sup>And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,<sup>22</sup>he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,<sup>23</sup>if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.<sup>24</sup>Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,<sup>25</sup>of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known,<sup>26</sup>the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.<sup>27</sup>To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.<sup>28</sup>Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.<sup>29</sup>For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.

2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Now Paul names the danger. Teachers are offering the Colossians a “philosophy” that sounds wise: keep food laws and holy days, practise harsh self-denial, honour angels as mediators, and pursue visions. Its message is “Christ plus”. Paul answers in three steps. First, stay rooted in Christ, as you received him, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. Second, in him the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and you are filled in him. You have already been circumcised, buried and raised with him; God made you alive, forgave all your sins, cancelled the record of debt by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the spiritual powers, leading them in triumph.

Third, therefore let no one judge you over food or holy days, which were shadows of Christ, the substance. Let no one disqualify you with self-made severity, angel worship and visions: such people have let go of the Head, from whom the whole body grows. Rules like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch” look wise but have no power to stop the flesh. The cure for sin is not more rules but union with the risen Christ, which chapter 3 unfolds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul wants them to know how hard he is striving for them, for Laodicea and for others who have never met him, so that they may be encouraged, united in love, and rich in understanding of God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He says this so that no one deceives them with persuasive talk. Though absent, he rejoices at their good order and firm faith. As they received Christ Jesus as Lord, so they should go on living in him, rooted, built up, established in the faith and overflowing with thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 — “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — is the epistemological foundation of the Reformed tradition’s approach to all knowledge. Cornelius Van Til’s presuppositionalism, Abraham Kuyper’s sphere sovereignty, Francis Schaeffer’s integrated Christian worldview: all are ultimately grounded in this text. All genuine wisdom and knowledge find their coherence and source in Christ. This does not mean that only Christians can know things; it means that all knowledge that is genuinely true is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” participating (knowingly or not) in the structure of reality that Christ created and sustains. The Christian intellectual task is to follow wisdom wherever it leads, knowing that it leads ultimately to the one in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered esoteric wisdom that seemed to go beyond what the gospel provided. Paul says: all the wisdom you are seeking is already hidden in Christ. You are not lacking wisdom; you have not been exploring deeply enough the one in whom wisdom dwells. Now: The Christian who turns to secular philosophy, psychology, or spirituality for the wisdom that Christ supposedly cannot provide has accepted the false teachers’ premise. All genuine wisdom, wherever it is found, is a trace of the one in whom all wisdom is hidden. The Christian engages with every source of wisdom while recognizing that Christ is its ultimate source and criterion.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,

Meaning first. Colossians 2 confronts the false teaching directly, and answers it with Christ. First, Paul tells of his struggle in prayer that they may be united in love and know Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, so that no one deceives them and they keep walking in Christ as they received him (vv. 1–7). Second, he warns against philosophy and human tradition not according to Christ. In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and believers are filled in him: spiritually circumcised, buried and raised with him, made alive and forgiven, the record of debt nailed to the cross and the hostile powers paraded in defeat (vv. 8–15). Third, the conclusion: let no one judge them over food, festivals or Sabbaths, which were shadows of Christ; or disqualify them with angel worship and visions; or bind them with rules like do not handle, do not taste, do not touch, which look wise but have no power against the flesh (vv. 16–23). Christ is enough.

For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you. Here is the heart of a true pastor. Paul lets the Colossians see straight into his inner life, and what they find is a man labouring for them. “Struggle” (agōn) is the root of our word agony: the all-out exertion of the wrestler in the contest, the same root he used of his ministry in 1:29. But notice his circumstances. He writes in chains (4:18), unable to visit or preach to them. So how does a caged apostle struggle for a church he cannot reach? Chiefly on his knees. His agony is the unseen labour of intercession, wrestling prayer and sleepless concern, exactly as Epaphras was always struggling on their behalf in his prayers (4:12). Pastoral love is not a warm feeling at a distance. It is hard, costly, hidden work, aimed at a goal: that their hearts be encouraged and brought to full assurance of Christ (v. 2).

And for those at Laodicea. Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae, a wealthy banking and textile city, the church later rebuked as lukewarm (Revelation 3:14–22). Paul wrote them a letter too, and wanted the two churches to swap letters (4:16). The same danger threatened the whole valley.

And for all who have not seen me face to face. Including Hierapolis and other churches in the valley. Paul had never been to Colossae; Epaphras planted the church (1:7). He would not have known these people in the street, and yet he agonises for them. That is a shepherd after Christ’s own heart. His care is not rationed to friends, or to converts who can repay him, but reaches sheep in a valley he has never visited, simply because they belong to Christ. A hired hand cares only for what the flock does for him; the true shepherd cares for the flock itself (John 10:12–13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s concern was anxious worry. It was earnest prayer and labour. He cast his cares on God; he did not carry them as a weight of dread (Philippians 4:6–7).

How do I struggle in prayer for someone? It is not about straining to feel intense or praying for hours. It means praying with persistence and with purpose: coming back to the same people again and again, asking for the things that matter most (as Paul does in v. 2 and in 1:9–12), and refusing to give up when nothing seems to change. It may mean praying when you are tired, or setting aside time you would rather spend elsewhere. Struggling prayer is ordinary prayer that keeps going, because you care what happens to that person’s soul.

In a sentence. Paul wants you to know how hard he is contending for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met him personally.
