On a Tuesday. Struggle in prayer this week for a church you have never visited: a persecuted church, a struggling plant, a missionary’s congregation. Learn one name from it and pray for that person by name. And take quiet comfort: somewhere, perhaps, an unseen believer is wrestling in prayer for you.

For worship. The church is held up by hidden hands folded in prayer, and above them all by the pierced hands of the great Shepherd, who knows his sheep by name in every valley of the earth, and who prayed for us before we were born (John 17:20). His care for his flock is never rationed and never tires.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,

What Paul asks for. Verse 1 said Paul wrestles for these believers; verse 2 says what for. And notice what he does not ask. Not that they be wealthy, comfortable or successful, nor even that the church grow in numbers, but three deeper things: that their hearts be strengthened, that they be knit together in love, and that they reach a rich, settled assurance in the full knowledge of Christ.

That their hearts may be encouraged. “Encouraged” (parakaleō) means strengthened, comforted: not a pat on the back but to be braced, given courage to stand. And the heart, in the Bible, is the whole inner person. Why do they need it? Because the false teachers press in with plausible arguments (v. 4), and a frightened, wavering heart is easily swept away, while a heart made sturdy can stand in the storm. This is the strengthening the Spirit himself gives, for he is the Helper whom Jesus sent (John 14:16), whose very name comes from the same root.

Being knit together in love. “Knit together” (symbibazō) means joined, united, as the joints of a body are (v. 19): parts woven and compacted into one. The binding agent is love, poured into our hearts by the Spirit (Romans 5:5). Love unites the church against division by false teaching. There is wisdom in joining the two. The lone sheep is picked off; the flock knit together stands. Heresy isolates and flatters the few; love weaves the whole body into one. And love is the soil in which true understanding grows.

To reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding. “Full assurance” (plērophoria) is complete, settled confidence: faith brought all the way to certainty, not anxious or perpetually unsure. And it is assurance of understanding: not a leap in the dark but a confidence that rests on actually grasping the truth. Understanding that is certain and settled.

And the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ. The mystery is not a secret doctrine for initiates, but a person: Christ (1:26–27). To know him is to know God’s mystery. This is the deathblow to the heresy. The false teachers dangled knowledge, mystery and fullness as prizes to be won beyond Christ, and Paul answers that the mystery is Christ, and its riches are already in him. Some manuscripts vary at this point; the ESV reading is well supported.

What it does not mean. It does not mean understanding comes without love. Paul joins them: knit together in love, to reach understanding.

Is it proud to be sure I am saved? No. It would be proud to be sure because of your own goodness, but Christian assurance rests on Christ, not on you. God wants his children to be sure: John wrote so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). Here Paul prays for the riches of full assurance. Doubts come to many believers, and they are not proof that you are not his. But the remedy for them is to know Christ better: his promises, his finished work, his faithfulness. The more clearly you see him, the surer you will be.

In a sentence. Paul’s goal is that they may be encouraged in heart and united in love, so that they may have the full riches of complete understanding, in order that they may know the mystery of God, namely, Christ,

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church to be knit together in love and confident in Christ. Then do something that knits: seek out the person on the edge, mend a cold relationship, or share with another believer something you have come to understand about Christ.

For worship. The Father does not want his children living on maybes. He wants them rich in the settled, glad certainty of knowing his Son, and he has made the Son knowable: born in a village, raised in a carpenter’s house, crucified in public, risen before witnesses. The things angels long to look into (1 Peter 1:12) have been opened to the humblest believer, and the longer a heart looks at Christ, the surer it becomes (2 Timothy 1:12).

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. In whom reaches back to the last words of v. 2: the mystery, which is Christ. Treasures are the precious things people dig and dive and travel the world to find. Wisdom and knowledge between them cover the whole range of what the heart longs to grasp: knowledge, the understanding of God and reality; wisdom, the skill of living rightly in its light. And all of them are stored up in Christ. “Hidden” (apokryphos) does not mean locked away from God’s people, inaccessible, but treasured up, stored away and kept safe, the way gold is kept in a vault, to be found by those who seek him. Christ is the strongroom in which God has stored everything worth knowing.

The sharp edge. There is an edge here, aimed at the false teachers. They peddled hidden wisdom: secret knowledge for the initiated few, reached by climbing past Christ into angel speculation and mystical experience. Paul takes their prized word and turns it back. The truly hidden treasures, all of them, are hidden in Christ, not in any system of theirs. So there is no wisdom worth having outside Christ, and no lack of it inside him. The Christian does not graduate from Christ to something higher; he goes ever deeper into Christ, who is himself the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30).

Two freeing things. First, you need not look anywhere else. You may quietly fear that the real riches belong to scholars and mystics, that you are a second-class believer outside the vault while cleverer people enjoy the gold. Not so. All the treasure is in Christ, and you have Christ; you already hold the key, and need only go further into the Saviour you already know. Second, the treasure has no bottom. A whole lifetime of knowing Jesus will not exhaust the riches stored in him.

The deed to the mine. Imagine a working man who spends years chasing rumours of treasure and signing up for one scheme after another, and then a lawyer tells him the deed to the richest mine in the country was made out in his name long ago. He already owns it; all his searching elsewhere was wasted effort; and the mine runs so deep that a thousand lifetimes could never empty it. That is you and Christ (Matthew 13:44).

What it does not mean. It does not mean other learning is worthless. All true knowledge belongs to Christ, and leads back to him.

Does this mean non-Christians can know nothing true? No. By God’s common grace unbelievers discover a great deal that is true, and Christians may learn from them. Paul is speaking of the wisdom that saves and makes sense of everything, which is found only in Christ. The doctor who sets your broken arm may not believe, and his skill is still real and a gift of God. But only in Christ do you learn who made the arm, why you are here, and how a sinner can stand before God.

In a sentence. in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

On a Tuesday. When you seek wisdom for a decision today, seek it in Christ and his word first. And if you have been feeling like a second-class Christian beside people who know more, open the Gospels and spend time with Christ himself. The treasure is not in knowing about the experts; it is in knowing him.

For worship. God did not scatter his wisdom across the universe in fragments for the clever to collect. He stored it all in his Son, and then opened the vault to fishermen and tax collectors. The treasure-house of heaven walked dusty roads and was hung on a cross as a fool, and in that foolishness of God the whole wisdom of God shone out, wiser than all the sages of the world (1 Corinthians 1:25). Every treasure worth having is in Christ, and Christ has given himself to us.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.

I say this in order that no one may delude you. With these words Paul reveals why he has pressed Christ’s all-sufficiency so hard: a danger is circling, and here he first names it plainly. Behind it lay what is often called the Colossian heresy: a mixture of Jewish rule-keeping (food laws, festivals, circumcision), harsh self-denial, the veneration of angels, and claims to secret knowledge. Its method was not to deny Christ outright but to add to him: Christ plus these rules, plus these mediators, plus this deeper experience. “Delude” (paralogizomai) means to deceive by false reasoning, to talk someone out of the truth the way a swindler reasons a man out of his money.

With plausible arguments. “Plausible arguments” (pithanologia) is persuasive speech, fine-sounding words. That is the whole peril. False teaching often sounds attractive and convincing; the error does not arrive looking obviously false. It comes dressed as wisdom (v. 23), sounding sophisticated and convincing. The pitch ran something like this: faith in Christ is a fine beginning, but for real fullness you must also keep these days, deny the body, honour these powers, reach this higher knowledge.

The little word plus. The packaging changes; the pattern never does. Today the same voice says: Jesus is essential, of course, but you also need this experience, this teacher’s system, these rules, to be truly filled. The tell is always the little word plus: Christ is not quite enough; add something. Paul’s guard is simple. The defence is to know Christ fully. Remember that all the treasures are already in Christ (v. 3), and you will not be talked out of him (2 Corinthians 11:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean persuasion or argument is wrong. It means arguments must be tested by Christ. Paul himself reasoned and persuaded (Acts 17:2–4; 18:4). The question is not whether an argument is clever, but whether it leads to Christ or away from him.

What if I cannot answer an argument against my faith? You do not have to win every debate to be right. Many false teachings sound convincing because their teachers are skilled speakers, not because they are true. If you meet an argument you cannot answer, do not panic and do not pretend. Say honestly that you will think about it, then take it to Scripture and to a wise believer or a good book. Christians have faced most arguments before. Meanwhile hold on to what you know: Christ died, Christ rose, and his word has not failed you. A question you cannot yet answer is not a reason to let go of him.

In a sentence. Paul tells you this so that no one may deceive you by fine-sounding arguments.

On a Tuesday. When you next hear a teaching, a podcast or a book that excites you, ask one question: does this add something to Christ that he has not already given? If it says Christ plus, it is offering you less.

For worship. Error comes in polished words; the truth came in person. The Son of God did not win the world by clever reasoning but by laying down his life, and he who is the truth (John 14:6) is also the Shepherd whose sheep know his voice and will not follow a stranger’s (John 10:4–5). No argument, however fine, can outshine the One in whom all the treasures are stored, and he does not let go of those he has bought.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.

For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit. Paul writes from a prison cell, to a church he has never visited, and says he is with them in spirit: present in thought, prayer and care (1 Corinthians 5:3). This is no mystical projection but the warm language of love that leaps over distance. His heart, his thoughts and his prayers are genuinely with them. Beneath the affection lies a deeper truth: believers are bound together in Christ by one Spirit, and miles cannot sever that bond.

Rejoicing. Here is a man in chains, cut off from freedom and comfort, and the word that falls from his pen is rejoicing. Over what? Not his release or better conditions, but the spiritual health of a congregation he has never seen. Their faith was his joy. That lays bare a true shepherd’s heart: his deepest gladness lies not in his own circumstances but in the wellbeing of God’s people. John says he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth (3 John 4), and Paul says elsewhere that he lives if his converts stand fast in the Lord (1 Thessalonians 3:8).

To see your good order. “Good order” (taxis) is a military term: soldiers drawn up in disciplined ranks. The church was still holding the line.

And the firmness of your faith in Christ. “Firmness” (stereōma) is the solidity of a battle line that holds, a solid front, a fortress wall that does not give way. Picture an army standing in perfect order, ranks unbroken, holding firm against the assault. The church is under attack from the plausible arguments of v. 4, yet their line holds. They had not yet broken ranks, and Paul writes to strengthen them before trouble spreads. This is why he commends them warmly before he warns them more sharply. And mark where the firmness comes from: your faith in Christ. Their solidity is not self-manufactured grit but rests on its object, a line that holds because the One it leans on cannot be moved (1 Corinthians 15:58; 16:13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church was in no danger. It means the danger had not yet overcome them.

Why does Paul praise them before warning them? Because that is how love corrects. He is not flattering them to soften the blow; he is telling the truth about what God has done in them, and the truth is good. A church that hears only warnings grows discouraged; a church that hears only praise grows careless. Paul gives both, in that order, so that they will hear the warning as coming from a friend who is on their side. When you need to correct a fellow believer, a child or a colleague, begin by honestly naming the good you see.

In a sentence. For though Paul is absent from you in body, he is present with you in spirit and delights to see how disciplined you are and how firm your faith in Christ is.

On a Tuesday. Hold your place in the ranks. Stand firm in Christ with your church. The soldier who drifts away from the line is the one the enemy picks off; be at the gathering, keep close to your brothers and sisters, and let them see that you are standing.

For worship. The fellowship of the saints is not broken by distance, or by prison walls, or even by death. One Spirit binds the whole body to its risen Head, who walks among his churches (Revelation 2:1) and sees their order and their faith more clearly than any apostle. What made Paul rejoice in a cell is seen and treasured by Christ on the throne, and one day his whole army will be gathered in one place, not to fight but to feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.

Therefore. This is the hinge of the whole letter, gathering everything Paul has said and turning it into a command. Because Christ is supreme and all-sufficient, because in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom, because you received him and your faith stands firm: therefore, here is what to do. Doctrine becomes duty. What is true of Christ grounds how you now live.

As you received Christ Jesus the Lord. “Received” (paralambanō) is the word for receiving a tradition handed down. And what they received was not just teaching about Christ but Christ himself, as Lord: received as Master, not an optional extra bolted onto the old life.

So walk in him. Walk is the Bible’s word for the whole daily conduct of life. So the point is searching: the way you began is the way you go on. You came to Christ with empty hands, resting on him alone, receiving him by grace; so keep walking the very same way. The Christian life is lived the same way it starts: by faith in Christ. No new method is needed. This is the deathblow to the heresy. The Christian life is not receive Christ to get started, then graduate to higher teachings. You do not move on from him; you go on in him. Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? (Galatians 3:3). However far you travel, you never leave the door you came in by: simple trust in Jesus.

Rooted and built up in him. Two pictures, and yes, Paul is mixing his metaphors cheerfully, as was normal in his world (Ephesians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 3:9). Rooted is from the garden: a tree sunk deep into the soil. Built up is from the building site: a house rising on its foundation. Even the tenses differ. Rooted (errizōmenoi) is a perfect: firmly planted once and for all. Built up (epoikodomoumenoi) is a present: continually, day by day. Think of a great oak whose roots drive deep into rich soil, drawing all its life from that ground and standing unmoved through every gale: that is the believer rooted in Christ. And think of a house going up on bedrock, brick upon brick: that is the believer built up in Christ, founded on him and steadily growing. Anchored and rising, settled and growing.

And established in the faith, just as you were taught. “Established” (bebaioumenoi) means confirmed, made firm. In the faith as Epaphras taught it (1:7). The false teachers were doing the opposite, pulling them away from the original gospel toward something newer and supposedly deeper. The mark of truth is not novelty but faithfulness to what the apostles handed down. When a teaching promises more than the plain gospel of Christ you were first taught, that is precisely the moment to be on guard (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 1:13–14).

Abounding in thanksgiving. Overflowing, brimming over: no thin trickle but a flood. And it is no afterthought. A heart overflowing with thanks for all it already has in Christ has no appetite for the false teacher’s offer of something more. Ingratitude is the crack through which discontent creeps in, and discontent is exactly the foothold the heretic needs; gratitude bolts the door. But how fast we forget. Israel was fed with bread from heaven every morning and spent the journey murmuring, and we do the same, sitting on a mountain of grace while muttering about the weather and the bills.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers do not grow. They are continually built up. But always in Christ, not beyond him.

How do I go deeper without going beyond Christ? By going further into the same things, not into new things. Read the Gospels again and again and get to know him. Learn what his death and resurrection accomplished, and what union with him means. Keep the means of grace he has given: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of his people. Obey him in the next thing he asks, because obedience opens understanding. Deep Christians are not people who found a secret; they are people who kept looking at Christ for a long time.

In a sentence. So then, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, rooted and built up in him, strengthened in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.

On a Tuesday. Thanksgiving must be cultivated, deliberately, against the grain of a forgetful heart. Stop, count the mercies, and name them: a Saviour, sins forgiven, Christ living within you, the sure hope of glory, until the grumble shrinks. You will find it nearly impossible to grumble and give thanks in the same breath, so fill your mouth with the better of the two (1 Thessalonians 5:18; Colossians 3:15–17).

For worship. The Christ we received with empty hands at the beginning is the Christ who carries us to the end. We did not take hold of a doctrine but of a Lord, and he has not changed since the day we first trusted him: the same welcome, the same patience, the same finished work. Every step of the long walk is taken in the Saviour who met us at the door, and he never runs dry and never gives way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to be captured by empty, deceptive philosophy rooted in human tradition and the world’s basic principles rather than in Christ. The whole fullness of God lives in Christ bodily, and believers are complete in him, who is head over every power. In him they have received a circumcision not done by hands, the stripping away of the old nature, and in baptism they were buried with him and raised with him through faith in God’s power. God made them alive with Christ, forgave all their sins, cancelled the record of debt that stood against them by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the hostile powers, exposing them publicly and triumphing over them in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.

See to it that no one takes you captive. In v. 4 Paul warned that someone might delude them; now he sounds the alarm and points at the enemy. See to it is a sharp watchman’s cry: beware! “Takes captive” (sylagōgeō) means to carry someone off as booty, to kidnap: the picture of a slave raider dragging away prisoners in chains. False teachers are spiritual kidnappers. And here is the thing worth pondering. If a man tried to seize you physically and march you off in irons, everyone would see it and you would fight. But when the kidnapping happens in the realm of ideas, when a teaching quietly carries off a person’s mind into bondage, almost no one notices, least of all the captive. He does not feel like a prisoner. He feels enlightened, thinks he is going deeper, being let in on something grand, while in truth he is being led away in chains. Spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress, which is exactly why Paul shouts rather than whispers.

By philosophy and empty deceit. “Philosophy” (philosophia) means love of wisdom. Here it is not philosophy in general, or all careful thinking (Paul reasoned with the philosophers at Athens), but this particular religious philosophy, which Paul calls empty deceit. In Greek it is one phrase: philosophy that is empty deceit. That is the true verdict on it: it promises fullness and delivers a void, and it does not merely fail but misleads. Mark the irony. It leaves a man empty, while in Christ you have been filled (v. 10).

According to human tradition. Its source is human, not divine. Trace its pedigree and it comes from men, not God, exactly what Jesus charged the Pharisees with: leaving the commandment of God to hold to the tradition of men (Mark 7:8).

According to the elemental spirits of the world. “Elemental spirits” (stoicheia) may mean the basic principles of religion, the ABCs, or the spirit powers thought to control the world, perhaps through the calendar and the stars, which people felt they must appease, as in Galatians 4:3, 9. The false teaching was earthbound, either elementary rules or dealings with spiritual powers. To crawl back under them is to return to the slavery Christ broke.

And not according to Christ. The decisive test: is it according to Christ? These four words are the hinge, exposing the fatal flaw in all the rest. The teaching is according to philosophy, according to tradition, according to the elemental spirits, but not according to Christ, who is the measuring rod against which every idea is laid. And this is wonderfully freeing. You do not need to become an expert in every cult and master every false system to be safe. You need to know one thing surpassingly well: Christ.

Where Christians differ: should Christians study philosophy? Some take this verse to forbid all philosophy. Verdict: Paul condemns philosophy that is empty deceit, rooted in human tradition and not according to Christ. Christians may study philosophy, and many great Christian thinkers have, but must bring every thought captive to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5) and judge all systems by Scripture. Philosophy is a good servant and a bad master.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be anti-intellectual. Christ contains all treasures of wisdom (v. 3). Paul himself reasoned with philosophers (Acts 17:18–31), and Christians may and should study every field of learning, testing all of it by Christ and his word.

The bank teller. A bank teller learns to spot forged notes not by memorising every counterfeit ever printed, but by handling the genuine note so constantly that anything false feels wrong the instant it touches his hand. So with you. Know Christ deeply, his supremacy, his sufficiency, his finished work, and when a teaching diminishes him, adds to him or sidelines him, you will feel the wrongness of it at once, however clever it sounds. The question is never merely whether an argument is hard to answer, but whether it is according to Christ (1 John 4:1; Galatians 1:8).

What does captivity to human philosophy look like today? Rarely a robed philosopher. More often it is the quiet assumptions of the age, absorbed without noticing: that you are what you feel, that truth is whatever works for you, that the physical world is all there is, that God exists to make you happy, that freedom means having no master. Some come from outside the church, some from inside it, dressed in Christian words. You do not need to be afraid of every idea. Ask of each: what does this say about Christ, about sin, about how a person is made right with God? If the answer pushes Christ to the edge, it is not according to Christ.

In a sentence. See to it that no one takes you captive through hollow and deceptive philosophy, which depends on human tradition and the elemental spiritual forces of this world rather than on Christ.

On a Tuesday. Test the ideas you meet today, in books, news and conversation: are they according to Christ? Pick one message you heard this week, from an advertisement, a show or a sermon, and lay it against Christ. Does it make him bigger or smaller?

For worship. Christ is not one voice among many in the marketplace of ideas. He is the truth by which every voice is measured, the wisdom of God in person, and the deliverer who breaks every chain that ideas can forge. To be held captive by him is the only true freedom.
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,

For in him the whole fullness of deity. For tells us this verse is the reason behind the warning of v. 8. Why must the Colossians refuse capture and cling to Christ? Because in him dwells the whole fullness of deity. That is the deathblow to every Christ-plus scheme: there is nothing to add to Christ, because all of God is already in him. And mark the stress: in him, in Christ and nowhere else, not in the angels, not in the powers, not in the impressive philosophy. The whole fullness (pan to plērōma): all of it, nothing left over, nothing residing elsewhere. “Deity” (theotēs) is the strongest word available: Godhead, the divine nature itself, not just divine qualities. Christ is not a creature filled with divine attributes but the One in whom the complete divine nature resides. The whole of it, not a portion.

Dwells bodily. “Dwells” (katoikeō) is present tense: continues to dwell, permanently, to take up residence, God at home in Christ, even now in his exalted state. And the crowning word: “bodily” (sōmatikōs), in a human body. The incarnate Christ, now risen, is fully God in human flesh. This is the incarnation at full stretch: the infinite fullness of God dwelling in the man Christ Jesus, flesh and all. All of God, in a body you could have stood beside. It is the strongest statement in Scripture of the full deity of the incarnate Christ.

Three blows against the error. This is the foundation of Paul’s whole case, and it strikes the false teachers from several sides. Against their angels and elemental spirits: if all the fullness of deity is in Christ, those powers have no fullness to offer, so why seek lesser mediators? Against their scattered fullness, pictured as spread thin across a chain of beings: Paul says it is concentrated, entire and undivided, in Christ alone. And against their contempt for the body: that one word bodily rebukes every teaching that seeks God by escaping the physical, for God himself dwells bodily in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the divine nature was turned into flesh. It means the eternal Son, fully God, took human nature, so that God dwells fully in the man Christ Jesus.

Is Jesus still a man now, in heaven? Yes. The Son did not take a body for thirty-three years and then lay it aside. He rose bodily, ascended bodily, and dwells (present tense) bodily, and he will return in the same way he went (Acts 1:11). That means there is a human being at the Father’s right hand who knows what it is to be tired, tempted, grieved and in pain (Hebrews 4:15). The God you pray to has a human face and human scars. He is not distant from what you are going through; he wears your nature still.

In a sentence. For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form,

On a Tuesday. When God feels distant or abstract, remember where he has chosen to be known: in a man. Read a Gospel story today and say to yourself as you read: this is God.

For worship. In Christ we do not hold a fragment of God or a junior deputy. The hands that uphold the universe once held a carpenter’s tools; the eyes that see every heart once grew heavy with sleep in a boat on Galilee. Nothing of God is missing from him, and nothing of our humanity was too lowly for him to take. Fully God, truly man, and given to us, now and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.

And you have been filled in him. The little word and carries us straight from Christ to ourselves. Verse 9 said the whole fullness of deity dwells in him, and verse 10 draws the staggering inference: and you have been filled in him. Paul builds the word link deliberately. The fullness (plērōma) dwells in Christ, and you have been filled (peplērōmenoi) in Christ: the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members. Since God’s fullness is in Christ, and believers are in Christ, they lack nothing.

Three things in four words. The tense is a Greek perfect: a completed action with lasting results. Not that you are slowly being filled or might one day be, but that you have been brought to fullness, and remain so. It is passive: God filled you; you did not fill yourself. And it is in him: yours not by your own attainment but by union with Christ. Here is the hammer blow to the heresy, which told the Colossians they were lacking and needed more rituals and experiences to reach fullness. Paul says: you are already complete in Christ. How can anyone add to fullness?

Who is the head of all rule and authority. Christ rules over all spiritual powers: he is the source and sovereign over the very rulers and authorities the false teachers urged the church to revere. Paul has said Christ created them (1:16), and he will say Christ disarmed them at the cross (2:15); here he is their head. So the beings the Colossians were tempted to fear and flatter are themselves his subjects. Why seek help from angels or spirits, when you are joined to their Lord?

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have nothing more to grow into. They grow in experiencing what they already have. Nor does it mean you are sinlessly perfect or that you personally possess deity. It means you lack nothing for salvation, nothing for access to God, nothing for true completeness: it is all yours in Christ.

If I am complete, why do I feel so incomplete? Because there is a difference between what you have and what you have yet to enjoy. A man with a fortune in his account who frets that he is poor does not need to earn more; he needs to wake up to what is already his. Your sense of lack is real, and some of it is the right longing for the glory still to come (Romans 8:23). But do not let it become a reason to chase extras. The answer to feeling incomplete is not a new experience or technique but a deeper grasp of what you already have in Christ, and a patient trust that he will finish what he started.

In a sentence. and in Christ you have been brought to fullness. He is the head over every power and authority.

On a Tuesday. You are complete in Christ. Stop looking for something extra to make you whole. And if you carry a vague dread of fate, of dark forces, of whatever pulls the strings behind life, say it plainly: the One I belong to is the head over every power that exists.

For worship. Not one power in the universe outranks your Lord. There is nothing left to fear and nothing left to add (Ephesians 1:21–22; Romans 8:38–39). The fullness of God dwells in Christ, and we are filled in him: the overflow of his life is our life, and it will never run dry.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.

In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands. The false teachers were evidently pressing the old physical rite of circumcision, and Paul cuts the ground away. In Christ you have already received the true circumcision, spiritual circumcision: the cutting away of the sinful nature, which the Old Testament promised. Even in the Old Testament the real thing was circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Romans 2:28–29). It is not done by human hands with a knife, but by God. So the Colossians need no physical circumcision.

By putting off the body of the flesh. What is cut away is not a scrap of flesh but the body of the flesh: the whole old sinful self, stripped off like a garment (3:9). That does not mean a believer no longer feels sinful desires. It means the person you were in Adam, ruled by sin, died with Christ, so sin is no longer your master, even when it still tempts you (Romans 6:6–7).

By the circumcision of Christ. Either the circumcision Christ performs, or Christ’s own circumcision, his death, in which his body was cut off and in which the believer shares. Either way, union with Christ achieves what circumcision pointed to. At the cross the old self was decisively cut away, and no human knife can add anything to it.

Having been buried with him in baptism. Paul sets baptism beside circumcision as a sign of the same reality. Baptism signifies union with Christ in his death and burial (Romans 6:3–4). To go down into the water is to be buried with him: going under the water pictures burial. The old life is not merely improved but put in the grave alongside Christ’s buried body.

In which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God. And rising pictures resurrection with Christ. Baptism does not stop at the grave. As the believer comes up out of the water, it portrays the next thing: raised with him. Union with Christ is union with his resurrection as well as his death, the old self buried, a new self raised to new life; this is the ground of 3:1, if then you have been raised with Christ. And mark how it happens: through faith. The union is received by faith in God’s power that raised Jesus. It is not the water that raises anyone, not the ritual working by itself, but the mighty power of God laid hold of by faith. Faith is the empty hand that receives; God’s power actually raises.

Who raised him from the dead. The same power raises believers to new life. Paul says God raised Jesus; elsewhere the Spirit raised him (Romans 8:11), and the Son says he has authority to take up his life again (John 10:18). This is no muddle but a window into the Trinity: the resurrection is the one, undivided act of the one God who is Father, Son and Spirit. And here is the comfort folded in. The greatest display of power in history, the full might of the triune God raising Jesus, is the very power that raised you with him and is at work in you now (Ephesians 1:19–20).

Why all this, in the middle of a warning? The false teachers were saying: you need more; be circumcised, keep our rules, climb higher. Paul’s reply is to show what has already happened to you in Christ. You have received the true circumcision, the old self cut away by God. You have died and been buried with Christ, that chapter closed. You have been raised with him by the same power that raised Jesus from the grave. What, then, could anyone add? You cannot improve on death and resurrection.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Paedobaptists argue from this verse that baptism is the new covenant sign replacing circumcision, and so, as circumcision was given to infants, baptism should be too. Verdict: The circumcision Paul links with baptism is the spiritual circumcision of the heart made without hands, and the raising happens “through faith.” What replaces physical circumcision is regeneration, and baptism signifies that inward reality, which is received by faith. So the sign belongs to those who show the reality: believers. The app holds believer’s baptism, while warmly respecting paedobaptist brothers and sisters who read the covenant signs differently.

The paedobaptist case, fairly put. Those arguments are serious and deserve a fair hearing. Paedobaptist Christians, with the Westminster Confession, point out that circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham’s infant sons, that Paul here links the two signs directly, and that the promise is to you and to your children (Acts 2:39). Many godly and learned believers hold this view. But Paul does not say that baptism replaces circumcision. He says Christ’s inward circumcision is what circumcision pointed to, and baptism is the sign of that, received through faith. The 1689 London Baptist Confession therefore says that those who actually profess repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus are the only proper subjects of this ordinance (29.2).

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians hold that God gives new birth through baptism. Verdict: Paul ties the raising to faith, not to the water. Baptism is more than a picture; it is God’s appointed sign of union with Christ, and a public confession of it. But it does not work apart from faith. And the picture of burial and rising fits immersion most naturally, though Christians who pour or sprinkle see the washing as the main image.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism itself saves. It signifies union with Christ, received by faith.

I trust Christ but have never been baptised. Should I be? Yes. Baptism is Christ’s own command to his disciples (Matthew 28:19), and in the New Testament those who believed were baptised, usually very soon (Acts 2:41; 8:36–38; 16:33). It does not make you a Christian, but it is the way Christ has given for you to confess publicly that you are joined to him in his death and resurrection. If you are unsure or afraid, talk to the pastor or elders of your church. And if you were baptised as an infant and now trust Christ, ask them to help you think it through from Scripture, with patience and charity toward the church that baptised you.

In a sentence. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not performed by human hands. Your whole self ruled by the flesh was put off when you were circumcised by Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through your faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

On a Tuesday. You are not half-finished or second-rate; you have been through the grave and out the other side in Christ. When an old sin pulls at you today, say: that person was buried with Christ. Then live as the raised person you already are (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 3:1–4).

For worship. When we trusted Christ we were so totally joined to him that everything he did became ours: his death our death, his burial our burial, his resurrection our resurrection. The power that rolled the stone away has raised us too. The rites the false teachers peddled are only shadows of a reality we already possess in full, and it is all the work of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.

And you, who were dead in your trespasses. Paul does not say we were sick or struggling; he says we were dead. Spiritually dead: spiritual corpses, unable to respond to God, unable to raise ourselves or contribute one thing to our own rescue (Ephesians 2:1, 5). And he names what killed us: trespasses, the very thing we lay dead in.

And the uncircumcision of your flesh. The second layer of the ruin. The Colossians were Gentiles, outside God’s covenant people; and deeper still, the phrase pictures the unrenewed heart with nothing yet cut away. We were doubly lost: dead in guilt, shut out as strangers.

God made alive together with him. One word in Greek, synezōopoieō: resurrection language. God did for us exactly what he did for Christ in the tomb. This is regeneration: God gave new life, in union with the risen Christ. The dead cannot make themselves alive. Notice what it does not mean. Not that we were partly alive and God topped us up; the dead do not help raise themselves. Not self-improvement or turning over a new leaf: you do not improve a corpse, you raise it. And not that we earned it by a decision, for God made us alive even when we were dead (Ephesians 2:5). This is grace at its purest: not God helping those who help themselves, but God giving life to those who had none.

Having forgiven us all our trespasses. “Forgiven” (charizomai) is built on the word for grace: forgiven freely, graciously. Notice that Paul shifts from you to us; he includes himself. And then comes the word to stop the heart: all. Not some, not the small ones, not only the sins up to the day you believed. All: past, present and future; great and small; the ones you remember and the thousand you have forgotten; the secret ones no one knows, and the scarlet ones that make you wince in the dark. God did not pardon most and keep a private reserve of charges. There is no sin of yours lying outside this word: not the one that haunts you at three in the morning, not the one you have never confessed to a living soul, not the besetting sin you keep stumbling back into. And it is no cheap amnesty, no looking away. It is possible only because Christ bore every one of those sins himself (Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19).

By canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. The record of debt is one Greek word, cheirographon: a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor himself, an IOU. Picture a ledger of all we owe God, every command broken, an itemised account with its legal demands standing in writing against us. That signed bond of guilt, our debt to God’s law, was the thing that condemned us, and the figures were beyond all paying. And God cancelled it. The word (exaleiphō) means to wipe out, as writing was washed off papyrus: not deferred or reduced but erased, as though the debt had never been written (Isaiah 43:25).

This he set aside, nailing it to the cross. When the Romans crucified a man, they nailed his charge above his head; over Jesus it read, King of the Jews (John 19:19). But Paul says it was our certificate of debt that was nailed up at Calvary. And press the question the picture raises: it was Jesus who was nailed there, so how was our record nailed with him? Because our debt was laid on him. The charge against us was paid in full by his death. This is penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty that we deserved, in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13).

What was nailed to the cross: the law, or our debt? Some take it as the law of Moses itself, which condemned. The more likely reading is that it is the record of our debt, our signed guilt before God’s law, which Christ cancelled by paying it. Either way, the law can no longer condemn those in Christ. That does not abolish God’s moral will: the ceremonial law is fulfilled, but love still keeps the commandments (Romans 13:8–10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God ignored the debt. It was paid by Christ.

If all my sins are forgiven, why must I still confess them? Because forgiveness has two sides. As our Judge, God has forgiven us once for all; there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). As our Father, he still wants us to confess the sins that spoil our fellowship with him, and Jesus teaches us to pray daily, forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:12; 1 John 1:9). We confess not to stay saved, but because we are his children. A son who has broken his father’s window is not disowned, but he does not pretend nothing happened either.

In a sentence. When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having cancelled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross.

On a Tuesday. Your debt is cancelled. When guilt accuses you today, point to the cross. Name the sin that haunts you most, and say over it: forgiven, all of it, nailed to the cross. Then go and forgive someone who owes you far less.

For worship. The document of our guilt did not drift to the cross on its own. It was fastened there in the flesh of the Son of God, who took our debt as his own and carried it into death. When the nails were driven through his hands, the bond that stood against us was driven through with them. He took the charge sheet that had your name on it down into the grave, and it never came back out. The debt is not outstanding somewhere, waiting to resurface. It is buried in the tomb of Jesus, and the empty tomb is the receipt stamped paid in full.
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.

Who the rulers and authorities are. They are not human kings but the spiritual powers: the fallen angelic and demonic beings, the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12). These are the same powers Christ created (1:16) and rules as their head (2:10), and, crucially for Colossae, the very powers the false teachers were urging the church to fear and appease (2:18). They are real, personal, malevolent beings, and they held humanity in a threefold grip: as the powers behind our sin, as accusers wielding the law’s condemnation against us (the record of debt of v. 14), and through the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15). The Colossians lived under their shadow, and Paul announces that the shadow has been broken.

He disarmed the rulers and authorities. “Disarmed” (apekdyomai) means stripped, as defeated soldiers were stripped of weapons and armour. And what was the powers’ great weapon? Not brute force, but our sin and its just condemnation. The devil is the accuser of our brothers (Revelation 12:10); his whole case rested on the unpaid debt of our guilt. Now see how this verse is welded to the last. In v. 14 God cancelled the debt and nailed it to the cross; in v. 15 he disarms the powers, because the debt was their weapon. Once the record of guilt is wiped out and sin is fully paid, the accuser has nothing left to accuse with, the jailer has lost his keys, death has lost its sting. The spiritual powers of evil lost their power to accuse and enslave.

And put them to open shame. Made a public spectacle of them, before the whole watching unseen world of angels and powers, and through the gospel and the church wider still (Ephesians 3:10). And here is the deep irony. At Calvary it looked as though the powers had won, for they crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). But in that very act they were undone. Their apparent triumph was their defeat.

By triumphing over them in him. “Triumphing” (thriambeuō) is the technical word for a Roman triumph. A Roman general celebrated victory by parading through the city in his chariot, his conquered enemy kings dragged in chains behind him, stripped and displayed to the jeering crowds. Paul casts Christ as that triumphant General and the rulers and authorities as the captive kings shuffling behind his chariot. At the cross, Christ led the defeated powers in his victory parade. What looked like Christ’s defeat was his triumph, and the very instrument of death became the chariot of victory. In him may also be translated in it, the cross.

The knockout blow. This is the climax of the whole argument. The false teachers told the Colossians they had to fear and appease these powers to be safe. Paul’s answer is devastating: the cross did not only forgive your sins (v. 14); it defeated the very powers you are being told to dread. Why bow to, or bargain with, or tremble before an enemy your own Lord has already conquered and led in chains?

What it does not mean. It does not mean evil powers no longer exist or act. They are defeated but not yet destroyed; their final end comes at Christ’s return (Revelation 20:10).

If Satan is defeated, why does he still seem so active? Because he is defeated but not yet removed, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and still fights on in the hills. He still tempts, deceives and accuses, and the New Testament tells believers to be watchful and to resist him (1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11). But he cannot condemn you, because your debt is paid; he cannot own you, because you belong to Christ; and he cannot win, because his end is fixed. Think of a fierce guard dog on a short chain: it still barks and lunges and frightens the timid, but it is bound and cannot drag down the one who belongs to its Master. Stand in Christ’s victory, and the devil will flee from you (James 4:7).

In a sentence. And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.

On a Tuesday. You may not fear principalities by that name, but you may have your own dread of the unseen: of evil, of the devil, of dark forces working against you. You are not called to fear the spiritual world or to buy it off with charms, rituals or anxious precautions. You are called to stand in the finished victory of Christ. When fear comes, name it before God, and thank him that the enemy is beaten.

For worship. The powers that frighten us are defeated foes. The Son of God went into the enemy’s stronghold, let them do their worst, and turned their weapon into his chariot. The crown of thorns was the beginning of their humiliation and the empty tomb was the parade. He who was hung up naked before the crowds has stripped the principalities bare before heaven, and he will finish what he began when the serpent’s head is crushed for good (Genesis 3:15).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So no one should judge them over food and drink, festivals, new moons or sabbaths; these were shadows of what was to come, and the reality is Christ. They must not let anyone disqualify them who insists on self-abasement, the worship of angels and claims of visions, puffed up by an unspiritual mind and not holding on to Christ the head, from whom the whole body grows. Since they died with Christ to the world’s basic principles, why submit to rules like “do not handle, do not taste”? Such regulations, based on human teaching, look wise with their strict religion and harsh treatment of the body, but they are powerless to restrain the flesh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you. Therefore draws the conclusion from everything before it. Because you have been filled in Christ (v. 10), because the record of debt was cancelled and nailed to the cross (v. 14), because the powers have been disarmed (v. 15): therefore do not let anyone drag you back under a system of religious rules. Because of Christ’s complete work, believers are free. Do not let anyone condemn you or set conditions. The false teachers were passing judgment: condemning the Colossians for not keeping their rules, making them feel second-class, disqualified. Paul forbids it flatly. Your standing is in Christ, not in menus and calendars.

In questions of food and drink. The food laws of Moses, rules about clean and unclean food, and perhaps ascetic rules besides (v. 21).

Or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. The three kinds of holy days in Israel’s calendar: annual festivals, monthly new moons, weekly Sabbaths (1 Chronicles 23:31; Hosea 2:11). All three are included. And there is a reason these things can no longer be made binding, which Paul gives next: they were a shadow of the things to come (v. 17), signposts pointing forward to Christ. The rest the Sabbath pictured is found in him (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the feasts are fulfilled at his cross. To make them a condition of acceptance is, in effect, to deny that Christ is enough.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath. Some say Christians must keep the seventh-day Sabbath; others that the fourth commandment transfers fully to Sunday with all its strictness. Verdict: Paul includes the Sabbath among the shadows fulfilled in Christ (v. 17). Christians are not bound by the Mosaic Sabbath law, and no one may judge them for not keeping it. Christ is our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is the day the church gathers for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): a privilege and a gift, and a wise pattern of rest, not a legal burden.

Does this include the weekly Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that Paul means only the ceremonial sabbaths of Israel’s festivals, and that the weekly Sabbath remains a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:3), now kept on the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath. That view is held by many godly believers and deserves respect. But Paul’s list, festival, new moon, Sabbath, is the Old Testament’s standard way of naming the yearly, monthly and weekly holy days together (1 Chronicles 23:31). The more likely reading is that the weekly Sabbath is included, a shadow fulfilled in Christ. Christians gather on the first day as a glad and ancient practice, but no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5).

The same error in modern clothes. The exact rules change; the dynamic never does. It is the same error whenever a secondary or man-made practice is made the measure of true spirituality and people are judged by it. A real Christian would never touch a drink. You must follow this diet or this fast to be holy. You must keep, or must not keep, Christmas or Lent. You must use only this Bible translation, sing only these songs, school your children in this one way. Wherever someone takes a matter Christ has left free and turns it into a test of whether you are accepted by God, and looks down on you for failing it, that is the Colossian error in a Sunday suit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean rest and worship are unimportant. It means they are not means of righteousness. Nor is Paul calling such observances sinful: a believer may hold his own convictions about days and food (Romans 14:5–6), but no one may make them the measure of anyone’s standing.

So may I judge a brother who keeps these things? No. The rebuke cuts both ways. Do not let anyone make you feel like a second-rate Christian over such things, and do not sit in judgment on a brother who differs from you (Romans 14:1–4). The believer who keeps Sunday strictly and the one who keeps it more freely, the one who abstains and the one who drinks with thanksgiving, are both accepted by the same Christ. And this is no licence to despise all discipline. The gospel never frees us to sin, only from it. It is liberty of conscience: Christ alone is the ground of our acceptance, and no one may add a single rule to him (Galatians 5:1).

In a sentence. Therefore do not let anyone judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a religious festival, a New Moon celebration or a Sabbath day.

On a Tuesday. Do not let anyone burden your conscience with rules Christ has fulfilled. Rest in him. And check your own heart: is there a practice you quietly use to feel superior to other believers? Give it back to God as a gift to enjoy, not a badge to wear.

For worship. Christ is the rest every Sabbath pointed to, the feast every festival foreshadowed, the new light every new moon hinted at. In him the whole calendar of shadows has come to its fulfilment. We do not keep days to be accepted; we gather on the day he rose because we have been accepted, and there is no more joyful reason to gather.

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.

These are a shadow of the things to come. These, the food laws and holy days of v. 16, are a shadow (skia): an outline cast by an object. Think what a shadow is: the dark outline an object throws, with the shape of the thing but none of its substance. You cannot shake a shadow’s hand. The whole ceremonial law was exactly that: a God-given shadow cast ahead of a coming reality, and the reality it traced was Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1). The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God. The Day of Atonement outlined his once-for-all sacrifice. The Sabbath outlined the rest he gives. The tabernacle outlined God come to dwell with his people. A shadow is real and useful: it truly tells you something is on its way. But it was never meant to be clung to as though it were the thing itself.

But the substance belongs to Christ. The word for substance is literally body (sōma), and the contrast is beautiful: the shadow set against the body that casts it. The solid body that threw this entire shadow play, the whole Old Testament system of feasts and foods and sacred days, is Christ himself. The reality that cast the shadow is Christ. And once the body has arrived, why cling to its shadow? When your friend walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall. To return to the ceremonial rules now that Christ has come is to prefer the outline to the person.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament is worthless. Shadows are real and point to the real thing. Studying them helps us see Christ. Nor does it mean that God’s moral law, summed up in love for God and neighbour, was a shadow; it is the ceremonial rules, the signposts, that have reached their destination.

How should I read the Old Testament laws, then? Ask what each one was pointing to. The sacrifices point to Christ’s once-for-all death; the priesthood to Christ our great high priest; the food laws, which marked Israel off from the nations, to the holiness of God and the clean heart he gives in Christ (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The moral commands, such as do not steal or honour your father and mother, still show us God’s will, and the New Testament repeats them. Read it all with the question Jesus taught on the Emmaus road: where is this about me (Luke 24:27)? You will find the whole of it lit up.

In a sentence. These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Read a passage of Leviticus or Exodus this week, and ask what it shows you of Christ. Then thank him that you do not have the shadow only, but the substance.

For worship. Nothing was lost when the shadows passed. Every lamb that bled at Passover, every goat led away into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement, every quiet Sabbath evening was a finger tracing the shape of Jesus before he came (Matthew 5:17; John 5:39). Now he has come, and the finger rests on him. The worshipper who once held an outline now holds the hand of the One who cast it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,

Let no one disqualify you. “Disqualify” (katabrabeuō) comes from the games: to rule against someone, like an umpire denying a prize. The false teachers set themselves up as umpires over the Colossians’ faith, pronouncing them out of the running unless they took up the teachers’ programme. Do not let anyone tell you that you do not qualify for the prize because you lack their experiences. Paul’s reply: do not let anyone rob you of a prize already yours in Christ, for the Father has already qualified you (1:12). And the programme had three strands.

Insisting on asceticism. “Asceticism” (tapeinophrosynē) is literally humility, but here it is false humility: harsh self-denial, fasting as a spiritual technique. The Greek says the false teacher delights in humility, but a twisted humility: self-imposed severity toward the body, rigorous fasting and harsh treatment of the body as a path to higher spirituality (named again in v. 23). It looked humble, even impressive, but it was a performance of lowliness, not the real thing.

And worship of angels. Either worshipping angels, or joining in the worship angels offer, in visionary experiences. The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and mystical experiences of the angelic world. Either way, giving religious devotion to angelic beings as mediators and guardians, channels through which to approach God, is plainly wrong. It dethrones the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5) and bows to the very powers Christ is head over (2:10). Angels themselves refuse it: when John fell down to worship one, the angel told him not to, but to worship God (Revelation 19:10).

Going on in detail about visions. “Going on in detail” (embateuō) means entering into, a word used in the mystery religions for initiates entering the sanctuary. They took their stand on visions they claimed to have seen. The teacher paraded the things he had seen, mystical experiences won through his disciplines, and built his authority on them: I have seen what you have not; follow me and you can too. It was spiritual one-upmanship by experience, making private revelations rather than Christ and his word the measure of who is advanced.

Puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind. Literally, the mind of his flesh. For all their spirituality, their minds were fleshly and proud. For all the impressive display, the man is simply puffed up, swollen, inflated, and without reason, for there is nothing actually there. And here is the irony at the heart of it. The man who beats his body to escape the flesh, who scales the heavens in visions to rise above it, is driven the whole time by the flesh: by the fallen nature’s craving for status and superiority. The austerity feeds his pride; the visions feed his self-importance; his humility is vanity in disguise.

Still with us. All three strands are still with us: holiness equated with severity; the fascination with angels, spirit guides and other mediators slipped between the believer and Christ; and the experience-chasing that rates a Christian by his dramatic encounters. Beneath them all runs the same error: a spiritual elite making ordinary believers feel disqualified unless they add some practice or experience to Christ, and, underneath the show, the same fleshly pride (1 Corinthians 8:1). The safeguard, in every age, is the next verse: hold fast to the Head.

Where Christians differ: praying to angels and saints. Some traditions encourage prayer to angels or departed saints for help and intercession. Verdict: Paul warns against worship of angels, and Scripture forbids worshipping any creature (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). There is one mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Believers pray to God through Christ alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fasting is wrong. Jesus expected his followers to fast (Matthew 6:16). It means fasting as a technique for spiritual superiority is wrong. Nor does it deny that angels are real and serve God’s people (Hebrews 1:14). It means we do not pray to them, seek them or build our faith on encounters with them.

What if a Christian friend tells me about a dramatic vision or experience? Listen kindly, and do not mock. God is free to work in his people’s lives in ways that move them deeply. But test it by Scripture, and notice where it points: to Christ and his word, or to the person and their experience? Be wary of any experience that is used to claim a higher rank, to add teaching beyond the Bible, or to make others feel second-class. The closed canon of Scripture is sufficient for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). You do not need someone else’s vision to know Christ fully; you have his word, and his Spirit to open it.

In a sentence. Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you. Such a person also goes into great detail about what they have seen; they are puffed up with idle notions by their unspiritual mind.

On a Tuesday. Do not let anyone make you feel second-class for lacking their spiritual experiences. You have Christ. And if you have had a striking experience of God, thank him for it quietly, and do not use it to measure others.

For worship. The prize is not awarded by the umpires of spiritual one-upmanship. It was won by Christ and given freely to every one of his people, the weak and the ordinary as fully as the gifted. He needs no angel to bring us to God, because he is God come to bring us home.
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.

And not holding fast to the Head. “Holding fast” means to grip tightly, to cling, and the Head is Christ (1:18; 2:10). In a single phrase is Paul’s diagnosis of the whole heresy. This is the root problem of the false teachers: for all the visions and disciplines and angel talk, they had let go of Christ. They shifted their grip from the Saviour to rules, experiences and spiritual beings, and that is fatal, because everything depends on keeping hold of the Head. All true spirituality holds on to him. It is the exact opposite of the believer rooted and built up in him (2:7), and it implies our part: hold on, do not drift, do not loosen your grip when something newer and more impressive comes along.

From whom the whole body. The church, the body of Christ (1:18). Christ is the Head, the church his body, and from the Head, and nowhere else, the whole body draws its life.

Nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments. Medical language. Paul fills in the anatomy: the body is nourished, fed, and knit together, bound into one, through its joints and ligaments, the connecting tissues that both link the parts and carry the supply down from the head to every limb. Christ, the head, supplies life to the body through the connections between its members. Life flows from Christ the Head, through all the connections, into every member, so that the body is at once fed and held together, and therefore grows. Believers grow through their relationships with one another in the church (Ephesians 4:15–16).

Grows with a growth that is from God. True growth comes from God, through Christ, not through rules or visions. The increase is his own doing, not something the body manufactures by technique (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

The branch and the vine. Here is the whole thing in a picture. Cut a branch from the vine and it does not grow; it withers, because all the life was in the vine (John 15:5). Sever a hand from the arm and no exercise will make it grow. That is exactly what the false teachers were unwittingly doing. By drawing people off Christ onto their rules and visions, they were cutting the branch from the vine, offering a fancier life while severing it from its only source.

What it does not mean. It does not mean growth happens without effort. It means its source is God.

Can I grow as a Christian without belonging to a church? Not as God intends. Paul says the body grows through its joints and ligaments, the connections between believers. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb. Other believers teach you, correct you, pray for you, need your gifts, and show you Christ in ways you would never see alone. There may be seasons when you are cut off by illness, persecution or distance, and God is not limited then. But if you are able, join yourself to a faithful local church, and be known there. Holding fast to the Head and staying joined to the body go together.

In a sentence. They have lost connection with the head, from whom the whole body, supported and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows as God causes it to grow.

On a Tuesday. Your growth is not a technique to master but the natural fruit of staying joined to Jesus. Your part is to hold fast to the Head, close to Christ in faith, his word and prayer, and God himself supplies the increase. Stop hunting for life in programmes and rule-keeping. Then think of one believer through whom God has fed you, and tell them.

For worship. Every ounce of life in the church flows down from her risen Lord. He feeds the smallest member through the plainest joint: a word from a friend, a prayer in a kitchen, a sermon in a small hall. The Head who was crowned with thorns now crowns his body with a growth that is God’s own, and no member joined to him has ever been starved.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations—“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.

If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world. The if is not a doubt but a settled fact: since you died with Christ. The elemental spirits (stoicheia, as in v. 8) are the basic governing principles and powers of the old order: the whole system of religious rules and the forces behind it. And Paul says you died to all of it. United to Christ in his death (2:11–12), you were severed from that old regime and released from its jurisdiction, for death dissolves every old bond (Romans 7:1–6). Since you died with Christ, you are no longer under that old order of rules and powers. The elemental rules have no more claim on you than a master has on a slave who has died.

Why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations. “Submit to regulations” (dogmatizō) means to be subjected to decrees. To take up that world’s regulations again is to behave as if you were still alive in the world, as if the death had never happened. It is a freed slave voluntarily walking back into the slave quarters and picking up his old chains.

Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch. The slogans of the false teachers. Notice their character: every one a prohibition, a religion of forbiddings, and pettily piled up, rules multiplying, each stricter than the last. Touch is lighter than handle, so even the faintest contact is banned.

(Referring to things that all perish as they are used). Then Paul lets the air out of the whole thing. Food and drink are used up and gone. They cannot touch the soul: as the Lord said, what goes into the stomach does not defile the heart (Mark 7:18–19).

According to human precepts and teachings? From Isaiah 29:13, quoted by Jesus against the Pharisees, who taught as doctrines the commandments of men (Mark 7:7). Human rules, not God’s commands. Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.
