These have indeed an appearance of wisdom. They look impressive and spiritual: wise, rigorous, deeply devoted. The fasting looks like devotion, the strict rules like holiness, the severity like depth. That is exactly their danger: a convincing surface with no reality beneath.

In promoting self-made religion. “Self-made religion” (ethelothrēskia) is will-worship: worship invented by one’s own will, worship a man chooses for himself rather than worship God commands. The word is found nowhere before Paul, and the coined word exposes the root: self-will dressed up as devotion.

And asceticism and severity to the body. With it go harsh treatment of the body as a path to holiness and a paraded humility. It all looks magnificent.

But they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh. The devastating verdict. For all the show, the system fails at the one thing it claims to do: it cannot curb sin. Rules cannot change the heart. They may restrain behaviour outwardly, but they feed pride and leave sinful desires untouched. External prohibition does not conquer the flesh; it only relocates it. Starve the body, and the flesh does not die; it grows fat on pride, swelling with self-righteous satisfaction in its own discipline. Rules may even inflame the very sin they forbid (Romans 7:5–8). Only union with Christ, dead and risen, defeats the flesh (3:1–5).

Weeds cut at ground level. Such rules are like cutting weeds off at ground level: the garden looks tidy for a day, but the roots are alive and the weeds come straight back. Only Christ digs out the root. The cure for sin is not a tighter rule book; it is a living Saviour. You have died and been raised with him, so the way forward is not to climb back under the rules but to hold fast to the Head and live the new life from above, where Christ is seated (3:1; Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16).

Where Christians differ: rules for holiness. Many churches add rules beyond Scripture: no alcohol, no dancing, strict dress codes, as tests of holiness. Verdict: Christians may make wise personal choices and churches may give wise counsel, but when human rules are made a test of spirituality or bound on others’ consciences, they become self-made religion. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and nothing is to be required beyond his word (Westminster 20.2). The power to defeat sin is found in Christ, not in rules.

What it does not mean. It does not mean self-discipline is useless. Paul disciplined his body (1 Corinthians 9:27). It means discipline cannot replace Christ.

Does this make fasting and self-discipline pointless? No. Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), Paul disciplined his body and kept it under control (1 Corinthians 9:27), and bodily training is of some value (1 Timothy 4:8). What Paul condemns is rules imposed as the way to holiness or acceptance with God. Discipline as a means of growth, done in faith, is good.

So how do I actually fight a sin I keep falling into? Not by rules alone, though wise boundaries can help: if you know you are weak, do not walk into temptation (Romans 13:14). The heart of the fight is Christ. Remember that you died with him and were raised with him, so sin is no longer your master (Romans 6:11–14). Set your mind on things above, where he is (3:1–2). Put sin to death by the Spirit, not by willpower alone (Romans 8:13): pray, confess it honestly, bring it into the light with a trusted believer (James 5:16), fill your mind with his word, and feed on his love. The flesh is starved most effectively when the soul is feasting on Christ.

In a sentence. Since you died with Christ to the elemental spiritual forces of this world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its rules: “Do not handle! Do not taste! Do not touch!”? These rules, which have to do with things that are all destined to perish with use, are based on merely human commands and teachings. Such regulations indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-imposed worship, their false humility and their harsh treatment of the body, but they lack any value in restraining sensual indulgence.

On a Tuesday. Here is the point in plain words: you died with Christ to the old world of rule-keeping, so do not crawl back under man-made rules as though you still belonged to it. If you have been fighting a sin with rules alone, turn to Christ today. Tell him the truth about it, and ask him to change your heart, not only your behaviour.

For worship. The Lord who died and rose again does not hand us a rule book and leave us to it. He joins us to himself, kills the old life in his death, and raises a new one in his resurrection. What no rule could do, he has done. The freedom he gives is not the freedom to sin, but freedom from sin, and it is the freedom of the Son: if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36).

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 2 showed that rules cannot defeat sin. Chapter 3 gives the real cure: union with the risen Christ. Since you have been raised with him, set your heart and mind on things above, where Christ reigns; your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory. Therefore put to death the old sins (sexual immorality, greed, which is idolatry) and strip off anger, malice, slander and lies, because you have already put off the old self and put on the new, which God is renewing in his image. In this new humanity race, religion, culture and class no longer divide: Christ is all, and in all.

Instead, as God’s chosen and beloved people, put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience and forgiveness, and above all love. Let Christ’s peace rule, let his word dwell in you richly through teaching and song, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks. Finally Christ’s lordship enters the home: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, each with a duty, and those with power given the harder command.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul draws the consequence of union with Christ. Because believers have already been raised with him, their ambitions and thinking should be directed to heaven, where Christ reigns, rather than to the earthly concerns that once ruled them. Their old life has ended and their real life is now kept safe with Christ in God, out of sight for the moment. When Christ appears, that hidden life will be revealed, and they will share his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.

Meaning first. Colossians 3 shows the true way to holiness, after chapter 2 tore down the false way of rules. The power for a holy life is not a stricter regime but union with Christ: believers have died and been raised with him, their life is hidden with him in God, and they will appear with him in glory, so they set their minds on things above (vv. 1–4). Because of who they now are, they put to death sexual sin and greed, which is idolatry, put away anger, slander and lies, and wear the new self, in a people where Christ is all and in all (vv. 5–11). As God’s chosen ones they put on compassion, forgiveness and love, with Christ’s peace ruling, his word dwelling richly, and everything done in his name (vv. 12–17). Then Paul carries that lordship into the household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, all serving the Lord Christ (3:18–4:1). The whole chapter answers one question: what does a person do with his days once Christ has become his life?

If then you have been raised with Christ. The “if” turns the argument. All through chapter 2 Paul pulled down the rule-bound, ascetic religion of the false teachers, ending with the verdict that such regulations have an appearance of wisdom but are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (2:23). Now comes the positive alternative, built on two halves of one truth: if you died with Christ, you are free from the world’s rules (2:20); if then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above. The cure for a failed religion of rules is a new direction: not down into severity to the body, but up toward the risen Christ. And the “if” means since, as in 2:20. Paul is not asking whether they belong to Christ; he is building his command on the fact that they do.

Raised already. “Raised with Christ” is not a promise about the distant future but a statement of what has already happened. United to Christ (2:12), you share his resurrection now. What does that actually mean? Two plain things. God counts you as one with his Son, so that his death for sin and his rising to new life are reckoned as yours (Romans 6:4–5). And the Spirit who raised Jesus now lives in you, giving a new heart that loves God and wants what is above (Romans 8:11; Ezekiel 36:26). And see how this answers the heresy. The false teachers urged the Colossians to climb, through fasting, visions and the worship of angels, to reach the heavenly realm. Paul says they need not climb a single rung, for in Christ they have already been raised there and seated with him (Ephesians 2:5–6). Every religion that is not the gospel is a ladder. The gospel is the news that someone came down the ladder, took hold of you, and carried you up.

Seek the things that are above. The verb (zēteō) is present tense: keep seeking, keep pursuing, keep making Christ’s kingdom your aim and your treasure. It means the reorientation of the whole bent of a life, its desires, aims, treasure and ambition, around the risen Christ rather than the passing things of earth. It is a question of what a man finally lives for, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21).

Where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Paul locates the things above with precision. They are not a vague spiritual atmosphere; they are wherever Christ is, and Christ is seated at the right hand of God, the place of supreme honour and authority promised in the psalm the New Testament quotes more than any other (Psalm 110:1). And he is seated. The priests of the old covenant never sat down in the sanctuary, because their work was never finished; this priest sat down because his was (Hebrews 1:3; 10:11–12). The Christ you are told to seek is the living, enthroned Lord of the universe, with the very powers the false teachers feared disarmed beneath his feet (2:15). The crucified one is the crowned one, reigning there as your representative and advocate (Romans 8:34). Our head is there, so our hearts belong there.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring earthly duties. The rest of this very chapter deals with marriage, children and work, and Paul plainly expects his readers to do them well. To seek the things above is not to leave the earth but to see it from the throne: to do your work, love your family and carry your burdens as someone whose life is anchored where Christ is. Nor is it a technique for spiritual experiences: you are told to seek not visions of heaven, which the false teachers were peddling (2:18), but Christ, who is there.

How do I actually seek the things above in an ordinary day? Begin by deliberately turning your attention to where Christ is: a few minutes with Scripture and prayer in the morning, before the day’s demands start talking. Then carry one question into the day: what does the risen Lord want done here, and how would he value this? When you make a decision about money, time or ambition, ask which choice treats Christ’s kingdom as the treasure. Gather with his people on the Lord’s Day, where heaven’s realities are preached and sung. And when you notice your heart has drifted to anxiety or getting, do not berate yourself; simply turn it back. Seeking is a direction you keep returning to, not a feeling you must sustain.

In a sentence. Since, then, you have been raised with Christ, set your hearts on things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.

On a Tuesday. Before your day fills with earthly concerns, lift your heart to Christ seated in heaven. Then, at some point in the afternoon when the pressure is highest, stop for ten seconds and remember where he is: not anxious, not hurried, not wondering how it will turn out, but seated. Your work today is real and it matters. It is not, however, holding up the universe. Someone else is doing that, and he has sat down.

For worship. The throne of the universe is not empty, and it is not occupied by a stranger. The one seated at the Father’s right hand still bears the wounds he took for us, and he sits there as our head, our brother and our high priest, with our names on his heart. Every power that threatened the Colossians is under his feet, and every power that threatens us. He has finished the work and he holds the throne, and he has joined us to himself so completely that where he is, our life now is. Glory to the risen Christ, whose seat in heaven is the true address of every believer’s heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.

Set your minds on things that are above. Verse 2 deepens verse 1. There Paul said seek; here he says set your minds (phroneō), another ongoing command that means more than passing thought. It is the settled bent of the mind, the whole orientation of a person’s thinking and valuing, the same word Paul uses when he says have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus (Philippians 2:5). Seeking engages the will; setting the mind engages the thoughts. Whatever you habitually dwell on and prize, set that on the things above: on Christ, his glory, his kingdom and his return. Aim the thoughts upward, and the life will follow.

Not on things that are on earth. The counterweight is deliberate. Earthly things here are not the earth itself, which God made and called good, but the perishable things treated as ultimate: the food rules and regulations of 2:21–22, and the sinful desires Paul is about to name in 3:5. Both are earthbound in the same sense. The ascetic and the sensualist look like opposites, but they have the same address: one is preoccupied with what he must not touch, the other with what he must have, and neither is looking at Christ. The two cannot both be the mind’s true north. A mind set on the flesh makes an earthbound man; a mind set on the Spirit makes a heavenly-hearted one (Romans 8:5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean becoming so heavenly-minded that you are no earthly good. Heavenly-minded people make the best earthly servants, because they are no longer using the earth to fill a hole only God can fill. Nor does it mean despising your body, your work or honest pleasures; that is the asceticism Paul has just demolished. The question is what your mind is finally set on: what you treasure, what governs you, and what you interpret everything else by.

The expatriate. Think of a man living and working abroad. He does his job well, pays his taxes, learns the language and is kind to his neighbours. But his heart is set on home, and everything he does is coloured by where he truly belongs: he is not crushed when the local currency falls, and he does not mistake the posting for his life. So it is with the Christian, for our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20). Live and labour on earth with your mind set on home.

If my thoughts drift constantly, am I failing at this? No; the command assumes drift, which is why it is in the present tense: keep setting. A mind is set the way a compass needle is set, not by never moving but by always swinging back to north. You do not fix your thoughts by grim concentration. You feed them. What you read, watch, scroll and talk about will shape what your mind returns to when it is idle, so give it things worth returning to: Scripture memorised, a psalm sung, a truth about Christ turned over on the commute. Wandering is the condition of every believer this side of glory. The question is where you come back to.

In a sentence. Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.

On a Tuesday. Notice where your mind goes when nothing is demanding it: in the queue, in the car, in the minute before sleep. That is where it is set. If it is always the same worry, the same craving or the same grievance, do not merely try to stop thinking it; give your mind somewhere better to go. Choose one verse about Christ this week, write it where you will see it, and let it be the place your thoughts come home to.

For worship. There is nothing above to set the mind on but Christ, and Christ is enough to fill a mind for ever. He is the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were made, the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (1:15–16; 2:3). The angels have been looking at him since before the world began and have not exhausted him. We are invited to think about the most glorious being there is, and to find that he has been thinking about us first.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

For you have died. “For” gives the ground beneath the command. Why seek the things above? Because that is where your life actually is. The two halves of the new identity are now in place. You have been raised with Christ (v. 1), so you reach upward; you have died (v. 3), so the earthbound life is behind you. The verb is past and finished. In union with Christ’s death, the old you, the self that belonged to the world and lived for its things, has died and been buried with him (2:20; Romans 6:2–7). The man who lived for earthly things is dead, and a new man has been raised in his place.

And your life is hidden with Christ in God. The verb (kryptō) is in the perfect tense: it has been hidden, and it stays hidden. And the phrase carries two glorious senses at once. First, hidden means safe. Your life is stored away in the most secure place in the universe, and it is double-wrapped: your life in Christ, and Christ in God. No enemy, no sin, no devil and not death itself can reach in and snatch it, for no one will snatch them out of my hand, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). Second, hidden means concealed. Your true life and glory are not on display yet. The world cannot see it, and for now it looks ordinary, unremarkable and often weak. But hidden is not lost. It is stored, waiting for the day it will be unveiled (v. 4).

Treasure in a strongroom. In the ancient world people hid what they valued most: coins buried in a field, valuables lodged in a temple strongroom. Paul uses the word for that. Your real life, your standing with God, your very self, is not held in your own trembling hands; on your worst day, when you feel like a failure and a fraud, it is still safe, because it hangs not on your performance but on Christ. And you are not yet what you will be. You may look ordinary, ageing and weary, like an acorn in winter ground that looks nothing like the oak, but the glory is real and it is coming: we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared (1 John 3:2). You do not have to achieve your life, guard it or prove it. It is kept with Christ in God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have no real life now, or that the Christian life is a waiting room. The life is real and present; it is simply not yet visible in its full glory. Nor does “you have died” mean you can no longer sin or feel temptation. The rest of the chapter commands believers to put sin to death precisely because it is still active in them. What died was your old identity and its claim on you, not every trace of its habits.

If my life is hidden and safe, why does it so often feel fragile? Because you are looking at the part that is not hidden: your moods, your health, your circumstances, your recent failures. Those are real and they do fluctuate. But Paul is not describing how your life feels; he is describing where it is kept. A deposit in a bank vault does not become less safe because the depositor has a bad week. When you feel fragile, do not try to feel stronger. Look away from yourself to the place where your life is, and remember who is holding it. Assurance grows by attending to Christ, not by taking your own temperature.

In a sentence. For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God.

On a Tuesday. Your life is hidden with Christ. Whatever happens today, it is safe. When the review goes badly, the diagnosis comes back, or someone you love lets you down, say it to yourself plainly: this touches my circumstances; it cannot touch my life. Then do the next thing in front of you as someone who has nothing ultimate to lose.

For worship. The God who hid Moses in the cleft of the rock while his glory passed by has hidden us in his Son, and the Son in himself. We are kept by the One who keeps the stars in their courses. We did not put ourselves there, and we cannot take ourselves out. Our Saviour went into the darkness of the tomb, which hid him from every eye for three days, so that our lives might be hidden in a place no darkness can reach. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose keeping is stronger than our weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

When Christ who is your life appears. Having spoken of present realities, Paul now lifts the eyes to the day of Christ’s return. Your life is hidden with Christ now, and it will not stay hidden. When he appears, it will blaze into the open in glory. The pattern is hidden now, revealed then. And notice the breathtaking phrase: Christ who is your life. Paul does not say Christ merely gives us life, as though it were a gift we hold apart from him. He says Christ is our life: its source, its substance and its centre. He is not an addition to your life, one good thing among many; he is your life. What does that actually mean? That everything you most truly are comes from him and is kept in him: your pardon is his death, your righteousness is his obedience, your new heart is the work of his Spirit, your future is his glory. Take him away and nothing of the new life is left. So Paul could say, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Galatians 2:20). This is the final answer to a heresy that offered Christ plus something: Christ is not part of the package. He is the whole of it.

Appears. The word (phaneroō) means to be brought out of hiding into open view. Right now he is hidden, enthroned at God’s right hand and unseen by the world; but a day is fixed when he will be revealed in glory before the whole creation. And mark the word when, not if. His appearing is certain; only the hour is unknown. It will be one appearing, public and visible to all, not a secret coming in stages (Matthew 24:27, 30–31).

Then you also will appear with him in glory. Your destiny is bound to Christ’s. As your life is now hidden with him, so it will be revealed with him, and not in shame but in glory. The hidden life of verse 3 will be displayed at last, and you, who look like nothing much now, will share the glory of Christ, transformed into his likeness. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2; Romans 8:17–19). Think of an heir to a great throne who has lived his whole life unrecognised, in working clothes, and then the day of the coronation comes. He is led out, robed, and revealed before all as the king’s own son. That is the believer’s future, tied to Christ’s own appearing, which cannot fail.

The hinge of the chapter. This verse is where the argument turns. Having settled who you are and who you will be, Paul draws the practical conclusion in the next breath: put to death therefore (v. 5). Future glory is the great motive for present holiness. Everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3). People who know where they are going start dressing for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will become divine or be absorbed into God. They will share his glory as glorified human beings, body and soul, still creatures, still themselves, made perfectly like their Lord. Nor does it mean that glory waits until the end with nothing before it. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); the soul does not sleep. But the full public unveiling, with resurrected bodies, comes when he appears.

What will glory actually be like? Scripture gives us more than we often notice. It will be a body raised imperishable, never again sick, ageing or dying (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). It will be a character finally free from sin, so that you will love God and others without the drag you feel now. It will be seeing Christ face to face, which is the heart of it. And it will be shared: you will appear with him and with all his people, in a renewed creation (Romans 8:21). Glory does not mean becoming a spotlight; it means being made fully what God always meant you to be, and reflecting his light without distortion.

In a sentence. When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

On a Tuesday. Think of one thing you are tempted to do today because no one will ever know, and one thing you are tempted to skip because no one will ever notice. Now picture the day when everything hidden is revealed with Christ. The first will look foolish then; the second will not have been wasted. Live today in the light of that morning.

For worship. Our story does not end in the grave or in obscurity. It ends with the King coming in his glory, and every hidden life he has kept brought out into the light beside him. He will not be ashamed of us on that day. He who is our life will show us to the universe as his own, robed in a glory he won and gives away. Lord Jesus, you are our life; come, and let what is hidden be seen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they must put to death everything in them that belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desire and greed, which is idolatry. These bring God’s wrath, and they once lived that way. Now they must also get rid of anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy talk, and stop lying to one another, since they have taken off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after its Creator’s image. In that new humanity the old divisions of race, religion, culture and class no longer count; Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.

Put to death therefore. “Therefore” reaches back to verses 1–4: because you have died and been raised with Christ, because your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory, therefore put the old sins to death. This is the great pattern of the Christian life: become what you are. You died to the old life as a finished fact (v. 3); now you put to death its lingering expressions, daily. And note the contrast with chapter 2. This is not the asceticism Paul has just condemned, rules imposed from outside that cannot touch the flesh (2:23), but the killing of sin from the inside, by people already dead and raised with Christ.

The violent word. The verb (nekroō) means kill, execute. Not manage, not tame, not go easy on: kill. Sin is an enemy to be executed, not a pet to be domesticated. You have died with Christ once for all (v. 3), yet you must put sin to death daily, and the finished fact is what fuels the ongoing fight. The killing is done not by rules that punish the flesh but by the Spirit: if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live (Romans 8:13). John Owen, the great Puritan, put it in a sentence his readers never forgot: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

A sentence already passed. Why can a believer fight sin with hope instead of despair? Because the enemy he is told to execute has already been condemned. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, God condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3), and our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). At the cross sin lost its right to rule us; in the daily fight it loses its grip. The believer is carrying out a sentence Christ has already passed and paid for, and he does it by the power of Christ’s risen life within him. That is why the command begins with therefore: the killing flows from the cross, and draws its strength from the empty tomb.

What is earthly in you. Literally, your members which are on the earth: the sinful desires and habits of the old life that still cling to the believer and work through his body. Paul is not calling the body evil. He is naming the places where sin still has a foothold and saying that the foothold must go.

Sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire. Paul names four, and the order digs from the outward act down to the inward root. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for every sexual act outside marriage: the outward deed. Impurity (akatharsia) moves inward to the defiled imagination and the polluted inner life. Passion (pathos) goes deeper, to the ungoverned lust that masters a person. Evil desire (epithymia kakē) reaches the very bottom: the wrong craving of the heart itself. Sin is not merely bad behaviour to be tidied on the surface; it runs all the way down into what the heart wants, which is why rules alone can never cure it. They trim the deed and leave the desire alive.

And covetousness, which is idolatry. Then he crowns the list with a startling word. Covetousness (pleonexia) is greed, the restless craving for more, and Paul calls it flatly what it is: idolatry. Why? Because to covet is to set the heart’s supreme desire and trust on something other than God, looking to created things for the security and worth only God can give. Whatever a man treasures above God is his functional god, and the greedy man bows at an altar he would never admit was there (Ephesians 5:5; Matthew 6:24). It climaxes the list because it lays bare the idolatry beneath all these sins: every one of them is, at root, seeking in something other than God the life only God can give. And it wears a respectable coat. Take care, said Jesus, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15).

How do I actually put a sin to death? Name it plainly, as the enemy it is, not as a weakness or a phase. Refuse it at the first stirring, not after you have entertained it for an hour. Starve it: remove what feeds it, whether that is a device in the bedroom, a route home past the shop, a friendship that always ends the same way, or the shopping app on your phone. Flee the situations where you know you fall (2 Timothy 2:22). Bring it into the light with a trusted believer. And do all of it leaning on the Spirit’s power and on Christ’s finished work, not gritting your teeth to earn God’s favour, but fighting from a favour already yours. The fight is from acceptance, never for it.

What if I have been fighting the same sin for years and keep losing? Then you are in a real war, which is itself a sign of life; the dead do not fight. Long struggle does not prove you are not a Christian. What would be alarming is making peace with the sin. So keep going, but look at how you are fighting. Have you been fighting alone and in secret? Tell someone. Have you been fighting the act and ignoring the desire underneath? Ask what the sin promises you, and seek that in Christ. Have you been fighting from guilt instead of grace? Go back to the cross every time you fall, at once, not after a period of self-punishment. The Spirit is patient, and he finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body is evil, or that sexual desire is itself sinful. God made the body and blessed sex within marriage. What must die is desire turned in the wrong direction and allowed to rule.

In a sentence. Put to death, therefore, whatever belongs to your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires and greed, which is idolatry.

On a Tuesday. Name one earthly desire that is ruling you. Then take one concrete step today to starve it, not just a resolution but an action: delete the app, cancel the subscription, change the route, tell the friend. And ask Christ for the power to keep it dead tomorrow. For the greed in particular, try this test: what would you find hardest to give away? That is often where the idol stands.

For worship. Covetousness grasps, and the Son of God let go. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He was offered all the kingdoms of the world and would not bow to get them; he had nowhere to lay his head, and he gave away even his life. He never coveted anything but his Father’s glory; he carried our idolatries to the cross, and now his Spirit finishes in us what he finished there. When Christ himself is our life, the idols lose their grip, because we have found the one treasure they were all pretending to be.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On account of these the wrath of God is coming.

On account of these the wrath of God is coming. Between the two lists of sins (vv. 5 and 8) Paul pauses to give the reason they must be killed and stripped off. Why deal so ruthlessly with these sins? Because they are exactly what God’s judgment is set against. The wrath of God is the dark backdrop that makes putting sin to death not optional but urgent (Romans 1:18; 2:5; Ephesians 5:6). And it is coming: real, and on its way, with a day of judgment fixed.

What God’s wrath is. It is not a bad temper or a petty loss of control, God flying off the handle. It is the settled, holy, righteous opposition of a perfectly good God to all evil: his just, judicial response to sin. Far from being a flaw, it is a mark of his goodness. A judge who felt no opposition to injustice would be no good judge, and a God indifferent to the abuse of children, the exploitation of the poor and the betrayal of a marriage would be no good God. The people who find the wrath of God most offensive in theory are usually those who have never been badly wronged.

One appearing, two outcomes. Paul has just written of the day when Christ appears (v. 4), and now of the wrath that is coming. They are not two events but one. God will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and he has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The appearing that will be glory for those whose life is hidden in Christ will be judgment for those who refused him, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). So the one face every human being will finally see is his. For some it will be the face of their life; for others, the face of their Judge.

A textual note. Some manuscripts add the words upon the sons of disobedience, which appear in the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. Whether or not Paul wrote them here, the meaning is the same: God’s wrath falls on those who persist in these sins without repentance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers will face God’s wrath. Christ bore it for them in their place, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and we wait for Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10). The point is not to frighten Christians about their standing but to show them how serious sin is, and why they cannot treat it lightly.

If Christ has taken the wrath for me, why should this warning move me? Because it shows you what your sin really is and what it cost. A man who has been pulled from a burning house does not wander back in to collect a souvenir. The warning keeps you from treating as harmless the very things that brought the cross on your Saviour. And it is a test: a person who carries on in these sins with no fight and no grief, while claiming to be safe, should ask honestly whether he has ever been rescued at all. For the believer who is fighting, the warning drives him not into fear but back to the shelter, where the wrath has already fallen on someone else.

In a sentence. Because of these, the wrath of God is coming.

On a Tuesday. When a sin starts to look small and manageable, say to yourself plainly what God says about it: this is one of the things his wrath is coming against, and one of the things my Saviour bled for. Then treat it accordingly. If you have never seriously considered whether you are sheltered in Christ from that wrath, consider it today, and come to him.

For worship. There was a day when the wrath of God against these very sins came down, and it did not fall on the guilty. It fell on the Lamb of God, who drank the cup to the bottom, so that for everyone who trusts in him not one drop remains. He was forsaken so that we would never be. The storm is real, and it is coming; but Christ has already stood in it for us, and the Judge on that day will be the Saviour who bore it.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.

In these you too once walked, when you were living in them. Paul is not claiming that every person outside Christ commits every sin on the list, or that all are equally vile. People apart from Christ differ enormously, and many are outwardly decent and restrained, because God’s common grace holds back the full flood of sin in the world. He is saying two things. This was the Colossians’ own former life, their habitual road. And these sins are the native air of life apart from God, the direction a heart turned away from him naturally runs, whether or not every sin shows its face in every person.

You too. Notice the tenderness of those two words. Even you, now God’s holy people, were once in this. It is meant to keep the believer humble: do not look down on those still trapped, for you were there yourself. And it is meant to keep him grateful: grace reached in and lifted you out. Such were some of you, Paul tells the Corinthians, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:3–5).

Once, but now. The word once sets up the pivot of the next verse: but now. This letter has already told us what stands between the two. You, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him (1:21–22). The way out of the old country was not a better effort but a body nailed to a cross. Christ did not merely show the Colossians a new road; he took their guilt on himself and brought them out as people God now sees as holy. That was your old country. You have emigrated, and he paid for your papers. Do not move back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never fall into these sins. They can and sometimes do, and Scripture records it honestly. It means these sins no longer define them or rule them. A Christian may stumble into the old country; he no longer lives there, and he is miserable when he finds himself back.

If I was a Christian from childhood, does “once” apply to me? Yes, though it may look different. You may never have walked in open sexual sin or drunkenness, and that is a mercy to thank God for, not a credential to boast in. But Paul’s point is that the heart apart from grace is turned from God at the root, and that was true of you too. The pride, self-will and quiet idolatries of a well-behaved child are the same country with tidier streets. Grace lifted you out as surely as it lifted the man with the dramatic story, only earlier, and that is more grace, not less.

In a sentence. You used to walk in these ways, in the life you once lived.

On a Tuesday. Remember what you once were, and thank God that it is in the past. Then think of someone who is still where you were. Pray for him by name, and if you have been looking down on him, stop. The only difference between you is the hand that reached in.

For worship. We did not climb out of the old country; we were carried out by a Shepherd who came looking for us when we were not looking for him. He knew exactly what we were walking in, every road and every habit, and he came anyway, and laid us on his shoulders rejoicing (Luke 15:5). He does not only forgive our past; he takes away its power to name us. Praise the God who does not leave his people where he finds them, and who will never take them back there.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.

But now you must put them all away. The great hinge from the old life to the new. Where verse 5 said kill, treating sin as an enemy to be executed, verse 8 says take off (apotithēmi), like stripping off filthy clothes and throwing them aside. And “all” sweeps up both lists. The first list (v. 5) was sexual and greedy, the sins of the appetites; this one is relational and verbal, the sins of the temper and the tongue. And here is the uncomfortable point: these are the sins respectable church members can commit for decades without anyone calling it sin.

Anger, wrath, malice. Two words for two kinds of temper. Anger (orgē) is the settled, smouldering kind: the grudge nursed, the banked fire of resentment that will not go out. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden kind: the flare-up, the outburst that explodes and subsides. Some of us are boilers and some of us are simmerers, and Paul names both. Beneath both lies malice (kakia): the ill will itself, the meanness of spirit that wishes another person harm, or is quietly pleased when harm comes to him.

Slander, and obscene talk from your mouth. Slander (blasphēmia) is injurious speech that runs a person down; it is the same word used for blasphemy against God, and the overlap is not an accident, because to tear down someone made in God’s image is to speak against his Maker (James 3:9). Obscene talk (aischrologia) is foul, shameful, abusive speech. And notice how far the list has travelled, from the hidden heart to the open mouth. The tongue is the drain through which the heart empties, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34).

Reviled, he did not revile. Every sin on this list was once aimed at one man. At his trial false witnesses slandered him, the high priest called his words blasphemy, the guards spat on him and mocked, and passers-by hurled abuse at the cross (Mark 14:55–65; 15:29–32). The tongue of the old humanity emptied itself on the Son of God. And when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Peter adds that he bore our sins in his body on the tree (2:24), and that includes the sins of our mouths. The anger and slander we are told to put away were carried by him, and his silence under them is the pattern of the new self.

How do I tell slander from a legitimate warning? Scripture itself names real dangers and sometimes real names (2 Timothy 4:14), so not every negative word is slander. Ask three questions. Is it true? Slander trades in falsehood and in the exaggeration that makes a story more interesting; a warning is accurate. Is it necessary, for a good end? A warning protects someone from harm; slander only wounds, entertains, or makes the speaker look better. And why are you saying it, and to whom? A faithful warning is given reluctantly, in love, usually to the person who can do something about it; slander is told with relish, behind the back, to anyone who will listen.

Is all anger sinful? No. Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5), and Paul says be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real wrong can be righteous: anger at cruelty, at injustice, at the abuse of the weak. What Paul tells us to put away is selfish anger, the kind that is about my rights, my comfort and my pride, and that wants to hurt. It is the kind that sits beside malice and slander in the list. A useful test: righteous anger is about God’s honour and other people’s good, is slow to arise, and moves toward putting things right. Sinful anger is about me, is quick, and moves toward getting even.

How do I put these off when I have tried to “just stop” so many times? Not by white-knuckle willpower in your own strength; that is the chapter 2 asceticism that cannot conquer the flesh. Putting off always comes paired with putting on (vv. 10, 12). You overcome a sin not by leaving a hole where it was but by replacing it: take off anger and put on compassion; take off slander and speak well of people behind their backs; take off lying and become a teller of truth. Sin is expelled not by a vacuum but by a stronger affection. And it flows from who you already are: you strip off these sins because you have already put off the old self (v. 9). It is the work of a lifetime, done by the Spirit. The old clothes feel familiar and you keep reaching for them, so you keep taking them off, day after day, while God keeps remaking you. Progress, not yet perfection (Ephesians 4:22–24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must suppress every strong feeling or never express displeasure. It means the sinful, self-serving forms of anger and speech must go. A believer can say firmly that something is wrong without contempt, sarcasm or a raised voice designed to dominate.

In a sentence. But now you must also rid yourselves of all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy language from your lips.

On a Tuesday. Pick the one sin on this list that your family would name if asked about you, and ask them if you dare. Then, the next time it rises, stop before you speak and replace it with its opposite: a soft answer instead of a sharp one, a blessing instead of a jibe, praise of the absent person instead of criticism. And if the words have already come out, go back and apologise without explanation. A sentence that begins I’m sorry, but is not an apology.

For worship. The only man who ever had the right to be angry with everyone in the room prayed for the men who were nailing him: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). The lips that will speak the last word over the world spoke pardon over his enemies. His words were always true and always kind, because his heart was full of grace, and he does not leave his people with their old tongues: he gives them his Spirit and is teaching them to speak like him. Blessed be the Lord whose mouth was the one mouth on earth in which no deceit was ever found.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.

Do not lie to one another. One more sin of speech, and not only bald untruths but half-truths, spin, flattery, broken promises, exaggeration, and the whole family of deceit. “To one another” presses it home: lying poisons the trust that holds the new community together (Ephesians 4:25). The new people of God are a people of truth, because their God is the God of truth and the devil is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). To deceive is to wear the old father’s likeness, not the new.

Seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices. The reason for all these commands. The old self, literally the old man, is not merely a bundle of bad habits but the whole person you used to be in Adam: your old identity under the reign of sin, together with its practices. Scripture says it was crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6). Both verbs here, put off and put on, are completed past acts, done decisively at conversion. So the foundational answer is: already done. He was taken off once for all, and the daily putting away of his leftover practices (vv. 5, 8) is the living out of a removal already accomplished.

And have put on the new self. Likewise you have put on the new self, the new person you now are in Christ, the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), your settled identity in union with the risen Lord. And it is corporate as well as personal, which is why verse 11 says the old divisions of race and class now fall away. Christ is forming not only new individuals but a new humanity.

Which is being renewed in knowledge. Yet the new self, already put on, is not static. The tense changes to the continuous: it is being renewed, made new day by day. And it is passive, because God is the one renewing it (2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 12:2). Here is the answer to the puzzle of already or not yet: it is both. The decisive change is done; the transformation is ongoing. And it is renewal in knowledge (epignōsis): not the secret knowledge the false teachers offered, but the personal knowledge of God as he really is in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3). The fall plunged the mind into darkness about God (Romans 1:21), and this renewal reverses it. Knowing God rightly is itself transforming.

After the image of its creator. This reaches back to Genesis. Man was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27). The image was defaced, though not erased, by the fall, and it is now being restored in Christ, who is himself the image of the invisible God (1:15). To be renewed after the Creator’s image is to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29; Ephesians 4:24). Salvation is not self-improvement. It is new creation, God stamping his own likeness on the soul again.

The restorer. Put the whole picture together. The change of clothes has already happened, once and for all, so the daily Christian life is to live as the man you now are, taking off the scraps of old clothing you still reach for. And while you do, God is at work on you like a master restorer cleaning a great portrait that has been painted over and grimed with age, patiently bringing back, stroke by stroke, the original image of the King that the fall had buried. You cannot always see the progress, and the cleaning can be slow, but the Master does not abandon a portrait he has begun to restore (Philippians 1:6).

Where Christians differ: is it ever right to lie, for example to protect life? The Hebrew midwives deceived Pharaoh, and Rahab hid the spies. Some Christians hold that deceiving people set on murder is not the lying Scripture forbids, since God dealt well with the midwives (Exodus 1:20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that every lie is a sin, though God may honour the faith and courage behind it. Verdict: the second reading is more likely, but such cases are rare and extreme, and godly believers have differed on them. They are not the subject of this verse. The command here is about trust among believers: Christians should be people whose word can always be relied on, in the small things as in the large.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old self is gone in every respect, so that a Christian no longer feels the pull of sin. The flesh still fights against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17). But the believer’s true identity is the new self, and the flesh is a squatter in a house that now belongs to someone else.

What counts as lying in everyday life? More than most of us admit. The excuse that is not quite the reason. The figure rounded up on the claim form. Saying you are fine when you mean you are not, to avoid a conversation that needs to happen. Letting a false impression stand because it flatters you. The CV that implies more than it says. Agreeing to do something you have no intention of doing. Truthfulness does not require you to say everything you think; silence and tact are not lies. But whatever you do say should be true, and you should not set out to make anyone believe what is false.

In a sentence. Do not lie to each other, since you have taken off your old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.

On a Tuesday. You have put on the new self, so dress the part today: speak truthfully. Watch especially for the small, convenient untruths, the ones that make a conversation easier or make you look a little better. When you catch one, correct it on the spot, even if it is awkward. And when you see the old clothes in yourself again, do not despair; take them off again, and thank the Restorer who has not stopped working.

For worship. The image we spoiled is being restored by the one who made it, and he is restoring it after the pattern of his own Son, who is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his nature. Christ never spoke a false word and never put on a false face. He is the truth, and he is making a people who look like him. One day the restoration will be complete, and every one of his people will bear his likeness without a blemish. Blessed be the Creator who did not discard the ruined portrait, but sent his Son to bear its ruin and to make it new.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.

Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised. This looks like a new topic but is not. Paul has spoken of putting on the new self (vv. 9–10); now he says that in this new self the old human divisions disappear. Here means in the new humanity Christ is forming. Paul names the great dividing lines of his world, in every category. Race: Greek and Jew, the deepest divide of all. Religion: circumcised and uncircumcised, the mark that had separated the covenant people from everyone else.

Barbarian, Scythian. Culture. A barbarian was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greek ears, the word imitating the sound of a foreign tongue; it was the ancient way of calling someone uncivilised. And the Scythians, nomads from north of the Black Sea, were the byword for the lowest and wildest of all, the people Greek writers used when they wanted an example of savagery. Paul deliberately reaches for the most extreme example he can think of. Even they are welcome as equals in Christ.

Slave, free. Class. In a city like Colossae, a slave was legally property and a free man was a citizen with rights, and the two did not eat at the same table. In the church they did. Philemon, a slave owner in this very congregation, was about to receive his runaway slave Onesimus back, carrying this letter, as a beloved brother (4:9; Philemon 16).

But Christ is all, and in all. Here is the glorious replacement for all those labels. Christ is all: everything, the sum and substance, the one thing that finally counts. In place of the old categories that ranked and divided, there is now a single defining reality. And Christ is in all: the same Christ lives in every one of his people, Jew or Greek, slave or free, polished or rough, and that indwelling is what makes them one. He lives in each of them by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10), so that every believer is joined to the same Lord, and through him to every other: the same Christ in the Scythian and in the Pharisee. And the wonder is this: the same Christ in whom all the fullness of God dwells (1:19) lives in plain, ordinary believers. You are not on the outside of the blessing looking in. Christ is in you, the hope of glory (1:27; Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean cultural, ethnic or social differences simply disappear. A Jew remained a Jew and a slave remained a slave, and men and women remain men and women. Paul himself goes straight on to give different instructions to wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters (3:18–4:1). The differences are not erased but dethroned: they no longer decide a person’s worth, his standing before God, or his place in the family. They are like accents in a choir, real and audible, but singing one song.

What does this look like in a church today? It means the businessman and the unemployed man share the bread and the cup as equals, and the elders are chosen for godliness, not for wealth or education or ethnicity. It means a congregation does not sort itself, without anyone deciding to, into tables of people who look alike. It means you take seriously a believer from another culture who prays and worships differently, as a brother and not a curiosity. And it means looking honestly at your own instincts: who do you naturally assume will be the most mature Christian in the room, and why? The world ranks; the church must not, because Christ does not.

In a sentence. Here there is no Gentile or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, but Christ is all, and is in all.

On a Tuesday. Your worth and identity are no longer measured by what the world ranks people by: nationality, job, class, education, whether you are somebody or nobody. The only thing that finally defines you is that you belong to Christ and Christ is in you. So this week, seek out one believer who is unlike you, older or younger, richer or poorer, from another background, and get to know them. Ask how they came to Christ. You will find the same Lord on the other side of the difference.

For worship. Christ has done what no empire, philosophy or revolution has ever managed: he has made one people out of every kind of person, without flattening them into sameness. He broke down the dividing wall in his own flesh, and now the Jew and the Scythian kneel at the same table, the slave and the master call the same Father, and none of them has anything to boast in but him. Heaven will be full of every tribe and language and people and nation, and every voice will be singing one name. Christ is all, and he is in all, and he is worthy of all.
verseByVerse.note: Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most uncivilised of barbarians.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s chosen people, holy and loved, they are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with and forgiving one another as the Lord forgave them, and above all with love, which binds everything together. Christ’s peace is to rule in their hearts, and they should be thankful. The word of Christ is to dwell richly among them as they teach and admonish one another and sing to God with gratitude. Whatever they do, in word or deed, they are to do it in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to the Father through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.

Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved. The clothing image continues. Having stripped off the old sins (vv. 8–9), you now put on the new virtues: you get dressed in the character of Christ. The Christian life is never merely stopping the bad; it is clothing yourself with the good, deliberately and daily, choosing to act in compassion and patience even before the feeling arrives. And Paul names who you are before he names a single virtue. Three titles, each of which once belonged to Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6–8), and all three describe God’s prior work on you.

Chosen, holy, beloved. Chosen (eklektoi): God set his love on you and picked you out before you had done anything to deserve it, even before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Holy: set apart as his treasured possession. Beloved: dearly loved, sharing the belovedness of his beloved Son, into whose kingdom he has transferred you (1:13). The identity comes before the commands, and the commands flow from it. You do not put on these graces to become chosen and loved; you put them on because you already are. And a person secure in being loved can afford to pour himself out for others. The beloved can afford to love.

Compassionate hearts, kindness. The first garments are tender ones. Compassionate hearts is literally bowels of mercy, the ancient way of naming the deep, gut-level feeling that moves when someone else is in pain. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is that compassion turned into action. Compassion feels; kindness acts. And it is the very kindness of God that leads us to repentance (Romans 2:4). Every one of these five virtues is a portrait of Christ, who was moved with compassion for the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36).

Humility. Strikingly, this is the very word the false teachers had twisted into ascetic show (2:18, 23), but here it is the real thing: a right estimate of yourself before God, knowing you are a sinner saved by sheer grace and therefore above no one, so that in humility you count others more significant than yourselves (Philippians 2:3). It is not thinking you are worthless or wallowing in self-hatred; that is self-absorption with a long face. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less.

Meekness, and patience. Meekness is also misunderstood. It is not weakness or spinelessness. The Greeks could use the word for a wild horse broken and tamed, all its power still there but now under control. Meekness is strength under control: the gentleness of someone who could retaliate and chooses not to. Jesus was gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29), and he also overturned the tables in the temple (John 2:15). Patience (makrothumia) is literally long-tempered: slow to anger, the same patience God shows to us, now worn toward others.

Bearing with one another. These virtues now meet real life. Bearing with one another means putting up with each other’s rough edges: the brother who talks too long, the sister who is always late, the personality that grates. It means making allowance, the way a family puts up with one another’s habits around the same breakfast table. Most church life is not about great wrongs. It is about small frictions, and love absorbs them without keeping a tally.

Forgiving each other, as the Lord has forgiven you. Then come the real wrongs, if one has a complaint against another. To forgive (charizomai, the verb built on the word for grace) is to release the debt, refusing the grudge and the revenge, just as God cancelled the record of debt that stood against you (2:14). And the measure is staggering: as the Lord has forgiven you. Freely, fully, at great cost, and while you were still his enemy (Romans 5:8–10). The man who knows how much he has been forgiven cannot easily hold a small debt over his brother; Jesus told a whole parable about the absurdity of it (Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:32).

Must I forgive only when the other person apologises, or at once? Both, in different senses. The forgiving heart, the release of bitterness and the readiness to forgive, you must have at once, whether or not the other ever asks: whenever you stand praying, forgive (Mark 11:25). You never nurse a grudge until the offender grovels. But full reconciliation, the forgiveness spoken and received and the relationship restored, is completed when the other turns and repents (Luke 17:3). Restoration by its nature takes two. So forgive from the heart at once, holding nothing back, and stand ready, even eager, to welcome the other back the moment he turns.

Must I seek reconciliation with someone who abused me? No, not in the sense of resuming closeness or trust. Forgiving from the heart means letting go of revenge and handing the wrong over to God, who judges justly. It does not mean trusting a dangerous or unrepentant person, resuming contact, keeping the abuse secret, or giving up church discipline or the protection of the law; the governing authority is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). Reporting a crime is not a failure to forgive. Reconciliation needs genuine repentance and changed behaviour shown over time, and safety comes first. A church that pressures a victim to reconcile has misunderstood both forgiveness and love.

And above all these put on love. Love is the crowning garment, the outer robe pulled on over the whole wardrobe. It is not mainly a warm feeling or romance. You can love, that is, seek the good of, a person you do not naturally like. It is a settled commitment of the will to seek another’s good and give yourself for it, at cost, regardless of merit or return: the love mapped out in 1 Corinthians 13.

Which binds everything together in perfect harmony. Why above all? Because love is the bond (syndesmos, a ligament, a belt, the same picture as the ligaments of the body in 2:19) that ties all the other graces together, and ties the whole body together, in perfect harmony. Without love the rest fall apart and ring hollow (1 Corinthians 13:1–3): humility without love becomes a pose, patience without love becomes cold endurance, and forgiveness without love becomes a transaction. With love drawn over them all, they are bound into one beautiful, mature character. And it is by this, Jesus said, that all people will know that you are my disciples (John 13:34–35).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring serious sin or pretending it did not happen. Forgiveness names the wrong and then releases it. It does not always remove the consequences, and it does not immediately restore trust, which has to be rebuilt. But it releases the debt and refuses revenge. Nor does bearing with one another mean tolerating anything at all; serious, persistent sin in the church is to be dealt with (Matthew 18:15–17), gently and with the aim of restoration.

How do I forgive when I still feel the hurt? Forgiveness is first a decision and then a process. You decide, before God, that you will not pursue revenge, will not keep bringing the matter up as a weapon, will not dwell on it to feed your resentment, and will not speak of it to others in order to damage the person. Then, when the memory returns with fresh pain, which it will, you make the same decision again and hand the wrong back to God. Feelings usually follow slowly. Pray for the person by name; it is hard to keep hating someone you pray for. And look again at the cross, where your own debt was paid.

In a sentence. Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which binds them all together in perfect unity.

On a Tuesday. Who do you need to forgive? Remember how the Lord forgave you, and forgive them today, in prayer, by name. Then pick one of the five garments that fits you worst, perhaps patience, perhaps humility, and put it on deliberately in one specific situation: the colleague who irritates you, the child who asks the same question again, the driver who cuts in. Do the kind thing first and let the feeling catch up.

For worship. Every garment in this wardrobe was first worn by Christ. He was compassionate to the leper, kind to the outcast, humble enough to wash feet, meek before Pilate, and patient with disciples who never seemed to understand. He bore with us when we were unbearable, and he forgave us while we were driving in the nails. Now he dresses us in his own clothes, chosen, holy and beloved, so that the world might see something of him in us. Glory to the Lord who first loved us, and who binds his people together with the love that held him to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.

And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts. The peace of Christ is the peace he won and gives, the peace he made by the blood of his cross (1:20). First it is peace with God (Romans 5:1). Out of that comes the settled calm he leaves with his people, for peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you (John 14:27), and the peace that should reign between them.

Rule. The word (brabeuō) is the umpire’s word: the referee who makes the call and settles the contest, the official at the games who awarded the prize. So let Christ’s peace be the umpire in your heart. When you are torn or anxious, when relationships are strained, when a decision pulls you two ways, let his peace make the call: refuse what would shatter it, and choose what preserves it. Do not let anger, fear or self-will referee your heart. Let the peace of Christ do it.

To which indeed you were called in one body. This peace is part of your calling. God did not call you to strife but to peace (1 Corinthians 7:15), and he called you in one body, into the one body of Christ, the one new humanity of verse 11, made of every kind of person. So this peace is not merely a private inner calm but the bond meant to govern the body’s life together. You are no lone Christian, and the same peace that umpires your heart is meant to keep the whole church one. In the context of verses 12–14, the umpire is most often deciding between a grievance and forgiveness.

And be thankful. A short command, but it is the first of three calls to thanksgiving in three verses (vv. 15, 16, 17), and thankfulness runs all through this letter (1:3, 12; 2:7; 4:2). Gratitude is the keynote of this section. And it belongs beside peace, because the thankful heart is the peaceful heart. Gratitude crowds out the grumbling and grievance that breed strife and anxiety, and the person counting his mercies has no room left to nurse his complaints (Philippians 4:6–7). Grateful people make peace; grumbling people break it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a feeling of peace is always a sign of God’s will, or that a feeling of unease always means no. Feelings can be mistaken, and a person can feel very peaceful about a sinful decision he has already made. The peace of Christ is not a mood to be consulted like an oracle. It is the peace that Christ has made and that his word describes. It governs decisions as we ask what would honour him and keep peace with God and with his people, tested always by Scripture.

So how do I let Christ’s peace decide something? Take a real decision or conflict. First ask what Scripture says about it; Christ’s peace never contradicts his word. Then ask which course keeps you at peace with God, with a clear conscience, and which course serves peace in the body of Christ rather than division. Ask whether a choice is being driven by fear, pride or the wish to win, and rule those out as referees. Pray, seek wise counsel from mature believers, and then act in faith. If two good options remain, you are free to choose, and the peace you have with God does not depend on choosing perfectly.

In a sentence. Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, since as members of one body you were called to peace. And be thankful.

On a Tuesday. Think of the one relationship in your church or family where peace is most strained right now. Ask what Christ’s peace would rule in that situation, and do the one thing it would call for: the message, the apology, the letting go. Then, before bed, name three specific mercies from today and thank God for them. Count them out loud if you have to. It is very difficult to be thankful and resentful in the same breath.

For worship. He is our peace. He did not negotiate a truce with God on our behalf; he made peace by his blood, taking into himself the hostility that stood between us and the Father and between us and one another. Now his peace stands guard over hearts that were once at war, and sits as umpire in churches made of former enemies. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift, the Prince of Peace, who left his peace with us when he went to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly. The phrase the word of Christ is rare in Paul (elsewhere only Romans 10:17). It means the message that is Christ’s, the gospel of which he is the heart, the apostolic teaching about him that the Colossians had received, the word of the truth, the gospel (1:5). Not narrowly the words of Jesus printed in red, but the whole word that proclaims him, embracing all of Scripture, which everywhere testifies to him. Note the pointed contrast: let Christ’s word fill you, not the philosophy and empty deceit of the false teachers (2:8).
