Dwell in you richly. To dwell (enoikeō) means to take up residence, to make a home, not to drop by as an occasional visitor. Richly means abundantly, in full and spacious measure. So the word of Christ is to be a resident, not a guest, furnishing every room of the heart. And “in you” is plural: among you, as a church. Paul is describing a congregation saturated with Scripture, not only individuals with good devotional habits. This, in fact, is how all the putting off and putting on actually happens: the mind is renewed (v. 10) as the word takes up rich residence within.

Teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom. The richly dwelling word overflows into a mutual ministry. Teaching is the positive passing on of truth; admonishing (noutheteō) is the corrective side, warning and urging a brother away from wrong. It is the same pair of words Paul used of his own ministry in 1:28. And mark one another: this is not the task of the official teachers alone but of every member, ordinary believers ministering the word to each other (Romans 15:14). It is done in all wisdom: skilfully and fittingly, with the discernment to know what word the moment needs. A verse thrown at a grieving friend can wound; the same verse given gently, at the right time, can heal.

Singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. The third overflow is song. Psalms are the inspired Old Testament songbook; hymns are songs of praise, perhaps like the great hymn to Christ in 1:15–20; and spiritual songs are songs prompted by the Spirit and full of his truth. Together they mean the full range of sung worship, and singing is itself a way of teaching one another (Ephesians 5:19). Sung truth lodges in the heart as almost nothing else does. Many Christians who can remember little of the sermons of their youth can sing the hymns from memory on their deathbeds.

With thankfulness in your hearts to God. Literally, with grace, or with gratitude, in your hearts. Singing is to come from the heart, not just the lips, and to be aimed at God, not at the audience. Worship is the word set to music in a thankful heart.

Where Christians differ: what should churches sing? Some Reformed churches hold to exclusive psalmody, singing only the inspired Psalms in worship. They note that all three words, psalms, hymns and songs, appear in the titles of the Greek Psalter, and that only inspired songs are fit for God’s worship. Others sing a wide range of songs. Verdict: the Psalms should have a central place in Christian worship, and many churches would be richer for singing far more of them. But the three terms most naturally describe a variety of songs, and the New Testament itself contains early Christian songs about Christ (1:15–20; Philippians 2:6–11; 1 Timothy 3:16). Churches may sing new songs that are faithful to Scripture and centred on Christ. The test is whether the word of Christ dwells richly in what is sung. Those who hold to exclusive psalmody do so out of reverence for God’s word, and they deserve to be honoured as brothers.

How do I know if a song is good to sing? Ask whether the word of Christ dwells in it richly. Is it true, faithful to Scripture in what it says about God, Christ, sin and grace? Is it about God more than about my feelings, though feelings are welcome? Does it teach something, so that singing it plants truth in the heart? Can a congregation actually sing it together, or is it a performance to watch? And does it lead to thankfulness? A song can be old or new, simple or complex. What matters is whether it carries Christ’s word to the heart.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only gifted musicians or good voices should sing. Every believer is commanded to sing, and God is not grading the tuning. Nor does it mean that Bible teaching is only for those with a gift for it. Elders have a particular charge to teach (1 Timothy 3:2), but every Christian is to speak the word to others.

In a sentence. Let the message of Christ dwell among you richly as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom through psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, singing to God with gratitude in your hearts.

On a Tuesday. Sing a psalm or hymn today, at home, in the car, over the washing up. Choose one you can sing from memory and notice what it teaches you. Then think of one believer who needs a word this week, encouragement or a gentle warning, and give it: a verse in a message, a sentence after church, a phone call. Let the word of Christ fill your heart and home, and overflow.

For worship. The Word who was with God in the beginning became flesh and dwelt among us, and now he sends his word to dwell in us. He sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed, and walked out to Gethsemane with the psalms on his lips. He is the theme of every true song the church has ever sung, and one day the whole creation will join the new song: worthy is the Lamb who was slain. Until then we sing with thankful hearts, because the one we sing about has put his own word in our mouths.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

And whatever you do, in word or deed. This is the sweeping summary of the whole section, and one of the most comprehensive statements of Christ’s lordship in all of Scripture. Whatever: nothing is left out. In word or deed: everything you say and everything you do, the two halves that cover the whole of life. Not merely the religious parts, but the entire ordinary round: work, family, meals, rest. There is no secular corner walled off from Christ.

Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. To act in someone’s name is to act as his representative: on his behalf, under his authority, for his honour, in dependence on him, and in a way worthy of him. So to do everything in Jesus’ name is to live as his in all things: to drive the van, pay the bill, speak the word and do the task as Christ’s representative, for his glory, by his help, in a manner that would not shame his name. This both consecrates the ordinary, because the humblest task becomes service of Christ, and constrains the sinful, because you cannot do in his name what dishonours it. So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Not a fence but a lordship. Here is the heart of the whole ethical section. The false teachers wanted a fence of external rules: do not handle, do not taste, do not touch (2:21). Paul gives instead the lordship of Christ, reaching into every word and deed from the inside. Rules can only cover the situations someone thought of in advance. The name of the Lord Jesus covers the ones nobody thought of.

Giving thanks to God the Father through him. The third call to thanksgiving closes the paragraph. Everything done in Jesus’ name is wrapped in gratitude to the Father, and it comes through him. Our thanks, like all our approach to God, comes to the Father through Christ, the one Mediator. This is the quiet final answer to the angel mediators of chapter 2: no other channel is needed, and none is allowed (1 Timothy 2:5). Lordship and gratitude: every word and deed turned into worship (Ephesians 5:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean adding the words in Jesus’ name to the end of things like a magic formula, as if the phrase itself did something. It means living as his. A prayer that ends in Jesus’ name is a good thing when it means we come through him; but the verse is about the whole of life carrying his name, not only our prayers.

What about the parts of my life that seem to have nothing to do with Jesus? There are none that he has excused himself from. Filling in a spreadsheet, changing a nappy, mowing the lawn and watching a football match can all be done in his name, if they are done honestly, gratefully, and in a way that does not dishonour him. Try a simple test: could I thank God for this, and could I do it with Christ beside me? If yes, do it heartily and enjoy it as his gift. If no, the verse has just answered the question for you. And if there is a part of your life you would rather he did not see, that is the part this verse is most kindly aimed at.

In a sentence. And whatever you do, whether in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

On a Tuesday. Take an ordinary task today, the most ordinary one you have, and before you start it, say quietly: Lord Jesus, I do this as yours. Then do it well, and thank the Father for it when it is done. Notice whether the task changes, or whether you do.

For worship. There is no corner of the universe where Jesus is not Lord, and there is no corner of our lives that he does not want. He did everything in his Father’s name: he worked in the carpenter’s shop, ate with sinners, slept in a boat and died on a cross, and all of it was worship. Now he takes our clumsy words and ordinary deeds, cleanses them, and carries them to the Father as offerings. Through him, then, we give thanks for everything, to the God who has given us everything in him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul applies this to the household, the basic unit of ancient society. Wives are to submit to their husbands as fitting in the Lord, and husbands are to love their wives and not be harsh with them. Children are to obey their parents, which pleases the Lord, and fathers are not to provoke their children and discourage them. Slaves are to obey their earthly masters sincerely, not to win favour, but working wholeheartedly as for the Lord, from whom they will receive the inheritance; wrongdoers will be repaid without favouritism. Masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, knowing they too have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. Over children and slaves his authority was close to absolute in law. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

The household code. With verse 17 Paul said everything is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, and now he brings that lordship into the home (3:18–4:1, as in Ephesians 5:21–6:9). Greek writers had household codes too, telling the head of a household how to manage his wife, children and slaves. Paul’s is different. It addresses the weaker parties, wives, children and slaves, directly, as responsible persons who stand before Christ for themselves. And it places real duties on the stronger parties, husbands, fathers and masters, all of whom are themselves under a Master. The phrase in the Lord, or its equivalent, appears in almost every line. The household is not a little kingdom under the husband; it is an outpost of Christ’s kingdom, and everyone in it answers to him.

Wives, submit to your husbands. Submit (hypotassō) means to order or arrange oneself under, and the form is voluntary: the wife places herself under, freely. It is not something the husband seizes or imposes, and nowhere in Scripture are husbands told to make their wives submit. It is her own glad, chosen deference to her husband’s God-given role of loving leadership, the headship of Ephesians 5:23. And it is to your own husbands: one marriage, not women in general deferring to men in general. Positively, it is a disposition of respect, support and trust: a wife coming alongside her husband as his partner, honouring and strengthening his leadership rather than competing with it, and, when a real decision must finally be made and they still differ, trusting his lead. Paul frames it as the reflection of something beautiful: the church’s glad submission to Christ (Ephesians 5:24).

As is fitting in the Lord. Paul grounds it not in custom but in the Lord, and the phrase does three things. It dignifies her submission, because it is an act of devotion to Christ, not capitulation to a husband’s superiority. It roots the command in Christ rather than in shifting culture. And it limits it: because her submission is in the Lord, it can never be a submission that dishonours the Lord. The same phrase that asks it also guards it.

What it does not mean. The word is so often abused that this must be said carefully. It does not mean the wife is inferior: she is fully equal in worth and standing before God, a fellow heir of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7; Galatians 3:28). Submission is a matter of role and order, never of value, just as the Son is fully equal to the Father and yet gladly does the Father’s will. It does not mean slavish obedience: tellingly, Paul tells children and slaves to obey (vv. 20, 22) but tells wives to submit, the gentler word. It does not mean silence or having no voice: she is a strong helper and counterpart (Genesis 2:18) who speaks, advises and may freely disagree, and godly women in Scripture did exactly that (1 Samuel 25). It does not mean obeying into sin: if a husband demands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). It is not earned by the husband’s worthiness, and it is not the submission of all women to all men.

Never a cover for abuse. Submission is not a licence for harshness or abuse, and the very next verse forbids the husband to be harsh. A wife is nowhere commanded to submit to cruelty or danger. Abuse, whether physical, sexual, emotional or financial, is a grave sin, and in many cases a crime. A wife who is being abused should seek safety and help, from the church and from the civil authorities, and she is not failing to submit by doing so. Where there is abuse, the church must protect the victim and call the abuser to account, never preach submit to the one being harmed.

Where Christians differ: is a wife’s submission still God’s will? Egalitarian Christians read this in the light of the call to mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21) and Paul’s statement that in Christ there is no male and female (Galatians 3:28). They see the household instructions as a cultural accommodation tied to the ancient world, now outdated, or as mutual only. Verdict: Paul grounds the wife’s submission in the Lord, and elsewhere in creation and in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:3, 8–9). That makes it permanent, not merely cultural. And Paul gives husbands a different command, to love, not to submit. But the wife’s submission is her willing response to her husband’s loving, sacrificial leadership, not a licence for him to dominate. It never requires a wife to sin or to endure abuse. Husband and wife are equal heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), with different callings in the one marriage. Egalitarian believers who hold their view from Scripture are brothers and sisters, and the debate should be carried on with charity.

What does it look like in an ordinary marriage? Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together, by agreement, and headship and submission rarely have to come into play. But picture the genuine deadlock. They have prayed, talked it through and weighed it honestly: a move, a major purchase, a direction for the family. They still disagree, and a decision must be made. There the wife trusts and supports her husband’s leading rather than insisting on her own way or making him pay for it afterwards. Day to day it looks like speaking well of him in public and in private, backing his leadership instead of undercutting it in front of the children, and treating him with genuine respect (Ephesians 5:33). The model is Sarah (1 Peter 3:5–6): a woman of strength who freely honoured her husband, not a doormat who had lost her voice.

What if my husband is not a Christian, or does not lead at all? Peter addresses the first case directly: a believing wife may win an unbelieving husband without a word, by her conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2). Her submission is still in the Lord, so she never follows him into sin, and she keeps her own walk with Christ, her church and her conscience. In the second case, where a husband is passive, submission does not mean pretending he leads when he does not. She may lovingly ask him to take responsibility, encourage every step he takes, and pray for him, without either seizing the role in contempt or abandoning the family to drift. And she should not carry it alone: wise counsel from the church can help them both.

In a sentence. Wives, submit yourselves to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Wives, find one way today to honour and support your husband’s leadership, as to the Lord: a word of thanks for something he did, backing a decision you were not sure of, speaking well of him to a friend. Husbands reading this verse: it was not written to you, and the moment you start quoting it at your wife you have already stopped obeying the next one.

For worship. The pattern of marriage was drawn in heaven before it was lived on earth. The Son, equal with the Father in glory, delights to do his Father’s will; the church, his bride, delights to follow the Bridegroom who gave himself for her. Every Christian marriage is meant to be a small picture of that love: a husband laying down his life, a wife gladly receiving it, both of them bowing before the Lord who is the true Husband of his people. Blessed be the Lord Jesus, the Son who delights to do his Father’s will, and the Bridegroom who never asks of his bride what he has not first given her.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.

Husbands, love your wives. The word is agapaō: not first a romantic glow but the deliberate, self-giving love of the will that seeks the wife’s good, the love crowned in verse 14. Paul states it briefly here; his parallel letter spells out the measure: love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). Nothing less than the sacrificial love of Christ for his people. So the husband’s headship is here defined, and it turns out to be headship by sacrifice, not headship by domination. He leads by giving himself away. And the present tense means keep on loving.

How counter-cultural this was. The household codes of the ancient world loaded the duties onto the lesser party and told the husband almost nothing except how to rule. Paul turns and lays on the man the harder command. Nobody in Colossae needed telling that a husband had authority; they needed telling that it was for her good, and that he would answer to Christ for it.

What love looks like. It is sacrificial: her good above his comfort. It is constant: a settled commitment, not rising and falling with his feelings or her loveliness on a given day. And it is active: it nourishes and cherishes her as a man cares for his own body (Ephesians 5:28–29). It looks like a husband who puts his wife’s good ahead of his own preferences, who cherishes and provides and listens, who serves her in small unglamorous ways, as the Lord himself knelt to wash feet (John 13:5), and who keeps loving her on the day she is hardest to love, because his love is a covenant, not a mood. In a word, it looks like Christ.

And do not be harsh with them. The word (pikrainō, from pikros, bitter) means do not be embittered: do not grow sharp or sour with your wife. Having commanded love, Paul at once names love’s opposite, because it is precisely the husband’s characteristic temptation. The very strength of his position can curdle into domination, and small resentments can harden into a cold, critical spirit toward the one he should cherish most. The present tense warns against the slow settling in of such a spirit: do not let bitterness take root. And Peter adds a sobering reason: a husband who does not live with his wife in an understanding way finds his prayers hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

The familiar clothes of harshness. It wears many disguises: the cutting tone, the sarcasm, the criticism that is never satisfied, contempt, the short temper, silence used as a weapon, and the winning of every argument by sheer sharpness. Often it is the strange sin of the man who is gentle and pleasant with everyone else, colleagues, friends and strangers, and saves his harshness for his own wife. The cure is the very character Paul has just commanded: the compassion, kindness, meekness and patience of verse 12, and the readiness to forgive rather than nurse a grievance until it sours (v. 13). A wife was never given to her husband to be a target for his bitterness, but to be loved as Christ loves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is only a feeling, or that a husband who no longer feels romantic is free to stop. Love here is action: serving, protecting, cherishing, providing, listening. Nor does avoiding harshness mean a husband can never disagree or raise a hard subject. He can and sometimes must. But he does it with gentleness, at the right time, for her good and not to win.

What do I do if I have been harsh with my wife? Confess it, first to God and then to her, plainly and without excuses: not I’m sorry you felt hurt, but I was harsh with you, and it was wrong. Ask her to tell you, honestly and without punishment, when it happens again, and receive it when she does. Look for the root: harshness usually grows out of an expectation she has failed to meet, or a pressure elsewhere you are taking out on her. Bring that to Christ. And if the harshness has become a pattern of control or intimidation, seek help from your pastor or a trusted counsellor at once. That is no longer a bad habit; it is a danger to her.

In a sentence. Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, do one unglamorous thing for your wife today that she did not ask for and will not expect. And listen to your tone of voice when you are tired. If it is sharper with her than with your colleagues, she is getting the worst of you, and Christ is calling you to give her the best.

For worship. The love that defines a husband’s duty was first poured out on a bride who was nothing to look at. Christ loved the church when she was unfaithful, unlovely and in rags, and he gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, cleanse her and present her to himself in splendour. He has never once been harsh with her. He bears her weakness, prays for her without ceasing, and will one day bring her home in glory. Every Christian husband is a small, flawed picture of the greatest Husband there is, and every Christian marriage points to the wedding supper of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.

Children, obey your parents in everything. Notice first that Paul speaks directly to the children. They were present in the church when letters were read aloud, and they are real members of the covenant community, able to hear God’s word and answer it. Obey (hypakouō) is literally to listen under: not merely to feel respect but actively to heed and do. And it looks different at different ages. For a young child it is plain, glad, prompt obedience in the daily round: coming when called, doing the chore, going to bed. This is the nursery of discipleship, where a little one first learns to submit to God by submitting to those God has set over him. For the older child and teenager, the relationship matures but the call remains, now expressed as honour and trust: keeping the household’s rules and receiving correction without rebellion.

In everything. The sweep is wide, but not absolute, for all human authority is held under God’s. The parallel reads obey your parents in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1), and a child is never bound to obey a parent who commands him to sin (Acts 5:29). But that exception is rare. The plain meaning, for nearly every child on nearly every day, is simply: obey, fully and gladly, even when you do not see the reason.

Obedience and honour. For the grown child who has formed his own household, the word shifts. The duty to obey belongs to the years under the parental roof, but the duty to honour never expires; it is the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2; Exodus 20:12). The adult child no longer takes orders as he did as a boy, but he never stops respecting, caring for, and providing for his parents as they age (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). Obedience belongs to childhood; honour is lifelong.

For this pleases the Lord. Literally, this is well pleasing in the Lord. And why does it delight him so? Above all because in obeying, a child walks in the footsteps of the Lord Jesus himself, the great obedient Son, who said I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me (John 6:38), and who became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). And here is the wonder: the eternal Son, by whom all things were made, spent his boyhood in a carpenter’s home and was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). So when a child obeys, he bears the family likeness of the Son who delighted to obey his Father. Two other reasons join it. The obedient home reflects God’s own good order, and the child’s obedience to his parents is, underneath, obedience to God, who set parents over him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children must obey parents who command sin, or who abuse them; God’s authority is higher, and a child who is being harmed should tell a trusted adult. And it does not mean adult children must obey their parents in everything. They honour them, listen to them with respect, and care for them, but they make their own decisions before God, especially within their own marriages (Genesis 2:24).

What about a child whose parents are not Christians? The command still holds, and in fact it may shine brighter there. A Christian child or teenager in an unbelieving home is to obey and honour his parents in everything that is not sin, and his cheerful obedience can be one of the most powerful testimonies they ever see. Where a parent forbids something God commands, such as faith in Christ itself, the child must follow Christ, but he should do so respectfully and humbly, without contempt, and look for every lawful way to honour his parents at the same time.

In a sentence. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Children, obeying your parents is a way of pleasing Jesus. Do it cheerfully today, the first time you are asked, without arguing. And if you are grown, ring your parents this week, or visit, and ask what you can do for them. Honour does not retire.

For worship. The Lord of glory once had a bedtime. He learned his letters, carried water, swept the workshop and did what he was told, and every hour of that hidden obedience was pleasing to his Father. He obeyed perfectly where we have not, and his obedience is counted to every child of God who trusts him, so that the smallest believer in the house is clothed in the obedience of the eternal Son. Blessed be the eternal Son, who became a child so that children might become the sons and daughters of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.

Fathers, do not provoke your children. The word (erethizō) means to irritate, exasperate, stir up to resentment. The parallel puts it sharply: do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). Here, as with the husband and the master, the one who holds the power is given the restraining word. A father’s strength is for building his children up, never for crushing them. The word is addressed to fathers because they bear the chief responsibility for the home, but it applies to mothers as well.

The many ways to provoke. Fathers exasperate their children in a hundred ways: by harshness and criticism that is never satisfied, by unfairness and favouritism, by punishing in temper, by impossible expectations, by domineering control, by hypocrisy, demanding what they will not do themselves, and by cold neglect that withholds all warmth and praise.

Across the years. It looks different at each stage. A young child is provoked by impatience and a sharp tongue over ordinary childish failings, the spilled cup, the mess; by anger out of all proportion; by rules that change with the father’s mood; by promises lightly broken. The good way is gentleness, clear boundaries held with warmth, generous affection and praise, and expectations that fit his age. The school-age child is provoked by constant criticism, by being compared to a sibling, by praise that never comes, by mockery and shaming. The good way is to encourage and to notice: specific praise for honest effort, real interest in his world, and discipline that is fair and explained.

The teenager and the grown child. The teenager is provoked by a control that will not loosen as he grows, by being treated as a little boy, by endless lecturing, by belittling, and by because I said so where a reason was owed. The good way is to let trust and responsibility grow together, to listen and reason, to choose the battles that matter, to keep the relationship warm, to own his own faults, and above all to point the young person to Christ rather than merely enforce a rulebook. Even a grown child can be provoked by a father who still dictates and criticises his choices, his spouse, and his way of raising his own children. The good way now is to honour the child’s adulthood: to advise when asked, and to bless rather than control.

Lest they become discouraged. The word (athymeō) means to lose heart, to have the spirit go out of you. Notice how discouragement shows at each stage: a bruised little heart in tears and timidity; a school child who gives up trying, because I will never be good enough for him, and quietly stops bringing his small joys to his father; a teenager whose discouragement erupts as open rebellion or, just as dangerously, sinks into withdrawal, secrecy, and a deadened, joyless compliance. Fathers are responsible for the spirit they create in the home.

The Father who sets the pattern. Through every stage one pattern holds, and it is set by the gospel. The earthly father is to father as God fathers his own: as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Psalm 103:13). God disciplines, but he never crushes; he is firm and tender, the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named (Ephesians 3:14–15; Hebrews 12:7–11). And the Christian father parents not to earn anything, but out of the fullness of a man who is himself a dearly loved child of that Father, passing on to his children the grace he has received.

Arms that blessed children. And the Father’s heart toward children has been shown in a face. Whoever has seen me has seen the Father, Jesus said (John 14:9), and Mark records how he treated children. When the disciples tried to send them away, he was indignant and said, let the children come to me; do not hinder them. Then he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them (Mark 10:14, 16). He never treated a child as an interruption, and he kept some of his sternest words for anyone who causes a little one to stumble (Matthew 18:6). A father who wants to know how not to provoke his children has only to watch the Son with them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fathers should not discipline. They must; a father who never corrects his child does not love him (Hebrews 12:7–11; Proverbs 13:24). It means discipline must be loving, fair, controlled, and aimed at the child’s good, never at venting the father’s anger. And it never means violence that injures, terrifies or humiliates a child; that is abuse, not discipline.

Is it too late if I have provoked my children? No. One of the most powerful things a father can do is go to his child, whether he is six or forty-six, and say: I was wrong, I was too harsh, I am sorry, will you forgive me? Many grown children have waited their whole lives to hear it. It does not undo the past, but it often opens a door that has been shut for years, and it shows the child the gospel in a way no lecture could. Then change the pattern, with God’s help and the counsel of others if needed. The Father in heaven delights to redeem what earthly fathers have damaged.

In a sentence. Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged.

On a Tuesday. Fathers, tell each of your children today one specific thing you appreciate in them, not their achievements but their character. Then notice how many of your words to them this week are correction and how many are encouragement. If the balance is badly wrong, put it right.

For worship. We have a Father who has never once provoked his children to despair. He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. He runs to meet the prodigal, he quiets us with his love, and he rejoices over us with singing. He gave his only Son so that we might be called his children, and that is what we are. Every faithful father on earth is a faint reflection of him, and every orphaned or wounded heart can find in him the Father it never had.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.

Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters. The word is doulos, slave. Slavery ran right through the Roman world, a large share of the empire’s population, and slaves were a large part of the early church. One of the slaves in this very congregation was Onesimus, returning to his master Philemon with this letter (4:9; Philemon). Paul addresses them as full members of the church, responsible before Christ for themselves. Obey in everything means the full scope of the master’s lawful direction, done thoroughly, not just the pleasant parts, with the unspoken limit that governs all such obedience: never into sin, for the Lord outranks every master. And mark the phrase earthly masters, literally masters according to the flesh: the human master is master only on the passing, earthly level, and there is a greater Master above him.

Roman slavery and ours. Roman slavery was harsh, and nothing here excuses it. But it was not the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries. People became slaves by capture in war, by birth, or by selling themselves to escape debt, and many were educated, held some money, and could in time be freed. Paul is not blessing the system. Elsewhere he quietly undermines it: if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity (1 Corinthians 7:21); he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10); and he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). He is teaching believers how to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would in time dissolve. The how-to-work of these verses carries straight across to any modern job; the conditions do not.

Not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers. Eye-service (ophthalmodoulia, a word Paul may have coined) is work that only happens while the master’s eye is on you: busy when watched and idle when his back is turned. The people-pleaser works to impress the man. It is one of the oldest temptations of the workplace, and it has not aged a day: the employee who looks busy when the manager passes and slacks when he is gone, who games the figures for the review, who works hard on the visible task and skimps the invisible one. The gospel has no room for as long as nobody is looking, because Someone always is.

But with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Against all that, work with an undivided heart, the same whether watched or not, in awe of the Lord who is always watching. Here is the great turn. You work well not because the master deserves it, or because he happens to be watching, but because you stand in awe of the Lord whose will this is. The audience of your work has changed. It is no longer the boss; it is God.

Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men. The Greek is vivid: work from the soul, putting your whole self in, not skipping the menial or unseen task. Here is why drudgery becomes worship. You are not, in the end, working for the man who signs your orders but for the Lord. Christ is your true Master, and every task is handed, as it were, directly to him. Hand the swept floor to Jesus, and a mean master cannot rob it of its glory (Ephesians 6:7). The Reformers drew from this the dignity of every lawful calling: the maid sweeping a room and the minister in the pulpit both serve God, and no honest work is too lowly to be done for him.

Knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. Now feel the force of the promise. Under Roman law a slave could not inherit; inheritances went to sons, never to slaves. Yet Paul promises this slave the inheritance, the whole eternal estate of God’s people (1:12), an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4). The man who owns nothing and can inherit nothing on earth is a full heir of God. He may get no wage, no thanks and no advancement from his earthly master, but the Lord sees, and he will repay, not with coins but with glory. And the inheritance is not wages earned. You receive it as a son, by grace; the reward is God graciously crowning the very service his own grace enabled.

You are serving the Lord Christ. Here is the clincher, and the heart of Christian work. When the believing slave does his master’s bidding, he is in reality rendering that service to Christ. The lowliest labour, done in faith, rises to the King of kings as service offered to him (Matthew 25:40). There is no higher title in the universe than servant of the Lord Christ, and Paul hands it to the people at the very bottom of Roman society.

For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality. The warning reaches both ways. To the slave: do not imagine your low place lets you get away with lazy or spiteful work. To the master, whom 4:1 turns to address: the one who wrongs his servant will not escape. God plays no favourites (Romans 2:11). He weighs the deed, not the rank, so the powerless need not fear that the powerful will buy their way out of judgment, and the powerful cannot hide behind their position.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slavery is good, or that the Bible endorses the trade that later carried millions from Africa in chains. Scripture condemns man-stealing as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10), and Christians who used these verses to defend that trade twisted them. Nor does it mean a worker must accept abuse, fraud or unsafe conditions without seeking redress. It means that within whatever situation God has placed him, the believer serves Christ with an undivided heart.

How does this apply to my job today? Directly. Your employer is your earthly master in the sense Paul means: someone with lawful authority over your work. So work as well when the manager is on holiday as when he is in the room. Do not pad your hours, take credit for others’ work, or skimp on the parts nobody checks. Do the job in a way you could hand to Christ. If your boss is unfair, you may seek a fairer job, raise concerns properly, or use lawful means of redress; Paul encouraged slaves to gain freedom where they could. But while you are there, your work is for the Lord, and he is the one keeping the record.

What if my work feels meaningless? Then this passage was written for you. Paul wrote it to people who did the most repetitive, unseen and unrewarded work in the empire, and he told them they were serving the Lord Christ. Meaning in work does not come only from the task itself; it comes from the One you are doing it for. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch, the parent changing the same nappy for the fifth time today: when it is done for the Lord, it is laid into the hands of the King. Your foreman may never say thank you. The Lord is keeping account, and he forgets nothing.

In a sentence. Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything; and do it, not only when their eye is on you and to curry their favour, but with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. Anyone who does wrong will be repaid for their wrongs, and there is no favouritism.

On a Tuesday. At work today, remember: you are serving the Lord Christ. Pick the task you most dislike, or the one nobody will ever check, and do it as well as you can, quietly, as a gift to him. Then, if you supervise others, ask yourself how you would treat them if you were sure their Master was watching you. He is.

For worship. The Lord Christ himself took the form of a slave. He who flung the stars into space knelt with a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then went out to be sold for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). He served without eye-service, for no audience but his Father, and he was paid with a cross. Now the servant who owns nothing, who is invisible to the great of this world, is the servant of the Lord Christ and the heir of all things. We carry our clumsy day’s work up to a Father who is delighted to receive it, through the Son who served us first.
verseByVerse.note: One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master in Colossae with this letter.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.<sup>2</sup>Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.<sup>3</sup>For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.<sup>4</sup>When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.<sup>5</sup>Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.<sup>6</sup>On account of these the wrath of God is coming.<sup>7</sup>In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.<sup>8</sup>But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.<sup>9</sup>Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices<sup>10</sup>and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.<sup>11</sup>Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.<sup>12</sup>Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience,<sup>13</sup>bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.<sup>14</sup>And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.<sup>15</sup>And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.<sup>16</sup>Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.<sup>17</sup>And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.<sup>18</sup>Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.<sup>19</sup>Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.<sup>20</sup>Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.<sup>21</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.<sup>22</sup>Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.<sup>23</sup>Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,<sup>24</sup>knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ.<sup>25</sup>For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The household code ends with a word to masters: treat your slaves justly and fairly, because you have a Master in heaven. Then Paul turns outward. Keep praying, alert and thankful, and pray for him: not that his prison door would open, but a door for the gospel, and that he would speak it clearly. Live wisely towards outsiders, seizing every opportunity, with speech that is gracious and seasoned with salt.

The letter closes with a page of names that shows the gospel in human form: Tychicus the courier, Onesimus the runaway slave now called a faithful brother, Mark the restored deserter, Epaphras wrestling in prayer, Luke the doctor, Demas who would later leave, Nympha and the church in her house, and Archippus, charged to finish his ministry. Paul signs with his chained hand: “Remember my chains. Grace be with you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.

Meaning first. Colossians 4 finishes the household code and closes the letter. Masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, since they too have a Master in heaven (v. 1). Then come three last exhortations: keep at watchful, thankful prayer, praying for Paul’s gospel ministry; walk wisely toward outsiders, making the most of every opportunity; and let your speech be gracious and seasoned with salt (vv. 2–6). Finally Paul sends news and greetings through a remarkable list: Tychicus the letter carrier, Onesimus the runaway slave now a faithful brother, Aristarchus his fellow prisoner, Mark the restored deserter, Epaphras wrestling in prayer, Luke the doctor, Demas, Nympha and the church in her house, and Archippus, charged to fulfil his ministry. He signs with his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you (vv. 7–18). The letter that exalted Christ over the whole universe ends with the same Lord ruling Tychicus’s journey, Onesimus’s homecoming and Archippus’s unfinished task.

Masters. The word is kyrioi, the very same word as Lord. In the Roman world a master held near-absolute power over his slaves. He could command, punish and sell them, and in law even kill them, with little accountability. A slave was reckoned property; Aristotle had called him a living tool, an asset valued for what he produced rather than a person with rights. The duties of the household ran one way only, from slave up to master. That is what makes this verse quietly revolutionary. Paul turns and addresses the masters, and lays an obligation on them.

Treat your bondservants justly and fairly. Justly (dikaios) means rendering what is right and due: honest dealing, fair provision, discipline that is just and not arbitrary. Fairly (isotēs) is literally equality, or equity: even-handed, impartial treatment, with a hint of the deeper truth that in Christ this slave is your equal and your brother. This went far beyond anything Roman law asked. The one-way street becomes two-way, and the slave is suddenly a person to whom justice is owed. Think of Philemon, a master in this very church, about to be told to welcome a runaway back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).

Knowing that you also have a Master in heaven. Here is the whole motive, and it is a masterstroke of wording: the master (kyrios) is told he has a Master (Kyrios). The man who holds the power is himself a servant; over the one at the top of the earthly ladder stands One who owns him completely. So Paul levels the hierarchy not by abolishing it but by pointing straight up. Deal justly with those beneath you, because you will answer for it to the Lord above you, the same Lord with whom there is no partiality (3:25; Ephesians 6:9). The master’s wealth and rank buy him nothing at that throne. The law of Moses had already said it of Israel’s own servants: you shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God (Leviticus 25:43).

Side by side at one throne. There is a humbling sweetness folded into this. Master and slave have the same Master in heaven. They kneel side by side at one throne, equals before the God who made them both and the Saviour who bought them both. At the foot of the cross the boss and the worker are two sinners saved by the same grace, and the Christian who holds authority wields it not as a little lord but as a fellow servant who never forgets the Master over his own shoulder.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul approved of slavery as an institution. He set principles that would in time undermine it: the equal dignity of slave and master, the accountability of every master to Christ, and brotherhood in the church (Philemon 16). Nor does it mean the verse has nothing to say today. The principle applies directly to employers, managers, and anyone with authority over the work and livelihood of others.

What does this look like for an employer or manager today? The old temptation survives intact: to see workers as resources, replaceable parts valued only for their output. We even call the department human resources. Justice and fairness look like a fair wage paid on time, honest contracts kept, safe conditions, no favouritism, and no treating people as disposable when it is convenient. They look like the owner who shares the gain fairly, the manager who disciplines by principle rather than mood, and the boss who treats the night cleaner and the senior partner with the same human dignity. They also look like telling people the truth about their position, and listening when they raise a grievance. The Christian in authority should be the most just and humane employer in town, because he knows whose servant he is.

What if I have power over others but not as an employer? The principle reaches further than the workplace. Teachers over pupils, officers over soldiers, landlords over tenants, carers over the vulnerable, church leaders over congregations, older siblings over younger ones: wherever you hold power over someone, you hold it on loan from the Master in heaven. Ask of every use of that power whether you would be glad to explain it to him. Power is not sinful; it is a stewardship, and the Lord pays particular attention to how the strong treat the weak.

In a sentence. Masters, provide your slaves with what is right and fair, because you know that you also have a Master in heaven.

On a Tuesday. If you manage or employ others, treat them justly and fairly; you will answer to your Master in heaven. This week, think of the person under your authority who is easiest to overlook, and ask what justice and fairness would require for them. Then do one concrete thing: the overdue conversation, the deserved credit, the correction of an unfair arrangement.

For worship. The Master in heaven is not like the masters of Rome. He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but took the form of a servant, and he who had every right to be served came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. He never once treated anyone as a tool. He knew his sheep by name. And because he is the Master of both the slave and the owner, he is the one Lord before whom all human power must finally bow, and under whom the weak are safe. Blessed be the Lord who rules with justice and serves with love.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They are to keep on praying, alert and thankful, and to pray for Paul too, that God will open a door for the message of Christ, for which he is in chains, and that he will make it clear as he should. They should act wisely towards outsiders, making the most of every opportunity, and their conversation should always be gracious and well seasoned, so that they know how to answer each person.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.

Continue steadfastly in prayer. The word (proskartereō) means to persevere, to hold fast, to keep at something doggedly. It is the word used of the first church, who devoted themselves to prayer (Acts 1:14; 2:42). Prayer is not to be occasional, but a steady devotion. And the very fact that Paul must command it tells us something tender: steadfast prayer is hard, and we need the encouragement.

Why prayer is hard. Prayer is hidden labour, with nothing visible to show for it. Answers often seem to tarry, and we grow discouraged. The flesh is weak, and prayer can feel like doing nothing. And there is an enemy who would far rather we did anything than pray. So Paul does not say pray when you feel like it; he says keep at it. It was for exactly this that Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow, to show that they ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Do not measure your praying by how it feels. Simply do not stop.

Being watchful in it. The word (grēgoreō) means stay awake, alert, on guard, like a sentry on night watch who dare not doze. It carries the memory of Gethsemane, where the Lord found his disciples asleep and said watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38). To be watchful is to pray awake, with the mind present; with open eyes, alert to what needs praying for and expectant for God’s answer, like a watchman looking for the dawn; and vigilant, alert to temptation and to the coming of Christ. Prayer’s great enemy is less hostility than drowsiness.

With thanksgiving. Thankfulness sounds yet again in this short letter (1:3, 12; 2:7; 3:15–17), now woven right into prayer. It keeps prayer from collapsing into a list of demands, lifting the eyes from what we lack to all God has already given. And that backward look fuels the perseverance Paul has just commanded, because the grateful person prays and keeps praying. Prayer without thanksgiving soon turns into complaint. We do not come to wring favours from a reluctant stranger, but as children to a Father who has already given us his Son (Philippians 4:6; Romans 8:32).

What it does not mean. It does not mean praying every second of the day, or that a Christian who works, sleeps and enjoys a meal is failing. It means a life marked by persistent, alert, grateful prayer: set times of prayer, and a habit of turning to God through the day.

What can I do when my mind wanders every time I pray? Almost everyone finds this, so do not conclude you are unfit to pray. Try praying out loud, quietly, or writing your prayers down; both keep the mind on track. Pray with an open Bible, turning a psalm or passage into prayer phrase by phrase, so you are answering God rather than inventing from nothing. Keep a short list of people and needs, so you are not searching for what to say. When your mind drifts, do not scold yourself; turn the distraction into a prayer and come back. And remember that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, interceding for us when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26).

Does persistent prayer change God’s mind? God is not reluctant, and he is not informed by our prayers of things he did not know. But he has ordained that many of his purposes are carried out through the prayers of his people, so that prayer is a real cause in his world, though never a lever on his will. Persistence is not wearing him down; it is depending on him, and in the waiting he is often changing us. Keep asking, because he invites you to, and trust that he will answer as a wise Father, sometimes with yes, sometimes with wait, and sometimes with something better than you asked.

In a sentence. Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful.

On a Tuesday. Set a regular time for prayer today, even ten minutes, and keep it tomorrow. Begin with thanks: name three specific mercies before you ask for anything. Then pray for one thing you have stopped praying for because the answer seemed slow. And when you notice yourself drifting during the day, let that be the signal to pray a sentence.

For worship. In the garden the disciples slept, and Jesus kept watch alone. He watched and prayed through the darkest night in history so that his weak and drowsy people might be kept, and the one who keeps his people neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4). Our feeble, wandering prayers do not reach the Father on their own merit; they come through the Son, and the Father who did not spare his own Son will not turn away the children for whom he gave him. Thanks be to God for a Saviour who stayed awake for us, and for a door into his presence that no drowsiness of ours can close.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison— that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison—that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.

At the same time, pray also for us. Stop and feel the weight of this. Paul, the apostle chosen by the risen Christ, the man caught up into paradise, a writer of Scripture and planter of churches across the empire, turns to a small congregation he has never met and asks them to pray for him. The greatest Christian of his age leans on the prayers of ordinary, faraway believers. Even the most mature Christian never outgrows his need of his brothers’ prayers (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19), and the humblest believer’s prayers truly count. Your prayers for your pastor are no formality. God has chosen to move his hand through them.

That God may open to us a door for the word. The open door is Paul’s picture for a God-given opportunity to preach (1 Corinthians 16:9; Acts 14:27; Revelation 3:8). Mark two things. First, it is God who opens it. Even the chance to speak of Christ is a gift of his providence, not the fruit of our cleverness. Second, and tenderly: a man in chains does not ask for the prison door to open. He asks for a door for the word. His own freedom is not his first concern; the gospel’s is. He could write elsewhere that he was bound with chains as a criminal, but the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9).

To declare the mystery of Christ. A mystery in Paul is not a puzzle but a secret long hidden in the heart of God and now thrown open: Christ in you, the hope of glory, including Gentiles in God’s people (1:26–27). The word presses the point that the gospel is not a system or a secret technique, as the false teachers offered their initiates, but a Person: God’s mystery, which is Christ (2:2).

On account of which I am in prison. Then, quietly, one of the wonders of this letter: Paul names the reason for his chains without a word of complaint against Rome, his accusers or God, and without a breath of self-pity. He looks past the magistrates and soldiers to the sovereign hand behind them, and calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1). He so believed in the reign of God that he could write from a cell that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12). That is what it looks like to believe that God is sovereign: peace where there might have been bitterness, and purpose where there might have been despair.

That I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak. Finally he asks for prayer not only for an open door but for a clear word. The verb (phaneroō) means to reveal, to make plain. The most gifted preacher the church has known does not presume on his own eloquence, but asks for prayer to speak plainly. An open door is wasted without a clear message on the far side of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about release, or that it is wrong to pray for freedom from suffering. Elsewhere he hoped to be released and to visit (Philemon 22). It means he cared more about the gospel than about his comfort, and that his first request was for the word to run.

What about my own prisons? The verse searches us. Most of us will never be in chains for the gospel, but we have our own confinements: unjust treatment, a shut door, an illness, a hard providence that will not lift. What do we do with them? Grumble at people and at God, or trust the sovereign hand and ask how Christ might be made known even here? The hospital ward, the job you cannot leave, the town you did not choose: each may be the place God has opened a door for the word. Pray for release if you wish, and pray first for the door.

How do I pray for missionaries and pastors? Use this verse as your outline. Pray that God would open doors: real opportunities, people ready to listen, freedom to speak. Pray for clarity: that they would explain Christ plainly and faithfully, without obscurity or compromise. Pray for courage, since Paul asked for boldness in the parallel (Ephesians 6:19–20). Pray for contentment and faith in hardship. And then ask them what they need, and pray specifically. A missionary’s newsletter is a prayer list in disguise.

In a sentence. And pray for us, too, that God may open a door for our message, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which Paul is in chains. Pray that he may proclaim it clearly, as he should.

On a Tuesday. Pray for open doors and clear words for one missionary and for your own pastor, by name, today. And pray it for yourself, whenever you try to explain the hope that is in you: Lord, open a door, and make me clear.

For worship. The word that Paul longed to declare is the Word himself, who was made flesh and whom no chain could bind. They bound Jesus and led him away, nailed him down and sealed his tomb, and on the third day he walked out, and the word of the gospel has been running through the world ever since. The Lord who holds the keys of death and Hades opens doors that no one can shut. Glory to the risen Christ, whose gospel cannot be imprisoned.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.

Walk in wisdom toward outsiders. Paul has asked them to pray for his witness (vv. 3–4); now he turns to theirs. The two belong together: pray for the gospel’s advance, and live so as to advance it. Having set forth the supremacy of Christ, the new life and the transformed home, Paul now sends that life out to the watching world. Outsiders are the non-Christians among whom they live, and Paul cares greatly how the church appears to them, because the world reads the gospel first in the lives of those who profess it (1 Thessalonians 4:12; 1 Peter 2:12).

In wisdom. To walk is the whole conduct of life, and in wisdom means with the skill, discernment and tact of the wisdom hidden in Christ (2:3), knowing how to live before non-Christians in a way that adorns the gospel rather than repelling people from it. It looks like integrity, kindness, a blameless life that disarms criticism, and the tact to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. And it avoids two ditches at once: compromise, blending into the world until no one can tell the difference, and harsh superiority, the sour, judgmental believer the world rightly recoils from.

The only offence. The only offence we should ever give is the offence of the cross. Christ crucified is a stumbling block to some and folly to others (1 Corinthians 1:23), and Paul would not remove that offence for anyone (Galatians 5:11). But he took great care that nothing else, no rudeness, hypocrisy or foolishness of ours, should stand in its way. If outsiders stumble, let it be over Christ and not over us. In pagan Colossae, walking in wisdom meant the Christian who was honest in the market and would not join the drunken temple feasts, yet was no sneering prig. Today it is the believer at work who is diligent and will not gossip or cut corners, the neighbour who is quick to help, the Christian online who does not meet every quarrel with cruelty. Your daily conduct before your unbelieving colleagues is itself an argument, for Christ or against him.

Making the best use of the time. The phrase is vivid: literally, buying up the opportunity (exagorazomai ton kairon). The word for time is not the ticking clock (chronos) but the opportune moment (kairos), the open window. The picture is a shrewd merchant snapping up a bargain before it is gone. It means seizing every God-given opening to commend Christ before it passes, because the days are evil, as the parallel adds (Ephesians 5:16). Opportunities are fleeting and life is short; the open window with this neighbour or that relative may not come again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean being pushy or manipulative, turning every conversation into a sales pitch or treating people as projects. Wisdom notices when a word would be welcome and when it would only be noise. It means being wise, alert and ready, so that when the window opens you are not asleep.

How do I spot an opportunity without forcing one? Listen more than you speak. Opportunities usually arrive as questions, griefs or crises: someone mentions a death in the family, asks how you stay so calm, confesses a fear, or notices you went to church. The window is often a single sentence, and the wise response is often a single sentence back, honest, gentle and brief, with an open door to say more: can I tell you what has helped me? Pray each morning that God would put such moments in your path and make you notice them. Then, when one comes, take it, and leave the result to him.

If I am shy, am I failing at this? No. Walking in wisdom is first a matter of how you live, and a shy believer who is honest, kind and faithful is already speaking loudly. You do not need to be an extrovert to buy up opportunities. A card to a neighbour who has lost someone, an invitation to a carol service, a book given with a short note, or a quiet answer when asked why you believe: these are open to anyone. God has used quiet people for far more of the world’s conversions than famous ones.

In a sentence. Be wise in the way you act toward outsiders; make the most of every opportunity.

On a Tuesday. Name one unbeliever you see regularly, at work, next door or in your family. Pray for them by name this morning, and ask God for one opportunity this week to speak or act for Christ toward them. Then watch for it, and when it comes, buy it up.

For worship. Christ walked in perfect wisdom among outsiders. He ate with tax collectors, spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well, touched lepers and welcomed children, and the common people heard him gladly. He never wasted a moment, and he never forced one: he would not be hurried before his hour, and when it came he set his face toward Jerusalem and did not turn aside. Blessed is the Saviour who came to seek and to save the lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.

Let your speech always be gracious. Note the sweep: always, all your talk, not merely your religious talk. Gracious is literally with grace. It means speech that is kind and winsome, not harsh, sarcastic or preachy. And more, it means speech that actually gives grace to those who hear (Ephesians 4:29), as the gracious words that came from the mouth of Jesus drew the crowds (Luke 4:22).

Seasoned with salt. Salt gave food flavour and kept it from spoiling, and Greek writers used salt as a picture of wit. So salted speech is not bland, insipid talk but speech with savour, interest and substance, worth listening to; and it is wholesome, free of what is corrupt or coarse. This is the opposite of the modern sense of salty speech, which is crude. Paul means tasteful and lively, not foul.

Grace and salt together. Hold the two together and you see the balance. Speech that is gracious but not salted is kind but bland: gushing, sentimental, saying nothing memorable. Speech that is salted but not gracious is clever but cruel, witty at someone else’s expense. The Christian’s tongue is to be both at once: kind and interesting, warm and with bite, truthful and winsome, just as the Lord spoke words that drew people in yet carried a point and stayed in the memory. In practice it is answering a hostile remark with unexpected kindness, seasoning a hard truth so it can be heard, and trading the coarse joke and the sour complaint for words that build people up.

So that you may know how you ought to answer each person. The aim of it all is to be ready to give a fitting reply to each one who asks. Mark each person: not a single canned formula fired at everyone, but an answer suited to this individual, his question, his objection, his need. What sort of questions? The watching world’s honest enquiries and challenges: why do you live like that? Why are you so hopeful? Peter says the same: always be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Wisdom listens before it speaks.

The soil and the fruit. See how the verse hangs together. Gracious, flavourful speech is the soil, and readiness to answer is the fruit. Winsome everyday words draw people to ask; harsh or insipid talk shuts the conversation before it begins. You need not have a sermon by heart, only a gracious, salted tongue and a heart ready with a fitting word (Proverbs 15:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean compromising the truth to be pleasant, or never saying anything that could offend. Jesus never traded truth for applause. It means speaking truth graciously, so that if people are offended, it is by the truth and not by us.

What if someone asks a question I cannot answer? Say so honestly. I don’t know, but I would like to find out, is a gracious answer, and it often opens a second conversation. You are not required to win every argument; you are asked to give a reason for your hope, and the simplest reason is often the strongest: what Christ has done for you, and why you trust him. Then go and find out, read, ask your pastor, and come back. People are usually more moved by a Christian who is humble and honest than by one who has a quick reply for everything.

In a sentence. Let your conversation be always full of grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak today, ask: is this gracious? Is it seasoned with salt? Listen for one moment when you are about to be sharp or sarcastic, and replace it with something kind and true. And think through, in a few plain sentences, how you would answer if someone asked you today why you are a Christian.

For worship. No one ever spoke like this man. Grace was poured upon his lips; he knew how to sustain with a word him who is weary; he silenced his accusers and comforted sinners in the same afternoon. He answered the rich young ruler, the woman at the well and the thief on the cross each in the way that fitted, and every word was true and every word was kind. The Word made flesh is full of grace and truth, and he is teaching our clumsy tongues to speak with his accent. Blessed be the Lord whose words are spirit and life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with news and greetings that show the network of people behind his mission. Tychicus will bring the letter and his news, together with Onesimus, the runaway slave now a faithful brother. Aristarchus, Mark (Barnabas’s cousin), and Jesus called Justus send greetings, the only Jewish believers working with him, and a comfort to him. Epaphras, their own founder, wrestles in prayer for them and for Laodicea and Hierapolis. Luke the doctor and Demas greet them. Paul asks them to greet the church in Nympha’s house, to exchange letters with Laodicea, and to tell Archippus to complete his ministry. He signs the greeting in his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Community of the Gospel as the Body of Christ

The list of names at the end of Colossians is the practical expression of the ecclesiology of 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstract entity; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. The community of grace is always concrete, always named, always embodied in particular people with particular histories, gifts, and needs. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted on the visible, particular, local church as the primary form of the body of Christ: not an ideal church somewhere, but this church, these people, this place, this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Onesimus is the most striking name on the list. The runaway slave, the subject of the letter to Philemon, is now a “faithful and beloved brother” being commended to the Colossians. The gospel has done exactly what Paul said it would do in 3:11: it has abolished the slave/free distinction as a defining category. Onesimus and Philemon are brothers; Onesimus and the Colossians are family. Now: The community of the gospel is always the community of the surprising, the reconciled, the transformed. The people who would never have been in the same room together are gathered at the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,

Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. A modern reader is tempted to skim a page of ancient names. Do not. This closing roll call is a photograph of the gospel at work, and it quietly preaches everything the letter has argued. Listen to the words Paul keeps reaching for: beloved brother, faithful minister, fellow servant, fellow prisoner, a comfort to me. These are not colleagues but family. And the first name, Tychicus, is the courier. A native of the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), he travelled with Paul and was trusted with his letters more than once. He carried these pages from Paul’s prison to Colossae with Onesimus walking beside him, and he carried the letter we call Ephesians on the same journey (Ephesians 6:21–22), and probably the letter to Philemon too.

He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. Three titles land on one man. Beloved brother: family. Faithful minister: dependable service, the word from which we get deacon. Fellow servant: partnership, literally fellow slave, standing beside Paul under the same Master.

I have sent him to you for this very purpose. Notice that Paul does not send him merely to deliver paper. He has two jobs, and the second is the larger. Tychicus is to tell them how Paul is faring, since a church that had never met Paul was anxious about him; and then to encourage their hearts, the same longing Paul expressed for them in 2:2. The word of God arrived at Colossae in the hands of a man whose commission was to love the people he was sent to.
