Scripture reaches most people through somebody, a parent, a preacher, a friend who would not give up on them, and the messenger’s character is not incidental to the message. Paul could have sent a courier. He sent a brother.

As the Father has sent me. Behind Paul’s sending of Tychicus stands a greater sending. Every messenger of the gospel is a fellow servant in the Lord, sent under Christ, who was himself the Sent One. The Father sent the Son into the world not to condemn it but to save it (John 3:17), and the risen Jesus said to his disciples, As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21). So a messenger who travels a long road to encourage hearts is doing in small what Christ did in full: coming in person, at cost, to people who needed more than a letter. The gospel still arrives the way its Lord arrived.

Sent to reassure. And observe what Tychicus was not given: any authority over the Colossians, or any brief to inspect or correct them. Paul had plenty he could have said to a church flirting with false teaching, and he had said it in the letter. The man he sends in person is sent to reassure. Sometimes the most useful thing you can carry into a troubled congregation is not another correction but your own steady, loving presence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only famous Christians matter to God, or that the letter carriers of the church are unimportant. Tychicus was a faithful messenger whose name would be forgotten if not for a few greetings, and Scripture honours him by name. The Lord notices the people who carry the letters.

Why does sharing news matter in the church? Because the church is a family, and families want to know how their members are. Paul thought it worth a long, dangerous journey for the Colossians to hear how he was. News is the raw material of prayer and love: you cannot pray for someone whose circumstances you never hear about, or rejoice with someone whose joys are never shared. Prayer letters, a word of news after the service, a visit to someone housebound: these are not trivial. They knit the body together and encourage hearts, which is exactly why Tychicus was sent.

In a sentence. Tychicus will tell you all the news about Paul. He is a dear brother, a faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. Paul is sending him to you for the express purpose that you may know about our circumstances and that he may encourage your hearts.

On a Tuesday. Think of the Tychicus in your own church: the person who carries things, sets up chairs, drives the elderly, sends the news. Thank them this week, specifically. And ask whether there is someone you could go and encourage simply by turning up.

For worship. Every title Paul gives Tychicus belonged first to Christ. He is the beloved Son in whom the Father delights; he was faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:6); he took the form of a servant and came not to be served but to serve. And he is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Tychicus is beloved, faithful and a fellow servant only in the Lord, because the Lord first shared his own names with people like him. Blessed be the faithful Master who makes faithful servants, and calls the couriers of his word his family.

verseByVerse.quote: and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.

And with him Onesimus. Here is one of the great sentences of the New Testament hiding in a list of names. We know exactly who this is, because Paul wrote a whole letter about him. Onesimus was a slave in the household of Philemon, a member of the Colossian church. He had run away, and in Roman law a runaway slave was a criminal whose owner could have him branded, flogged, or worse, and who could expect no sympathy from any magistrate in the empire. Somewhere in his flight he had met Paul in prison and been converted (Philemon 10). Now he is walking back into the town he fled, carrying a letter to his master.

Our faithful and beloved brother. Read how Paul introduces him to the congregation that knew him as somebody’s runaway property. Not Onesimus, whom I am returning to his master. Not a word about his legal position. Our faithful and beloved brother: the identical phrase he has just used of Tychicus, a free man and an apostolic delegate. The two men are given the same titles in the same breath, and the Colossians are to receive them on the same terms. And Onesimus, a slave, is trusted as a messenger alongside Tychicus to tell them the news. The gospel has transformed his status before the church long before it changes his status before the law.

Who is one of you. Then four words that go further still. He is not an outsider being tolerated. He belongs. He is a member of that church, with the same standing as the man who owns him. Paul does not argue for this, soften it or explain himself. He simply states it, in a public letter that would be read aloud in the room where Philemon was sitting.

The doctrine walking through the door. Set this beside 3:11, a few paragraphs earlier: here there is not Greek and Jew, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all. Here is that doctrine walking through the door on two legs. Paul does not stage a revolt against Rome’s slave system; he does something slower and more corrosive to it, putting a runaway and a delegate side by side with the same titles. And there is a gentle play on the name, which Paul makes openly in Philemon 11: Onesimus means useful. Formerly he was useless, Paul says, but now he is indeed useful.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul excused Onesimus’s wrong. The letter to Philemon shows that he sought reconciliation and offered to make restitution himself: if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account (Philemon 18). Grace did not pretend the wrong had not happened. It paid for it, and made him a brother.

What should a church do with a new believer who has a criminal past? Receive him as Paul received Onesimus: as a faithful and beloved brother, one of us, not a project or a risk to be managed in whispers. Wisdom still matters: where there is real danger to others, especially to children, safeguards are a form of love, and a repentant person will understand them. Where restitution is owed, it should be made, as Paul arranged. But the man’s name in the church is no longer his record. Do not keep reminding him of his past, do not introduce him by it, and do not hold him at arm’s length. Christ has not.

In a sentence. He is coming with Onesimus, our faithful and dear brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond God’s grace. Think of someone in your church whose past makes you slightly uneasy, and this week treat them in a way that says: you are one of us. Sit with them, ask about their week, give them a job to do. And if your own past embarrasses you, read this verse again. That is what the gospel does with a history: it does not pretend the history away, and it refuses to let it be your name.

For worship. Onesimus walked home with a letter that said charge it to my account, and in that sentence the whole gospel was written small. We were runaways from our Master, with a record that deserved the worst. And the Son of God said to the Father: if he owes you anything, charge it to me. He paid what we had stolen and more, and then sent us home with a new name. Faithful and beloved brother: that is how Christ introduces the runaways he has redeemed. Glory to the Saviour who makes the useless useful and the outcast family.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was the runaway slave of Philemon, a member of the church at Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you. Three men, and each carries a story worth pausing on. Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 20:4). He had been seized by the mob in the theatre at Ephesus (Acts 19:29) and had sailed with Paul on the voyage that ended in shipwreck (Acts 27:2). Now he is in custody with him. The word Paul uses (synaichmalōtos) is literally fellow prisoner of war, a man captured alongside him in the same campaign. In Philemon 24 Paul gives the title fellow prisoner to Epaphras instead, so some have thought the companions took turns sharing his confinement. Either way, here is a Christian whose name we would never have known but for a greeting, who followed the apostle into a riot, a shipwreck and a cell.

And Mark the cousin of Barnabas. Read the next phrase carefully, because it is the sound of a wound healing. This is the John Mark who abandoned Paul and Barnabas partway through the first missionary journey and went home (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas wanted to take him again, Paul refused, and the disagreement was sharp enough to split the two men and end their partnership (Acts 15:37–39). Now Paul is writing ahead to make sure Mark gets a warm reception.

Concerning whom you have received instructions; if he comes to you, welcome him. Paul is aware that a church might have heard the story and be wary of Mark because of his past, and so he says it plainly: welcome him. Years later, near the very end, Paul will send for him: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). The deserter became indispensable. Grace does not discard those who have failed. It restores them, and it restores the people they failed, too, for Paul’s own heart had to change toward Mark.

The Gospel a restored man wrote. The early church held that this Mark wrote the second Gospel, and the book bears the marks of a man who knew both failure and grace. It does not spare the disciples: when Jesus was arrested, they all left him and fled (Mark 14:50). Yet it also records the angel’s message at the empty tomb: go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). The risen Lord sent word by name to the man who had denied him. The Gospel that bears his name preaches what his own life proved: a deserter can be called back. The welcome Paul now asks for him is simply the risen Christ’s way with his failures, passed on.

And Jesus who is called Justus. Jesus was a common Jewish name, the Greek form of Joshua, and this man also used the Roman name Justus. He is otherwise unknown, an ordinary believer with an ordinary name, remembered for ever because he stood by Paul.

These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God. Only three Jewish believers in Paul’s whole circle at that moment, and the word only carries a quiet ache. This is the man who could wish himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his kinsmen (Romans 9:3). He is apostle to the Gentiles by calling, and it evidently cost him something to look around a room and count three of his own people. Many Jewish believers of the time opposed his mission to the Gentiles, and some actively worked against him.

And they have been a comfort to me. The word (parēgoria) appears only here in the New Testament. It is a medical term, the root behind paregoric, a soothing medicine that eases pain. These three men were medicine to the apostle’s soul. Paul was not a self-sufficient hero. He needed friends, and he said so.

Fellow workers for the kingdom of God. One phrase here has puzzled readers. Paul speaks of the kingdom far less than Jesus does in the Gospels, and some conclude it is not the church’s present business, that it belongs to Israel or waits wholly in the future. There is a real truth in that instinct and it should be honoured: the kingdom in its full visible glory is still to come, when Christ returns. But notice what Paul writes: these men are, right now, fellow workers for it. And earlier in this letter he said that God has already transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (1:13). So the kingdom is already here, wherever Christ is owned as King, and not yet consummated, awaiting his return in glory. We live in it now and labour for its advance, while we wait for its dawning in full (Romans 14:17; Acts 28:31).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Mark’s earlier failure did not matter, or that the quarrel with Barnabas was trivial. Real damage had been done and real hurt felt. It means failure need not be final. Restoration took time, and it took change on both sides.

If I have failed in serving God, can I be used again? Yes. Mark deserted in the middle of a mission and became the man Paul asked for at the end of his life. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored by the lakeside to feed his sheep. God’s grace is not only for the start of the Christian life but for its failures along the way. Be honest about what happened, put right what you can, accept that trust may need to be rebuilt over time, and then take up whatever service is put in front of you, however small. The question is not whether you have failed but whether you will let him restore you.

In a sentence. Paul’s fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you his greetings, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas. (You have received instructions about him; if he comes to you, welcome him.) Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings. These are the only Jews among Paul’s co-workers for the kingdom of God, and they have proved a comfort to him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a Mark in your life, someone who let you down and whom you have quietly written off? Ask whether God has changed him, and whether he is asking you to welcome him back. And think of one servant of Christ who is carrying a heavy load. Be a comfort to them this week: a note, a meal, a prayer said with them rather than just for them.

For worship. When Jesus was bound, no Aristarchus stood beside him to share his chains. He went into the dark without a comforter, so that none of his servants would ever be without one. Now the King of the kingdom gathers the failures, the fearful and the forgotten and makes them his fellow workers. He gives a lonely apostle three friends to be medicine to his soul, and as his sufferings overflow to his people, so through him their comfort overflows too (2 Corinthians 1:5). Blessed be the forsaken Lord who never forsakes his own.
verseByVerse.note: Mark had once left Paul, causing a split with Barnabas; he is now restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.

Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you. Epaphras is the most important name in the list for the Colossians, because without him there would be no church at Colossae to write to. He was the man who first brought them the gospel. Paul called him our beloved fellow servant and a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf (1:7), and it was his report that prompted this letter. Now he is far from home, with Paul. And Paul gives him the title servant of Christ Jesus, literally slave (doulos), a title Paul uses of himself elsewhere (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1) and in this letter gives to no other individual.

Always struggling on your behalf in his prayers. The word (agōnizomai) is the athlete’s straining word, the root of our agony, used of a wrestler in the contest. It is the same word Paul used of his own labour in 1:29 and 2:1. This is not a man who mentions Colossae in his devotions. He is wrestling. Most of us think of intercession as the least strenuous thing a Christian does. Epaphras is hundreds of miles away and can do nothing else for these people, and the New Testament calls what he is doing combat. If prayer is genuinely wrestling, then the person who says all I can do is pray has misunderstood which activity is the strenuous one.

That you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. Mark the content of his prayer, because it is the whole letter distilled into one petition. Stand: firm, not shifted off Christ (2:6–7). Mature (teleioi): full-grown, the goal Paul named in 1:28. And note the sting, since the false teachers were offering an advanced inner circle. Paul’s maturity is not a grade above ordinary Christians; it is the growing up of people already filled in Christ (2:10). Fully assured (peplērophorēmenoi) is a wonderful word meaning carried all the way to settled conviction: not tentative, not hedging, not swayed by every new teacher. And all of it in all the will of God: not in esoteric secrets, but resting in the whole will of God made known in his Son.

For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis. Three towns within a dozen or so miles of one another in the Lycus valley: Colossae; Laodicea, the wealthy banking centre; and Hierapolis across the valley, about six miles from Laodicea, famous for its hot springs. Epaphras had evidently evangelised and cared for the whole valley, and Paul, who had never been there, formally vouches for him. Such a word steadies a congregation’s confidence in the man who taught them, especially when other teachers are trying to undermine him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wrestling prayer is only for spiritual giants or for those with a special gift of intercession. Epaphras was an ordinary believer from Colossae before he was anything else. Every Christian can wrestle in prayer, and every Christian is called to.

What do I actually pray for the people I love? Most of our praying, if we are honest, is for their circumstances to improve: health, jobs, exams, journeys. Those are good things to pray, and God invites them. But Epaphras wrestles for their maturity and assurance. He wants them standing, grown and certain. It is a larger ambition than comfort, and it is the one that survives whatever happens to their circumstances. Try praying Paul’s and Epaphras’s prayers for your children, your friends and your church: that they would stand firm in Christ, grow up into him, and be fully assured of his love and his will. Use the prayers of 1:9–12 as your words.

In a sentence. Epaphras, who is one of you and a servant of Christ Jesus, sends greetings. He is always wrestling in prayer for you, that you may stand firm in all the will of God, mature and fully assured. Paul vouches for him that he is working hard for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.

On a Tuesday. Wrestle in prayer for your church today, like Epaphras. Choose three people and pray for them not only about their circumstances but about their souls: that they would stand, grow and be sure. Keep at it for a week, and notice what it does to your love for them.

For worship. Behind Epaphras on his knees stands a greater Intercessor. In Gethsemane Jesus wrestled in prayer until his sweat became like great drops of blood, and on the night before he died he prayed for his disciples and for all who would believe through their word. He still prays, at the Father’s right hand, and he prays that we may stand. The church at Colossae was held up by the prayers of a faithful pastor and by the prayers of the Son of God. So are we. Glory to the High Priest who ever lives to make intercession for his people.
verseByVerse.note: Hierapolis lay across the valley from Laodicea.

verseByVerse.quote: Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.

Luke the beloved physician greets you. Nine words, two names, and between them one of the saddest contrasts in Scripture, though nobody reading the letter that day could have known it. This is the author of the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, and it is the only place in the New Testament where we are told his trade. It fits how he writes: the careful research of one who had followed all things closely (Luke 1:3), and a precise interest in illness. He is not listed among the men of the circumcision (v. 11), so he was most probably a Gentile, perhaps the only Gentile writer in the New Testament. And in the we passages of Acts he is a travelling companion who quietly writes himself into the story without ever naming himself.

Beloved. Beloved is Paul’s own word for him, and the picture it opens is worth having. Paul was a man with a physical affliction he could not shake (2 Corinthians 12:7; Galatians 4:13–14), flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned once and shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). Travelling with him, for years, was a doctor. And at the very end, when everyone else had gone, Paul wrote: Luke alone is with me (2 Timothy 4:11). God works through ordinary means, and using doctors and medicine is no lack of faith. The apostle who healed others by God’s power still travelled with a physician.

As does Demas. Three words, and no title. Tychicus is a beloved brother, Onesimus is faithful and beloved, Epaphras is a servant of Christ Jesus, Luke is the beloved physician. Demas gets his name and nothing else. Here he is still a fellow worker (Philemon 24). Whether or not Paul meant anything by the brevity, the sequel is on record. Years later Paul wrote: Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4:10). He is not accused of scandal or heresy. He fell in love with this present world, the ordinary, respectable pull of comfort, safety and a quieter life, and the pull was stronger than his attachment to a chained old man in Rome. That is how most people leave. Not with a repudiation but with a drift.

Two loves. Paul’s own words in that last letter set Demas against a better love. A few lines before he writes that Demas loved this present world, he speaks of the crown laid up for all who have loved the Lord’s appearing (2 Timothy 4:8, 10). The same verb stands in both places. Demas did not lose interest in religion; he found something he loved more than the coming of Christ. That is the root of every drift, and it is answered not by trying harder to love the world less, but by seeing more of the one who is coming. Christ who is your life will appear (3:4), and a heart that longs for that day has less room for the pull of this one.

Two possibilities side by side. So the verse holds two Christian lives side by side: the man who stayed to the end, and the man who did not. Both sent their greetings, and nobody in Colossae could have told them apart. Serving alongside great Christians does not guarantee faithfulness to the end. Let it make us watchful rather than smug, and let it make us pray, as Epaphras did, that we may stand.

Was Demas a true believer who lost his salvation? Scripture does not tell us his final state. Here he is a fellow worker; later he deserts. If he never returned, the Reformed reading is that he showed he had never truly belonged, for they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). And he may have returned; we are not told, and we should not pronounce on him. What we do know is that those whom God has truly called and justified, he keeps to the end (Romans 8:30; John 10:28–29). The doctrine of perseverance does not make warnings like this unnecessary. It is one of the means by which God keeps his people: he warns them, and they take heed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Demas was certainly lost, or that every Christian who goes through a cold season is a Demas. It means we must guard our hearts against the love of the world, which rarely announces itself and usually looks perfectly reasonable.

How do I know if I am drifting like Demas? Watch for the quiet signs rather than the dramatic ones. Prayer becoming rare and then optional. Gathering with God’s people slipping from weekly to occasional, always for a good reason. Scripture squeezed out by screens. Conversations with believers becoming awkward because you have less to say. Decisions about jobs, homes and money made without any reference to Christ’s kingdom. A growing irritation with Christians who seem too serious. None of these alone proves anything. Together they are a direction. If you see them, do not despair; turn back now, tell a trusted friend, and go back to the means of grace. The Shepherd goes after drifting sheep.

In a sentence. Our dear friend Luke, the doctor, and Demas send greetings.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly what in this present world is pulling hardest at you right now: comfort, security, success, approval. Name it before God. Then do one thing this week that deliberately puts Christ’s kingdom ahead of it. And thank God for the Lukes in your life, the people who have stayed.

For worship. There is one friend who never deserts. When all forsook Paul, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). When the disciples fled, Christ went on alone to the cross for them, and he has promised that he will never leave us nor forsake us. He is the Great Physician, who heals the sick soul, and the faithful Shepherd, who keeps his sheep to the end. We are drawn to love this present world, and he loved us more than his own life. He is faithful, and he will keep us.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, the author of Luke and Acts, was a doctor. Demas later deserted Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.

Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea. Laodicea keeps appearing in this letter (2:1; 4:13, 16). It lay about ten miles off, a rich banking town famous for its black wool and an eye salve, and Paul is knitting these valley congregations together: greet them, swap letters with them, pray for them. The churches were not to be self-contained little societies. Brothers here, as often in Paul, includes the sisters.

And to Nympha and the church in her house. Two things sit in this short verse, and both are easy to walk past. The first is Nympha herself. A woman is named, and a congregation meets in her home. For the first two centuries or more Christians met in houses, which had to be large enough, and their owners willing to fill them every week with people who might attract official attention. Nympha had means, and she used them. The New Testament names several such women: Lydia at Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40), Priscilla with Aquila (1 Corinthians 16:19), and Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12). The early church would have been homeless without them.

The church in her house. The second is the shape of it. The church in her house tells you what a first-century congregation actually looked like: not a hall but a room; not an audience but a group small enough to eat together. When Paul writes about bearing with one another and forgiving each other (3:13), he is describing people who sat in the same room every week and could not avoid one another’s faults. Our arrangements are different. The demand is not.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read a man’s name, Nymphas, and his house, as the ESV footnote mentions. The feminine reading is better supported, and it is the one most modern translations follow.

A shadow over Laodicea. There is a shadow over the name for anyone who reads on. A generation later the risen Christ dictates a letter to this same church, rebuking it because it says it is rich, has prospered, and needs nothing, not realising that it is wretched, pitiable, poor, blind and naked (Revelation 3:17). Paul greets them warmly here, and the warning is not yet needed. Churches can be greeted by an apostle and still drift. The Laodicea of Colossians 4 and the Laodicea of Revelation 3 are the same address. And yet even there the risen Lord does not give up on them. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, he says, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Revelation 3:20). The Lord who rebukes them still wants a place at their table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Nympha was the pastor or elder of the church. Hosting a church was a valuable and costly ministry of hospitality and generosity, and the New Testament honours it by name; the oversight of the church was given to qualified elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). Recognising both of these honours Nympha rightly and keeps the shape Scripture gives the church.

Could my home be used for the church? Very likely, and in more ways than you think. You do not need a large house. A kitchen table is enough for a Bible study for four, a meal for a lonely student, coffee after a funeral, a prayer meeting, or a place where a new family in the church can be made welcome. Hospitality is commanded of all believers (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), not only of the gifted. It will cost time and tidiness, and it will sometimes be inconvenient. That is what made Nympha’s gift a gift.

In a sentence. Give Paul’s greetings to the brothers and sisters at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.

On a Tuesday. Could your home be used for church life this month: a Bible study, a prayer meeting, a meal for someone on their own? Pick a date and invite someone. And pray today for a church other than your own, by name, as Paul did for Laodicea.

For worship. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head, and yet he has made his home in his people. He promised that where two or three gather in his name, he is there among them, and in every crowded room in Laodicea and every kitchen where believers meet today, he keeps his word. One day the house of many rooms will be opened, and the Host himself will serve his guests at the marriage supper of the Lamb. Blessed be the Lord who had no house of his own, and has gone to prepare a place for us in his Father’s.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.

And when this letter has been read among you. Start with the obvious thing that is not obvious to us. Read among you means read aloud, to the gathered congregation (1 Thessalonians 5:27). Copies were expensive and literacy limited, so for most Christians through most of the church’s history Scripture came in through the ears, in a room full of other people. Paul was writing for the ear, and the public reading of Scripture is still a central part of Christian worship (1 Timothy 4:13).

Have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans. The instruction is more significant than it looks. From the very beginning these were public documents for the whole people of God, not private mail. Paul expects congregations to swap his letters, copy them, and read one another’s. That habit, churches passing letters round the Lycus valley and beyond, is one of the first stirrings of what became the collected New Testament. Nobody convened a committee to decide it; it began with an apostle telling one small church to share what it had.

The word of Christ, passed hand to hand. Why should a letter from a prisoner carry such weight that churches must read it aloud and pass it on? Because the apostles did not speak on their own authority. Jesus promised them that the Spirit would teach them all things and bring to their remembrance all that he had said (John 14:26), and Paul received his gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12). What the Colossians were sending on to Laodicea was the word of Christ that Paul had told them to let dwell in them richly (3:16). In the apostles’ letters the risen Lord is still speaking to his churches.

And see that you also read the letter from Laodicea. What was the letter from Laodicea? We do not know, and honesty serves better than invention here. It may simply be lost: a letter of Paul’s that God did not intend to preserve, which need not alarm us, since Paul wrote at least one other letter to Corinth that we do not have (1 Corinthians 5:9). Many have thought it is the letter we call Ephesians, written as a circular to several churches and reaching Laodicea before Colossae; some early manuscripts lack the words in Ephesus in Ephesians 1:1. A forged Epistle to the Laodiceans appeared later, and the church rightly refused it.

Where Christians differ: lost letters and the canon. If an apostolic letter is lost, is the New Testament incomplete? Verdict: no. God in his providence preserved the books he intended for the permanent canon. Not every apostolic letter was meant to be Scripture for all time; or, if the letter from Laodicea is Ephesians, it was not lost at all. That a letter written by an apostle might not be preserved is not a gap in the Bible. It means God gave his church what he meant it to have. The canon is not everything the apostles ever wrote; it is what God caused to be kept. It is complete and sufficient for all things necessary for his glory and our salvation, faith and life (Westminster 1.2–3, 6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church created Scripture, or gave the books their authority by voting on them. The church recognised the Scriptures God had given, as a child recognises his father’s voice. The authority comes from God who breathed them out, not from the church that received them.

Should I worry that books were left out of the Bible? No. The books sometimes promoted as lost gospels were written long after the apostles, usually in the second century or later, and they teach things the apostles never taught. The early church did not suppress them out of fear; it recognised that they did not carry the apostolic voice. The books we have were received widely and early because they came from the apostles and their close companions and agreed with the faith once for all delivered. God, who inspired his word, has also preserved it. You can read your Bible as complete.

In a sentence. After this letter has been read to you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.

On a Tuesday. Read a letter of Paul aloud this week, all the way through in one sitting, as the Colossians first heard it. Colossians takes about fifteen minutes. Read it with your family or a friend if you can. You will hear the flow of the argument in a way that reading a few verses at a time can never give.

For worship. The God who spoke the world into being has not fallen silent. He spoke through prophets and apostles, and in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, and he has kept every word he meant us to have. Through fires and persecutions, copied by hand in candlelight and carried in saddlebags, his word has come down to us whole. The grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand for ever. Thanks be to God for his book, and for the Word to whom it testifies.
verseByVerse.note: The letter from Laodicea has not survived; some think it may be the letter we know as Ephesians.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”

And say to Archippus. We meet Archippus once more, in the letter to Philemon, where Paul calls him our fellow soldier and names him alongside Philemon and Apphia (Philemon 2). He was probably a member of that household, quite possibly their son, and seems to have had some ministry in the church, perhaps leading it while Epaphras was away. Something had stalled. Paul does not say what, and there is no rebuke in the words, but the charge would not be needed if all were well. Perhaps he was discouraged, or the false teaching had unsettled him, or the work had simply grown hard.

A public charge. Notice first that it is public. Paul does not write privately to Archippus; he tells the whole congregation to say it to him. There is wisdom in that. A church is meant to hold its members to what they have taken on. Encouragement is a duty of the whole church, not merely of the pastor, and a man who has gone quiet in his work is better served by a room full of people who expect something of him than by everyone politely looking away.

See that you fulfil the ministry that you have received in the Lord. Then the two words that carry the charge. The ministry is one he has received, a trust handed to him by Christ, not a career he chose. That changes its character entirely. You may resign from a job you selected, but a trust is somebody else’s property left in your hands. And he is to fulfil it (plēroō), literally to fill it full, to carry it through to the end. Not to begin it, not to maintain it respectably, but to finish (2 Timothy 4:5). And it was received in the Lord: given by Christ, and to be completed for him. The pattern is Christ’s own. On the night before he died he said to the Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). He too had received a work, and he carried it through to the cross. Every ministry in his church is a small trust handed down from that finished one.

The household on the road. There may be more here than we can see. Archippus belongs to Philemon’s household, and Philemon’s household is exactly where Onesimus is walking back to as this letter travels (v. 9). Whatever ministry had stalled, it had stalled in the one home in Colossae about to be tested hardest, the home that must decide how to receive a returning runaway. Paul does not join the two threads for us, and we should not force them.

The charge turns to face us. This is the only name in the entire roll call handed a charge of his own, and it swings the whole list round to face the reader. After nine people who carried letters, prayed, went to prison, came home, stayed and left, the one charge lands on an ordinary Christian whose ministry we cannot even identify. You have been given something too. See that you finish it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Archippus was in serious sin, or that he was being publicly shamed. The tone is that of encouragement to persevere. Nor does it mean only ordained ministers have a ministry to fulfil. Every member of the body has been given gifts and work by the Lord (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10).

How do I know what ministry I have received? Begin with what is already in your hands. Your ministry is rarely something exotic. It is usually the people God has placed around you and the gifts he has given you: the children you are raising, the Sunday school class, the elderly neighbour, the welcome team, the friend who is struggling, the work you were asked to do and said yes to. Ask mature believers where they have seen God use you. Notice what needs you see that others miss. And look at what you have started and let slide. That may be the very thing the Lord is asking you to finish.

In a sentence. Tell Archippus: see to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. What ministry have you received from the Lord? Write it down in a sentence. If you have let it stall, take one step this week to pick it up again. And if you know someone who has grown weary in their work for Christ, say to them, kindly, what the Colossians said to Archippus: you can finish this, and we are with you.

For worship. Paul called Archippus a fellow soldier (Philemon 2), and every soldier of Christ serves under a Captain who never left the field. He set his face like flint toward Jerusalem and did not turn back, and on the cross he cried, It is finished. No work he has taken up has ever been left half done, and that includes the work he is doing in his weary servants. He does not only command us to finish; he holds on to us until we do. Glory to the faithful Captain of our salvation, whose finished work is the strength of every unfinished one.
verseByVerse.note: Archippus was probably a member of Philemon’s household.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Paul dictated his letters to a secretary. It was Tertius who actually penned Romans, and he says so (Romans 16:22). At the close the apostle would take the pen himself. It served two purposes. It authenticated the letter, his handwriting being the seal of genuineness against forgeries (2 Thessalonians 3:17). And it was a piece of pure affection, his own hand reaching across hundreds of miles to a church that had never seen his face.

Remember my chains. Then, in that handwriting, three words. Roman custody often meant a wrist chained to a guard, so the hand that took the pen may well have been in iron. This is the letter that has told us Christ is the image of the invisible God, that in him all things hold together, that in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily. The man who wrote it was a prisoner while he wrote, and the last thing he does is ask them not to forget it.

Not self-pity, but an argument. It is not self-pity. It is partly a request for prayer (v. 3), and a call to solidarity, to remember those who are in prison as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3). But the chains are also an argument, and he knows it. Nobody wears irons for a lie. A church being offered a more sophisticated religion by teachers who risked nothing had been sent the gospel by a man paying for it in metal.

Grace be with you. The last word answers the first. The letter opened with grace to you and peace from God our Father (1:2), and it closes here, the shortest of all Paul’s closings. Everything between the two, the supremacy of Christ, the emptiness of the false teaching, the new life, the transformed household, the page of names, stands inside grace and is made of it. To a congregation being told they could climb nearer to God by rules, festivals, visions and severity to the body, the final word is the first word: not effort, not secret knowledge, but grace, the free gift of God in the Christ in whom they have already been filled. Some manuscripts add Amen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was seeking pity or attention. He was seeking prayer and solidarity, and reminding them what the gospel costs and what it is worth.

How do I remember the chains of Christians today? Paul’s request outlived him. Many believers today are imprisoned, beaten, or cut off from family and work for following Christ. Remember them first in prayer, by name and country where you can; organisations that serve the persecuted church publish specific requests. Write to prisoners where that is possible and safe. Give to support their families. Speak up for them to those in authority. And let their faithfulness shame our complaints and strengthen our courage. The same grace that held Paul in chains is holding them.

In a sentence. Paul writes this greeting in his own hand. Remember his chains. Grace be with you.

On a Tuesday. Remember the chains of persecuted believers today: find the name of one Christian in prison for his faith and pray for him by name this week. Then end your own day where Paul ended his letter. Whatever you did well or badly, whatever you finished or left undone, you go to sleep inside grace.

For worship. From grace, to grace, all the way home. The hands that wrote this greeting were chained for the sake of hands that were nailed. Christ was bound and led away, so that his people might be set free; he wore the chains of our sin so that grace might be with us for ever. Everything this letter has shown us, the Son who is before all things, the cross that disarmed the powers, the life hidden with Christ in God, the glory that is coming, comes to us as gift. Grace be with you: the last word of the letter is the first word of the gospel, and it will be the last word of history, when the Lord Jesus comes and every chain falls away.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed the greeting himself.

He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord.<sup>8</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,<sup>9</sup>and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.<sup>10</sup>Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him),<sup>11</sup>and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.<sup>12</sup>Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.<sup>13</sup>For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.<sup>14</sup>Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.<sup>15</sup>Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.<sup>16</sup>And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.<sup>17</sup>And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”<sup>18</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
